speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in recent meetings with dairy farmers from my riding of Northumberland, they have conveyed to me a desperation concerning their ability to survive the Government's new policies.
The recent freezing of industrial milk prices for the next 20 months, along with the budget cuts of $14 million a year from dairy spending, including the dropping of federal export subsidies and the cutting of funding for the Canadian Dairy Commission, all point to the fact that the Government is not interested in preserving the Canadian dairy industry.
Dairy farmers in my riding and across Canada want to know why they are being singled out for income freezes which will not allow their incomes to rise by as little as the rate of inflation.
I urge the Minister of Agriculture to reconsider his destructive policies which are contrary to the Government's own long-term dairy policy that included a complete commitment to supply management. The family farm dairy industry must be maintained.

Mr. Speaker, the Government of British Columbia has publicly threatened to withdraw from the national milk
marketing system. This has caused great concern to the province's 1,000 dairy producers, the majority of whom support the national milk marketing program.
One of the reasons for opting out is that the present distribution of the national market sharing quota or MSQ is completely unfair. British Columbia, with 12 per cent of Canada's population, has only 3.6 per cent of the national quota. Quebec, with 26 per cent of Canada's population, has 47 per cent, while Ontario and Quebec combined hold 78 per cent of the total national milk quota. This is a discriminatory allocation and must be rectified.
B.C. must stay within the national milk marketing system to protect the B.C. Dairymen's Association and to ensure the economic stability of the B.C. dairy industry. The only way to accomplish this is to adjust immediately the milk quota plan and give British Columbia its fair share.

subtopic: THE IMPORTANCE OF MAJOR JUNIOR HOCKEY
THE IMPORTANCE OF MAJOR JUNIOR HOCKEY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, If the Quebec Major Junior Hockey League is important to the central regions, it is also important to the remote regions. The Western Hockey League in Canada covers four provinces and a number of American states. The Ontario Hockey League covers a large territoiy.
However, in Quebec the situation is different. The Quebec Major Hockey League is based almost exclusively in the central regions, with the exception of Chicoutimi.
Abitibi and Temiscamingue contribute to the economy of Quebec's central regions. Our ore and wood chips are processed in Montreal and Trois-Rivieres.
Mr. Speaker, the Quebec Government should apply the principles of Canada-Quebec agreements on economic development to junior hockey and consider allow-

June 27, 1989
ing two divisions so that Quebec's resource regions would be represented as well.

Mr. Speaker, on July 7, 8, and 9 Brampton plays host to the biggest and best multicultural event in Canada.
For three days, visit the Ming dynasty court; relive the wild days of the Cossack brotherhood; shake hands with a real leprechaun, retrace the voyages of Prince Henry the navigator; dance the hula; meet the descendants of Canada's first settlers; celebrate Octoberfest early; star in a music hall variety show; view the exotic temple dances of India; do the Philippine bamboo pole dance of Tiniklang; hear the skirl of bagpipes and poetry of Robbie Burns; dance the mazurka in a Polish castle; travel with the Croatian people through 2,500 years of history; take a leisurely stroll from the Alps to the rugged terrain of Sicily; do the Zorba dance in an authentic Greek tavern; hear the old legends of the Caribbean Islands; visit the people of the desert in the Arabian pavilion which will take one back to biblical times. All this in just three days at Carabram in Brampton, Ontario.

Mr. Speaker, a Chinese citizen in Canada recently applied for refugee status and was rejected and taken to the Chinese Consulate to get his passport for the purpose of deportation to China.
If he was not a refugee before, the Canadian Government made him a refugee by reporting him to the consulate, since Canada told China that he had embarrassed the Government of China by trying to stay in Canada.
Already a Somali citizen, Abdi Aden, rejected by the refugee board and deported to Somalia, has been imprisoned because Somalia has the same sort of laws.
The Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mrs. McDougall) must take steps to avoid endangering more such innocent persons and to stop violating the United Nations law that forbids forcing a person to return to face persecution.
The Immigration Act has a remedy under the "self-exiled persons designated class", which authorizes the Government to protect citizens of the Soviet Union and five other Eastern European countries whose laws also provide punishment for embarrassing unauthorized departure or absence.
I call upon the Minister of Employment and Immigration to exercise her authority under the Immigration Act to save the liberty and life of Chinese and Somalians in Canada by adding China and Somalia to the countries on the self-exiled persons designated class list.

subsubtopic: REQUEST FOR REINSTATEMENT OF FUNDING TO CENTRE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Centre for Occupational Health and Safety, located in the great riding of Hamilton West, is under siege by the Tory Government.
For the last decade the centre has provided Canadians with comprehensive information on occupational health and safety matters. Last year alone, the centre provided Canadians with 350,000 copies of technical publications, had 1,200 Canadian firms communicate over 40,000 times with the centre's data base, and fielded over 100 hot line calls a day.
Obviously, the Conservative Government fails to understand that the centre needs government funding, because it has decided to eliminate the centre's $10 million grant by 1991.
The Hon. Member for Lincoln (Mrs. Martin) attempts to explain it all away by stating that the funding was "seed money for the difficult start-up period". A decade of support can hardly be labelled a start-up period.
Canadians cannot afford to lose such an important resource. I call upon the Government to reinstate funding for the centre immediately.
June 27, 1989

Mr. Speaker, all Canadians have been painfully reminded these last few weeks of the fact that many citizens of the world do not enjoy the same basic democratic privileges which we often take for granted. We have also been reminded of the fact that democratic privileges must sometimes be protected from those who would destroy them by force.
Therefore, it is important to pause for a moment on this the forty-fifth anniversary of the Normandy invasion by the Allied Forces to express a few sincere words of gratitude to those Canadians who in the past were willing to fight and to die, if necessary, to ensure the survival of democracy as we have known it.
Yesterday morning I had the opportunity to speak briefly to the delegates attending the thirty-fourth biennial convention of the Manitoba and North-West Ontario Command of the Royal Canadian Legion. On behalf of my constituents, I would now like to say a sincere thank you to the entire membership of the Royal Canadian Legion and indeed to all those veterans who fought in order that we could be free.
We will always be indebted to them.

subtopic: THE LATE HON. HOWARD CHARLES GREEN

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: THE LATE HON. HOWARD CHARLES GREEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today British Columbians and all Canadians mourn the loss of a dedicated politician and Canadian, Howard Charles Green.
Howard Green was bom in British Columbia five years before the turn of the century. After attending regular school in British Columbia and graduating from law school in Toronto, he served overseas with the fifty-fourth Kootenay Battalion during the First World War.
In 1935, at the age of 40, Mr. Green was elected to the House of Commons by the people of Vancouver South. He remained an active Member of Parliament until 1963, representing Vancouver Quadra for the last 14 years. First, as Minister of Public Works in the Cabinet of another great Canadian, John Diefenbaker, and then as
Secretary of State for External Affairs from June 1959 to April 1963, Howard Green took an active role in international discussions which greatly raised Canada's profile world-wide.
To the family of the late Hon. Howard Green, all in this Chamber extend our deepest sympathies.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
subtopic: THE LATE HON. HOWARD CHARLES GREEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to join with my colleague across the way in paying tribute to the Late Howard Green. He was a formidable Member of Parliament. He was the first Member for the then new riding of Quadra. He held that seat for a long period of time. He was our Member of Parliament when you and I, Mr. Speaker, grew up in Vancouver.
I remember him as one who kept in touch, particularly with young people at the university when we were attending the University of British Columbia. He was also a great Member of Parliament and a first-rate Secretary of State for External Affairs under the Late John George Diefenbaker. His quest for peace and for international comity was well known to the House and the country. He will be remembered with affection and with respect by everyone in Vancouver, British Columbia, and throughout the country.

subtopic: THE LATE HON. HOWARD CHARLES GREEN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am saddened by the news today of the loss of a very great Canadian, the Hon. Howard Charles Green.
Howard Green was a son of British Columbia and a great Canadian. He brought with him the spirit of the West, that fighting independence that he took with him into the Conservative Party and into the Diefenbaker Cabinet.
He fought for British Columbia as strongly as he fought for all of Canada. In his role as Secretary of State for External Affairs, Howard Green carved out the last important independent stand, pro-Canadian in international affairs. He had a pan-Canadian view of this country. He loved his Province of British Columbia. We will miss him and we will remember him.

subtopic: VOLUNTEER FIRE-FIGHTERS LIMIT OF TAX EXEMPTION
VOLUNTEER FIRE-FIGHTERS LIMIT OF TAX EXEMPTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there is no question in anyone's mind with respect to the splendid work done by volunteer fire-fighters, not only in my riding of Haldimand-Norfolk but all across Canada.
Volunteer fire-fighters served their municipalities with very little compensation. Generally, they are given honorariums to cover out-of-pocket expenses. I am confident that no one in this House would disagree with such remuneration. One would agree that their service is worthy of every penny.
The Government presently allows them a $500 tax exemption on honorariums that they receive. However, the inflationary costs incurred in the course of duty expenses often exceed the $500 tax exemption limit and volunteers are now being forced to pay income tax on these expenses.
These volunteers are donating their time and often risking their lives on behalf of others. Surely, we owe them more thanks than this.
Tax exemptions for volunteer fire-fighters in Canada should be mcreased to at least $1,000. This sum should be increased periodically to keep up with added costs and inflation.
This is the least Canada can do to recognize the great contribution these volunteers make to our country and offer some incentive for the civic minded individuals to continue this service to their communities and to Canada.

Mr. Speaker, within a few days we are expecting the business plan for VIA Rail as requested by the Government of Canada. I urge the Government of Canada, in considering its response to
June 27, 1989

this report, to seize the golden opportunity and the need for fiscal restraint present to us and therefore respond with a national transportation strategy design for the next century.
From a southern Ontario perspective, we have Canada's busiest airport in Toronto, the most congested highways in the nation, and the most heavily used rail and bus services in Canada.
Whatever the Government's options on VIA within the vital corridor from Windsor to Quebec City, I urge the Government to study them, not in isolation of rail service only, but within an integrated transportation strategy of rail, air, car and bus traffic.
While considering this strategy I implore the Government to develop it in consultation with the provinces and in a manner that is in harmony with sound environmental considerations for the future.

subsubtopic: IMPACT OF CUTS IN NOVA SCOTIA
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to be poor and unemployed in the City of Halifax is now going to be tougher than ever. Due to changes in cost sharing agreements the Halifax city Government has its back to the wall.
Cuts in social assistance are being forced that will create hardship not seen in our city since the terrible days of R. B. Bennett-$50 less per month in the shelter allowance alone. All this before the effects of the Government's ill-conceived, all-out attack on Atlantic Canadians through its pernicious Budget are truly felt.
The Nova Scotia Nutrition Council says that the children on social assistance do not receive proper nutrition in our province. They cannot because social assistance does not pay enough to provide it. The situation is now critical.
I call on the federal Government to reverse its search and destroy policy in the Atlantic region. Cuts to UI, to EPF, to ERDAs, closures of bases and fish plants will strain our municipalities beyond their endurance.
Tories, provincial and federal, must stop this wholesale slaughter of our social service safety net.

Mr. Speaker, my question is directed to the Minister of Finance. It is about his new national sales tax. You know the tax we are talking of, Mr. Speaker. It is that tax which the Minister says is so simple, so simple that for two years neither he nor his Department can come up with a booklet to explain it. That is the tax we are talking about.
Will the Minister confirm that he is slapping a new national sales tax of 9 per cent on reforestation equipment which is currently exempt from manufacturers' sales tax? At the same time will he confirm that he is slapping a new national sales tax of 9 per cent on pollution control equipment which is currently exempt, and on product safety testing equipment which is currently exempt, and on farmers' irrigation systems which are currently exempt?
Why does the Minister want to discourage anti-pollution equipment, reforestation, and safety equipment?

speechtext:

subtopic: REQUEST FOR LEGISLATION ON STANDARDS OF BEHAVIOUR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend has heard the Solicitor General advise that it would be completely inappropriate to comment in respect of any investigation that may or may not be ongoing. Mr. Speaker, we introduced a piece of legislation, which passed the House, dealing with lobbyists. I think most people acknowledged that it was a substantial step forward, a first for Parliament.
We introduced other legislation last year in respect of conflicts of interest, declarations by Members of the House of Commons and Members of the Senate in regard to their holdings and so on. Oral Questions THE CONSTITUTION

Mr. Speaker, the Prime Minister has said that a Constitution should bring Canadians together and should be accepted by all Canadians.
My question is to the Prime Minister. Since it is now clear that most Canadians outside central Canada reject the Meech Lake Accord and that public opinion will make it politically impossible for certain provinces to accept the Accord, will the Prime Minister now urge negotiation of a new Accord that will address the concerns of these provinces as well as the concerns of Quebec?

Mr. Speaker, I am surprised to hear the comment from my hon. friend. The Premiers of Canada met in Edmonton under the chairmanship of the Premier of Alberta, a province represented by my hon. friend. They said in 1986 that it was very important, given the incomplete nature of the work in 1982, that the Premiers request the federal Government engage in what was referred to as the "Quebec round" to bring Quebec back into Confederation.
That having been accomplished, it was their hope and that of the Leaders of every Party of this House, that we would then move on in a second round to deal with those matters of substance and concern to other Canadians. For example, the question of Senate reform is of great interest to the people of Alberta and western Canada. But clearly it was the considered view of all of the Premiers, particularly those from western Canada, as well as myself and the Leaders of the political Parties in this Chamber, that these other matters could not be dealt with properly until such time as the constitutional loop was closed.
Quebec was brought in on terms that were both reasonable and fair. That is what the Meech Lake Accord was all about. That is why it was endorsed by 10 premiers representing four different political parties from British Columbia to Newfoundland and Labrador. That is why it was endorsed very enthusiastically by the Leader of the Opposition, the Leader of the NDP and myself as Leader of the Progressive Conservative Party.
I want to tell my hon. friend that among other things, under the previous Constitution there was an inequality vis-a-vis the provinces where some provinces had vetoes and others did not. Alberta is now a first class province under the Meech Lake Accord and it was not before.

A supplementary question, Mr. Speaker. In my maiden speech a couple of months ago I said something about executive federalism. Yes, in fact the Premier of Alberta did endorse the Meech Lake Accord. The people of Alberta did not.
We in Alberta are also interested in seeing a meaningful Senate reform proposal from this Government, and we have not seen such to this date. We are looking forward to seeing that.
The Prime Minister will be aware that a recent poll in the Montreal Gazette shows that even in Quebec, only 44 per cent of the people actually support the Meech Lake Accord. Since these are hardly the kinds of numbers necessary to provoke a national unity crisis, why does the Prime Minister not urge the Government of Quebec to also show some flexibility instead of just twisting the arms of the smaller and politically weaker provinces?

Mr. Speaker, my hon. friend says that while the Premier of Alberta endorsed the Meech Lake Accord, the people of Alberta did not. On November 21 last, there was a general election and the Progressive Conservative Government which stood for a strong support of the Meech Lake Accord won 25 out of 26 seats in Alberta. That is a major endorsement.
Hear, hear!

Now my hon. friend refers to a very fundamental question of Senate reform which all of us I think desire to bring about in Canadian federalism. Senate reform can only be achieved if Quebec is brought back into the Constitution. It cannot be done without that condition precedent.
The Premier of Alberta understood that, the Leader of the Opposition understood it, the Leader of the NDP understood it. I think my hon. friend understands full well that if Alberta desires Senate reform, which it does, and if Senate reform would be beneficial to Canadian federalism, which it indeed would, then first and foremost we must find terms on which Quebec can honourably rejoin the Canadian constitutional family. We have
June 27, 1989

found them in Meech Lake, and I urge my hon. friend to strongly defend Meech Lake and endorse it across western Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour of tabling, in both official languages, the Third Report of the Standing Joint Committee on Scrutiny of Regulations.

The report concerns the formal documents regulations made under Section 4 of the Seals Act. These regulations specify the classes of public documents which must be passed under the Royal Seals. It is the view of the Joint Committee that the current regulations are invalid in that they were not approved by Her Majesty the Queen as required by Section 4 of the Seals Act.

The predecessor of the present Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs disagreed with the Committee's views but nevertheless agreed to table a Bill to amend the Seals Act in order to remove the requirement which provides that the regulations must be approved by the Sovereign.

As noted in the Third Report, "It will be for Parliament to decide whether to amend the Act in this fashion". The only recommendation of the Joint Committee is that any proposed legislation retroactively validate the existing regulations for greater certainty. I invite Hon. Members who wish a more complete explanation of the issues involved to read the Third Report of the Joint Committee.

Canada Film Year was established to bring Canadians into contact with Canadian films and stars, and to heighten the image Canadians have of Canadian films. From the outset, it was agreed that such a project must be mounted and maintained by the industry itself, and not be government-led. The role of government was to be limited to a supporting one. speakeroldname: Hon. John C. Crosbie (Minister for International Trade):
subsubtopic: INTERNATIONAL BIDDING ON GOVERNMENT SUPPLY CONTRACTS
speechtext:
International Bidding on Government Supply Contracts
1.	Contracts for purchases of goods by Canadian Government departments and agencies which are covered by the GATT Agreement on Government Procurement (usually referred to as the "Code") are open to competition among signatories of the Code where the value of the contract is $213,000 or more. The threshold for coverage is the result of agreement among the Code signatories and may only be adjusted by renegotiation pursuant to Article IX.6.
2.	Contracts for purchases of goods by the same departments and agencies covered by the GATT Code are also covered by the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement (FTA). The FTA threshold is $31,000. Contracts for eligible goods worth more than this amount and less than $213,000 are covered by the FTA. There is no provision in the FTA specifically requiring renegotiation of the threshold. Further bilateral negotiations on the FTA procurement provisions in general are, however, called for in Article 1307, but these will not take place until the completion of the current GATT round of multilateral trade negotiations.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to Motions P-6, P-7 and P-8, the motions proposed by the Hon. Member are unacceptable for the following reasons: First, the three motions made by the Hon. Member relate primarily to the security of Canada which is the responsibility of the Solicitor General whose reply on the Herbert Norman case is provided in response to Question Nos *69, *70, *71 and *72 answered this day.
Second, the Government's position on the Norman case was provided in response to a question during proceedings on adjournment motion on May 28, 1987.
Third, as indicated by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) on the matter on April 10, 1987, Herbert Norman was employed by the Department of External Affairs and all information that is permitted under the privacy and freedom of information legislation has been made available. Fourth, External Affairs departmental officials have in the past month re-examined the material reviewed under Access to Information requests received to date. There is no evidence to indicate that Herbert Norman was an intelligence agent of the Soviet Union or any other foreign power.
Fifth, in addition, departmental officials have been instructed to re-affirm that all of the department's documents on Herbert Norman have in fact been collected and reviewed, in other words, to re-affirm that relevant material is not lying unfound on some file in the Archives.
Sixth and finally, this re-examination of the Department's files will be for the entire period of Norman's service with the Department. It is a major undertaking in terms of resources and will take some time. It is hoped that this effort will ensure that history is provided with all possible documents related to Norman's services with the Department.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have a few brief words on second reading. I would like to respond to some of the questions that have been given to us by Members of the New Democratic Party.
First, people will be aware that some very serious problems have been suffered by the grain business in the last three years. Problems in the first two years were as a result of some pretty drastic falls in grain prices internationally and the Government was in a position to respond with payments based on price. In the 1988 growing season, we suffered some pretty severe weather problems. If you look at the records, the weather during 1988 for parts of the Prairies was as bad or worse than some of the worst years during the 1930s. As a result, there was a very poor crop. If you look at where there were some crops in the Prairies such as the northern part of the Prairies and parts of Ontario and Quebec, they had, in some cases, average crops. So when you see the

June 27, 1989
Supply
fall in production, you can realize that there were people that had very little if any crop.
The Government responded by putting in place a drought program based on two criteria: that the money be targeted and directed at the areas that had suffered the most. As I said, there were areas in the Prairies that actually had an average or even a little above average crop.
Second, that it be crop specific, and we did that. The result is what we see here today. I should also point out that this is the third part of the Government's response to the drought situation of 1988. We responded with a water program to assist the livestock producers in the spring of 1988. Second, we responded almost a year ago with a program to assist and encourage producers to produce feed for livestock. Third, we responded with the this drought program that we are here putting the appropriations through for today.
All along we maintained consultations with the producers themselves. We also maintained good consultations with the provinces. We believe very strongly that this type of program, as it has been in the past, needs to be a cost-sharing program. We have worked with the provinces in both developing the program through their crop insurance corporations and we are presently working with them to work out a satisfactory arrangement as far as the cost-sharing is concerned.
We need to mention the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). He has been very good to Canadian agriculture in some very difficult times. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) is here, and the Treasury Board has been very good in terms of arranging for cashflow. We are not able to respond to these types of situations as a Government without the co-operation of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the President of the Treasury Board. We want to say publicly that we appreciate the kind of support that we have had. I
I have some questions that have been given to me by some of the Members opposite. I believe it is appropriate at this time if I refer to them. The Hon. Member for Prince Albert-Churchill River (Mr. Funk) I notice is in the House. He is concerned that the rules require that an appeal may only be launched by a rural municipality or township on behalf of all landholders within the
township. He wants to know why we cannot do this on an individual basis.
There are two reasons for that. First, the recommendation that we receive from producers or producer organizations such as the Western Wheat Growers, the Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, the Ontario Corn-Growers Association, plus the provincial Governments all recommended that we do not run the program on an individual basis, that we run it on an average area basis. The reason for this is quite simple. There is no question that weather was the major problem, but within any region you are going to get variations in the yield based on the amount of fertilizer and the amount of chemical an individual farmer would use. If we went with individual coverage or individual targeting, then you are not giving anyone any credit for the type of management practices that they use themselves. Whereas if you go with an average for an area, you at least take some of those considerations partly into consequence.
Second, while it would be possible to do it on an individual basis, the Member is absolutely correct, administratively it would make it much more cumbersome and it would see the program delayed. Therefore for those two reasons, it was the recommendation of the individual farm groups and the farmers themselves that we use an average area for the reasons outlined, and second, if you look at the administration of it, then you can see that with the number of producers involved that it would lead to some pretty lengthy appeal processes.
I should say something about the appeal process. We are calling them review committees. We have them set up in each of the four provinces. Quebec is being handled a little differently. Of the five provinces, Quebec's money is being channelled through their Crop Insurance Corporation. But there are review committees set up now in the three western provinces and in Ontario to look at the data to see how it looks and how the individual review committees relate the data that we have collected from the Crop Insurance Corporation. Therefore that essentially is the reason. We did consider it and found, for practical reasons, that it would be difficult.
Second, looking at the principles behind it, decided that it would be better to go on an area basis. I should say the area now is a township, not a municipality. So it is a relatively small area. We feel very strongly that once the
June 27, 1989

overall data is in that most of the producers' concerns over the initial maps will be addressed in the final data.
The second question I have is from the Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Althouse) who is concerned, to read at least part of the question, that, "Saskatchewan is the largest recipient of drought aid with more than one-half of the moneys going to the province. Saskatchewan has crop insurance data showing average long-term yield for each quarter section. Why did the Government not take advantage of this existing data to speed the delivery of the drought program?" He goes on to say, "The New Democrats propose such a solution whereby crop insurance holders would have received their extra payment immediately leaving only uninsured producers to apply for assistance. Why that?"
I believe I answered the first part of that question in reply to the Hon. Member for Prince Albert-Churchill River. While it would have been possible, that was not the recommendation of the farmers and the provincial Governments for practical reasons.
As far as the second part of the question, it is a judgment call. It probably would have been easier to make payments to just the people who had crop insurance, but effectively you would be penalizing people who did not have crop insurance. You will find that the person who had crop insurance would get the drought payment; whereas the person who did not have crop insurance would not be eligible for either of them until later on.
Therefore we decided on that basis that we would try to treat everybody the same and make all the payments at the same time.
And let everybody wait.

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
The Hon. Member says that you make everybody wait. That may in fact be true, but if you are going to start splitting up the payments, some people get them sooner and some people get them later on. You will find that the overall process is delayed. When you see what is happening-I think I am relatively accurate in these numbers-only about 30 per cent of producers in Ontario are covered by crop insurance. Whereas if you go to Saskatchewan it is 70 per cent.
Supply
Therefore you are going to find some very big discrepancies across the country on the number of producers that would have received payment. So we decided that this program, while it is based on crop insurance numbers and data that we received from crop insurance, that we would use that data to develop the program so that everybody got treated the same in terms of when the payment was made and in terms of the amount of money that was paid.
The third question I have is from the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Laporte). "The announcement on November 10 was based on a $45 an acre payment being received in the case of wheat. Will that still be a realistic expectation for grain producers? How many farmers will be receiving the maximum amount?" How many farmers will be receiving the maximum amount? At the time we announced that the program that for producers-and this was a prairie number the Ontario number may be different than that-for those on the Prairies in a high yield area such as south of Winnipeg, the Red River Valley or in the Regina Plains or Rosetown, Kindersley that consistently have yeilds and high crop insurance coverage with a total loss of crop will have a payment in the area of $40 to $45 a tonne. That was an estimate, and that estimate still stands.
In response to how many farmers would be receiving the maximum amount, we will not know that until we have everybody's applications and are able to add up to see how many people have that maximum amount, whatever it is. But the estimate still stand, but it stands for people who have been in the highest yielding areas which have received little or no moisture have experienced high temperatures and therefore basically suffered a total loss of crop.
The fourth question I have is again from the Hon. Member from Prince Albert-Churchill River (Mr. Funk). The Special Canadian Grains Program's computer system produced an overpayment situation for many producers. Will this overpayment be deducted from the drought cheques and what about overpayments from the Western Grain Stabilization Program?
The answer to the first question is yes, we will be deducting any overpayments made under the Special Canadian Grains Program. From this program we will not be deducting from Grain Stabilization. I forget the number precisely but when you look at the amount of money that has been repaid under the Special Canadian Grains, I think we are down now to about two-tenths of 1 per cent of the number of producers who are still in an

June 27, 1989
Supply
overpayment position. It is a very small number, but that amount on the Special Grains will be deducted.
In terms of Western Grain Stabilization, we do not have the ability to cross-reference. It would be a very difficult job to do in terms of deducting an overpayment. The decision was made not to do it.
While there was an overpayment made as a result of the 1987-88 Western Grain Stabilization Act payment, it amounts I think to less than a quarter of 1 per cent of all of the money the program has paid out in the last four years. Of the amount of money that was overpaid, over half has been sent back by farmers and 52 per cent of the money has been received and 58 per cent of the farmers have returned their money. So it is over half in both cases. We are deducting the overpayment under Special Canadian Grains. We are not deducting the overpayment under Western Grain Stabilization.
The fifth question from the Hon. Member for Moose Jaw-Lake Centre (Mr. Laporte) is what federal-provincial arrangements have been made to fund future drought disaster programs? For example, we know that Quebec will be applying its drought money to crop insurance to lower producers' premiums. What arrangements are being made with each of the other provinces? The Member is correct, Quebec is using its share of the drought assistance to reduce the premiums in its crop insurance over the next three years. That is the choice the Quebec Government made. It was supported by UPA and that is how the matter is being handled in Quebec.
Second, we are working with the provinces as far as improving crop insurance, to come up with a better crop insurance program. The Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) has indicated that he is prepared to open the Act to amend crop insurance so that we have more options. Producers ask us if we would like to go from, for instance, 80 per cent to 90 per cent coverage. We respond that there is going to be a considerable increase in premium. The producers say "fine, give us the option". We cannot do that unless we open the Act. We
are going through consultations with the provinces now and for almost a year we have had discussions on the over-all safety net system in this country as far as grain is concerned. We have had quite good discussions with the industry and the provinces and that process is under way. While we do not have anything specific, these kinds of things take time. We are in the process as far as making crop insurance more responsive. Hopefully if we get into a situation like this again we will be in a better position to use crop insurance as a vehicle with more producers involved.
It is pretty tough in a province like Ontario to use crop insurance as a drought delivery program when-I think I am right-certainly less than half of the producers in the province take out crop insurance. If we can get a better crop insurance program with more producers enrolled we will be in a better position to use crop insurance in the future. I think that is the aim of of provincial Governments, producers and the federal Government to have these programs more predictable.
Farmers tell us, I think it is a good observation, that given the same amount of money, if we know about it ahead of time, can plan a budget that same amount of money will be more useful in our budgeting process than the same amount of money on an ad hoc basis without knowing far enough ahead exactly what it is. That is the direction in which we want to go and I believe everybody agrees with that.
The next question I have is from the Hon. Member for Mackenzie (Mr. Althouse). Will the Minister assure farmers that there will be no requirement for part of the drought payment to be used to finance insurance for future years as was the case with livestock. I am not so sure that the premise of the question is correct, Mr. Speaker. There was a requirement that if you are to be eligible for the second half of the livestock feed part of the drought assistance you have to join crop insurance. That was just for one year. I understand what the Member is saying. There was a requirement under the livestock assistance side, the feed security side, of the
June 27, 1989

drought program for producers to enrol. But there is no such requirement on the grains side of this drought payment. There is nothing there.
As far as asking people to sign up for one year, it does not obligate producers to do anything more than join for the present year which is the 1989 growing season or the 1989-90 crop year.
The last question I have is from the Hon. Member for Saskatoon-Humboldt (Mr. Hovdebo). Provincial agriculture Ministers say that they were not consulted prior to the announcement of the drought program. They have since stated clearly that they believe this was a federal program. Why did the Government place this expenditure before the House as two separate estimates when one would have sufficed? Actually the Member has two questions.
First, this has been an ongoing program with the provinces. We wrote to the provinces in the early part of October indicating that we expected the drought program we were developing to be cost-shared. We expected to have co-operation from the provinces in developing it. We have had good co-operation and we are still working with the provinces in terms of cost-sharing. I believe we will be able to reach an agreement that is fair for all of us.
We said again on November 10 when we announced the program-just with regard to that-that "consultations are under way with the provinces regarding program design and cost-sharing". We have said right from the beginning that this is the third stage of the over-all response by the Government to this situation.
I mention the water program, the feed assistance program and drought assistance program as far as grain is concerned. We have said from the beginning and say again that this is a cost-shared program. We believe we will reach an agreement with the provinces to share those costs.
Why did the Government place this expenditure before the House as two separate estimates when one would have sufficed? It is a choice by people at Treasury Board that this was the proper way to proceed. The original estimate of money was there in order that we could cash flow the amount of money we estimated under the initial payment. It comes to a little more than $850 million if you do the arithmetic. There is some money in there for two-price wheat and a couple of other programs. This is the way the Government cash manages. It in no way changes anything from the
Supply
announcement we made back on November 10 or anything we have said heretofore as far as this program is concerned. This Bill does not in any way indicate that the federal Government does not expect the provinces to contribute. It simply means that the federal Government is putting the money in place so that the program can pay the full amount of money. We expect cheques to begin going in the mail at the end of July so the full amount of money can flow depending on whatever financial arrangements we can make with the provinces on how they will participate.
That responds to the questions, Mr. Speaker. I will just leave a little bit more information in terms of estimates. We estimate that somewhere between $20 million and $30 million will be going to the Province of Quebec; $171 million to the Province of Manitoba; $417 million to the Province of Saskatchewan; about $150 million to the Province of Ontario and about $80 million to Alberta. That total will come, I think, fairly close to $850 million.
The initial payment which we made, we estimated that it would have been $260 million to $280 million, or even up to $300 million. We got out $218 million, for a couple of reasons. The people who applied had smaller acreages than we originally anticipated. For some reason, we still estimate that there are about 4,000 producers out there who would have been eligible had they sent in their application forms. There were less people who applied than we would have thought, based on our maps and based on the amount of applications which were sent out as a result of the phone calls and the requests for applications. There was more money available to be sent out, if producers had sent in their applications forms.
The process is well under way. We have had good co-operation with the municipalities and the district agricultural offices, the AGREP offices. We will be using them in terms of how the review process is going to work. I believe very strongly that when this program is all over, it is going to be seen to have been a very good program. We will have been able to accomplish the two objectives which we have stated, and that is to target the amount of assistance directly at producers who suffered the biggest loss.
Second, we will be doing it on the basis of being crop-specific so that we do not pay a person the same for a bushel or for an acre of oats as we do for an acre of com in Ontario, or for an acre of canola, as we do for an acre of some of the horticultural crops in Ontario.

June 27, 1989
Supply
I am pleased to be here this afternoon putting this appropriations Bill through so that the money is there in order that we can meet the timeframe and the targets which we set out in this program so that producers will be in a position to receive their share of this program when the cheques start to go in the mail at the end of July.

Mr. Speaker, I am relieved to be on my feet today speaking on this Bill and speaking in support of it. The rural community across Canada was very, very disappointed, needless to say, when the Estimates were tabled in the House of Commons a couple of months ago. We were relieved that this money will be finally coming out to them. Even though it willbe the end of July, we are sure it will be much appreciated.
I had the opportunity to be in Saskatoon yesterday and I was looking at the crops and was very much relieved that they appear in very good shape. They have had adequate rainfall this year. I was talking to many people from across the three Prairie provinces and they are very optimistic as far as their crop prospects are concerned.
In terms of Ontario, we too have excellent crop prospects this year, unlike last year when we suffered very severe drought. We will have an excellent crop of wheat, hay, corn, soya beans.
I want to draw this point to the Minister's attention, that in Kent and Essex Counties, which are not in my constituency, they have had so much rain that they have not been able to get their crops planted this year.
I hope that the Minister will remember the precedent that the previous administration set back in 1984 when a similar situation prevailed in northeastern Saskatchewan. We actually had a drought across the southern part of the Prairie provinces. Yet, northeastern Saskatchewan had a severe weather problem and excess rain. They were not able to get their crops planted. Because of that fact alone, they could not plant their crops, and they did not qualify for crop insurance. I
I hope that the Minister will keep an open mind on the situation in southwestern Ontario for these people who have not been able to plant their crops and consequently do not qualify for crop insurance. If they need help later
in the summer, will the Government consider this and give them whatever help they can.
I want to also point out that I appreciated my colleagues here in the House of Commons on this side of the House keeping us abreast of what is happening in terms of the areas that are missed. We all know that rain does not start or stop at a township line or a county line, but it goes across one boundary into the next.
I want to thank my colleagues here for keeping us abreast of what is happening in the various areas, as well as the producers themselves. In my particular constituency of Lambton-Middlesex, we had a tremendous response when I asked them if they would more closely identify those areas that are left out and did not show up on the original maps.
Part of the reason for this is perhaps that if a couple of concessions in a township had adequate rainfall, and in some cases they did, and had reasonably good crops, and the rest of the township was severely affected by the drought, the average of the total township would not bean adequate indication of some of the hardships being faced by those farmers.
There were several who assisted us in this, members of the Federation of Agriculture, both in Lambton and Middlesex counties and people in the Soya Bean Growers Marketing Board. They went up and down the concessions and took statements from all of the farmers to identify those areas that were most severely affected and that were not included in the maps.
I refer here in particular to Metcalfe township, Mosa township and part of Ekford. Also, in the northern end of the Middlesex County, we had part of Adelaide and West Williams.
Going across into Lambton, as strange as it may seem, we had a terrific rain there on July 16 last year. We had between nine inches and ten inches in a matter of couple of hours. That was even more devastating than the drought because it came in such a hurry and created flash floods that packed the ground to the extent that the crops never did recover, because it turned very, very dry for the rest of the summer. I have to pay a special tribute to Ron Huctwith and the people in the central and Warwicktownship for gathering together the information on this particular instance, who were able to make a
June 27, 1989

submission to the Associate Deputy Minister who is in charge of this program.
Then of course, over in the boundary line between Sarnia-Lambton and Lambton-Middlesex and the boundary line of MooreTownship and Enniskillen Township, my colleague for Sarnia-Lambton (Mr. James) and I both put forward information as to the area that was missed in that particular area adjacent to Sombra Township that qualified for both com and soya beans. Yet, right across the town lines they were left out because of the process which was used.
I hope that these areas will be looked at, whether it is by the review committee or by the Minister when the time comes, to make sure that those farmers were not disqualified from this program.
I am also pleased that the assistance is going out to something like 130,000 producers across Canada. Assistance is going out at a time when they have a lot of crop input costs to pay for. It will be prior to the harvest of western Canada but during the wheat harvest in southwestern Ontario.
I hope that from the lessons learned in the administration of this one that we will be able to cope with such an emergency better in the future. I realize that there is a tremendous backlog of people who did not get application forms, and they are very worried, but I have to give credit to the Associate Deputy Minister for trying to put together a program which will meet the needs of those most severely affected.
I do not want to hold up the passage of this Bill. We on this side certainly support it. We want to get this money out in the hands of the farmers as quickly as possible. With those few comments, we will certainly be supporting the Bill on this side of the House.

Mr. Speaker, I rise to speak on this Bill to provide approximately $850 million for the drought assistance program. You will remember, Mr. Speaker, that it was during the election that this program was announced. There was a whole summer when we sat looking at the prospect of drought. My colleagues and I spent the summer preparing a drought program which we introduced in early September or late August, whereby we proposed a method of payment and the kind of program which could be used to provide some
Supply
relief for farmers right across the country who were suffering from the drought.
As farmers in Saskatchewan certainly recall, though the program was not as well discussed in the other provinces, the program would have cost something in the neighbourhood of $1.4 billion. In provinces where average crop insurance coverage is 70 per cent, as in the case of Saskatchewan, there would have been a top-up of an additional 30 per cent under this program, and that 30 per cent of average yield would have been provided whether the farmer had crop insurance or not. Those who had crop insurance, because they would have already been inspected and received cheques, would simply have the crop insurance agency in the province issue the additional 30 per cent and their cases would have been completed.
We recognized that that program would have paid crop insurance holders more rapidly than those who had not taken the precaution of having crop insurance, but we justified that by saying that it was in the best interests of all farmers in Canada to participate in crop insurance and we should not provide the kind of program that would discourage people from participating in crop insurance. Paying early, as soon as possible after the crop insurance inspection was completed, we submitted, would have encouraged participation in crop insurance programs.
At the moment, in Saskatchewan somewhere between 70 and 75 per cent participate in crop insurance. Saskatchewan was also the province that had suffered the most damage. Over half of the money in the program would have gone to Saskatchewan so half or little better than half of the administrative problems would have been solved by adopting that program. It would have paid out on a fairer and more equitable basis. In the event that most of a township save a few sections in one comer got rain, that producer in the comer that did not get rain would not be left without coverage, though the program the Government eventually proposed did leave him without coverage.
The election campaign proceeded. After it had been going on for about five or six weeks, I suspect the Government conducted a poll and found it was having some difficulty with its lack of a policy for drought relief. On November 10, about two weeks before the election date, the Government came out with an announcement of approximately $850 million for the program we are debating today. Government Members attempted to sell the program by saying that it was a Government program that had been well thought out, there had been consultations and that the Government had been working on this

June 27, 1989
Supply
well thought out move for many years. Many farmers thought that they were finally seeing results from the promises made by the then Minister of Agriculture who said in December 1985 that a disaster program was being planned by his Department so that farmers would not have go through the uncertainty they went through in the previous year of drought.
As the program unfolded, it became very obvious that the Government had not taken precautions and that the bureaucracy was not ready to handle the program as announced. At that time, there was absolutely no data on township average yields or township actual yields on which the program was to be based. The bureaucracy had to commence from scratch to put together a program.
To make the situation worse, expectations were built up very high by government Members who, during the election campaign, said that this was a firm commitment on the part of the Government and that the program could be implemented very quickly. Post-election, the new Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski) indicated that cheques would be in the mail. At one point he said that they would be in the mail before Christmas and then he changed that by saying that the applications would be in the mail before Christmas. In fact, we all know that most producers did not receive their applications until well into March. This reinforces my contention that the Government did not do any planning for this program and was not prepared for it. It pulled it out of thin air on the basis of a poll which showed that it would lose certain rural seats on the prairies unless it came up with some sort of a drought program.
That is now water under the bridge. The Government has indicated that it has not managed the program well and that it is incapable of managing such a program. It has not answered questions about the delays in the program to any satisfaction. The civil servants who have been given the task of carrying out the program are now defending themselves by saying that the cheques will be in the mail about the same time as the Special Grains Program payment cheques were in the mail last year, and that therefore the program can be deemed to be a success. We will see. That was not the promise made by the Minister of Agriculture and members of the Government during the election campaign and after the election. They were leaving the impression that payments would be made very quickly.
Government Members also left the clear impression that there was full co-operation with the provinces. That impression began to fall apart very quickly. As recently as March, the Premier of the Province of Saskatchewan who is also the Minister of Agriculture told the legislature in Regina that this was a federal program and the provinces had made no commitment to participate. The question had arisen, of course, because the estimates had been tabled with only half of the money listed in the first draft. Gradually the Government began to admit tacitly that there had been no result from discussions with the provinces that would yield any money, so it introduced as Supplementary Estimates the balance of the funds. Now we have returned to the House for approval from the Agriculture Committee for this amount of money which, in the words of the Minister, is to cover the special drought payments as well as something for two-price wheat and some other programs on which he did not elaborate but about which we expect we will find out more when we go into Committee of the Whole.
In the interests of getting this legislation through the House, even though it provides much less than we thought was necessary to deal with the problem adequately, I suggest that the House now go to Committee of the Whole.

Mr. Speaker, I rise today to support this Bill, but I have a few comments I would like to make. Having said that I support the Bill, I would also like to say that I am somewhat critical of the Bill and the way it was handled by the Government.
I understand that the intent of the Government is to fine tune this Bill so that it applies to townships rather than to counties or districts. The Government should have faced the reality of the situation and realized how difficult this type of fine tuning was to handle. If it had been handled in the manner in which similar types of assistance programs were handled in the past, farmers would have received their money by now and could have been using it. The money that will go to the producers because of the poor crops last year is money needed by those producers to assist in their cash flow for this year and the purchase of seed. Unfortunately, even with the
June 27, 1989

best efforts of Agriculture Canada and the Minister's office, they are not going to receive that money as quickly as all of us would have liked.
As mentioned by other Hon. Members, the fine tuning of this Bill has caused a discrepancy between farmers on opposite sides of the same concession roads that happen to be in a different township. The crop insurance figures from townships that are being used basically to calculate who gets what are showing discrepancies.
When bringing this Bill into the House today to grant extra funds, the Minister made the comment that this was an ongoing program. However, he must realize that that is not the accepted explanation in that this announcement, as he said, was interestingly made 11 days before the election last fall. The announcement was that the program would be cost shared on a 50-50 basis with the provinces. More than one province has denied that that consultation process took place. I feel that that should have taken place, and some of those other problems would not have happened.
The Minister also made the comment that there are approximately 4,000 producers who would be eligible if they had sent in an application. The Minister may recall some questions that we asked in the House, and also to some of the members of the ministry and the staff. In Ontario in particular, many, many producers did not receive their form until the deadline was past. I put out two press releases in my riding encouraging producers to make sure they put their application in, and that the Minister has stated that he will honour those. I respect and appreciate that fact. However, there were producers who received the application, looked at the date on the application which they sometimes received weeks after the deadline, did not notice the press release, and there was nothing on the application stating that even though the application was received late, it should be still sent in, and now another deadline has past.
Supply
We worked hard to advise the producers. That money is needed by the farmers, it is owed to the farmers, and they deserve it. We worked hard, but there were producers who decided that it is too late and there is no use sending in the application, so I lost on that one.
I support the Bill. I am sure in hindsight that the Minister and his staff will look at how this was handled. The phone lines were busy and it was difficult. However, I will not hold up the debate in discussion any longer in order that we can pass this Bill and the farmers can receive their money.

Most of those people have not been able to get their crops in. I wonder if any of these moneys, or if other moneys are available, to help those farmers out of this tough situation. The Minister may be aware that many of those same farmers suffered a drought last year. This year they

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
The Hon. Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) raised that issue when he spoke. I certainly take the observation. However, this program is designed for drought assistance. There is no provision in this Bill to assist producers who may now be facing some equally serious problems as far as flooding is concerned.
I stand to be corrected, but I believe that for producers who have decided to take out crop insurance there is a provision in the crop insurance for them to be compensated if they are unable to seed for flooding reasons, or for whatever other reasons. There is some compensation available for producers. I know that that is the case on the prairies. I assume that the same applies in Ontario for producers in the riding of the Hon. Member. There should be compensation if they have in fact taken out crop insurance for the present year.

I have had discussions with the Minister in the past. There are drought relief committees to be appointed. I believe the Province of Ontario has six, and three that have already been appointed by the federal Government have been in southwestern Ontario. I have had discussions, and I have great concern that no one has been appointed from eastern Ontario, and to the best of my knowledge, there have been no appointees to the other three committees. Horticulture is a major sector of agriculture in Ontario and it is not represented.
What action has been taken on that to date?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext:
The Hon. Member has raised this question, and the two of us have had private discussions. The Hon. Member makes a very good point. Review committees were designed to assist the over-all administration of the program to serve the producers. There are four in Alberta, four in Manitoba, six in Saskatchewan, and six in Ontario. The six in Ontario are made up by three from the federal Government and three from the provincial Government.
We have been rather disappointed that the province has not seen fit to appoint those three. We are going to have to deal with that issue. The Hon. Member is absolutely correct that we need better geographical representation.
The Hon. Member also makes a very good point in terms of horticultural crops. I understand from his own personal background that he has had a very good career as a farmer growing many kinds of special crops, and if anyone is qualified to make those comments, he probably is, as far as the House is concerned. We take his point, and we will do our very best to address it as quickly as we can.

I wonder if the Minister could outline for us the amounts of additional funding he has in here. For example, he mentioned compensation for the two-price wheat system, and a couple of other items. Could he elaborate on those, and give us some figures?

speakerposition: Minister of Western Economic Diversification; Minister of State (Grains and Oilseeds)
speechtext: There is a whole host of programs that do not add up to nearly the amount of money for the drought program. I mentioned two-price wheat. The Canada Grain Commission has a certain amount of funding in here. Stop-off charges for millers are here. The International Grains Institute is here. Fees for membership for International Wheat Council contributions to the Canada Grains Council-the grain related funding that the federal Government is involved in-is here. For instance, we cost-share with the Canadian International Grains Institute, the Canada Grains Council and other kinds of things, depending on the organization. I believe some funding for POS in Saskatoon is in here as well. Those are the types of things I was referring to.

Mr. Chairman, I have a few questions to ask of the Minister.
Before I proceed, however, I would like to pay tribute to my colleague, the Hon. Member for Mackenzie, for the work that he has done on this issue. If it had not been an election period and the Government needed to have a separate program from what the NDP was proposing, it might well have been the Hon. Member's proposal that would have been accepted. I think a lot of difficulties would have been resolved if it had been.
I am still concerned about the business of individual producers versus townships. The Minister suggested that management factors played a big part in this. My own experience in my constituency is that in the parkland areas the rain was very spotty. One of the Minister's officials in committee the other day acknowledged that fact. His family farms 12 miles from where I farm. The rainfall was very spotty. Often, most of a township was in
June 27, 1989

relatively good shape but for people on the other side of a forested area or on the other side of a valley it could have been very bad.
I still do not see any mechanism included in this proposal whereby those kinds of real inequities are addressed. The Minister's officials said that fairness, equality and equity were still the objectives of the program. Those individuals caught in this type of situation could be totally wiped out if there is not some mechanism whereby the farmer who has virtually total crop loss falls into a township where the average is relatively good. I am not happy at all. I would hate to see this Bill go through without some assurance that if it is demonstrated after looking at the data that there are cases like this that there might not be some mechanism to address it.
In digging around on this program I noticed that the Minister when talking about the maximum total available per acre still quoted the figure of $40 to $45.1 noted that with interest since it has been told to me that there is still a 10 per cent leeway at the top end of the payments here and that if the totals, once they are run through the computer, exceed $850 million, in fact that will revert to a lower level. Can the Minister confirm that this might still be true?

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, June 26, consideration of the motion of Mr. Epp that Bill C-19, an Act to amend the Canadian Exploration and Development Incentive Program Act, be read the third time and passed.

subtopic: CANADIAN EXPLORATION AND DEVELOPMENT INCENTIVE PROGRAM ACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as I warned Hon. Members last Friday, they could have either supported the hoist motion advanced by the Hon. Member, the critic for the official Opposition, or failing that, they could hear me yammer on for a few more minutes. The House decided, and here I am.
I would like to say that it is indeed unfortunate that the House seems determined to give third reading to this Bill today to pass it into law. I say this is unfortunate for a variety of reasons; principally because it will hurt the small, independent Canadian oil companies and the independent Canadian companies that supply the oil patch in the Western Sedimentary Basin, especially in Alberta.
It should be noted at the start that the passage of this Bill will in no way affect the large international companies. Indeed, it will not affect the large Canadian companies involved in the patch. Because they already will have made up their allowable exploration and drilling expenditures prior to the termination date set in the Bill, the premature termination of the program. It is the small companies that will have just been undertaking their exploration and drilling programs that will have spread those programs over the four quarters of activity in the year that will be caught short and harmed by the passage of this Bill. In this sense, this Bill is discriminatory
against precisely that sector of the industry which most needs and, indeed, most deserves the assistance that the program otherwise would grant.
Right off the top, this is an inequitable Bill. Indeed, it is a harmful Bill from the point of view of the small, independent Canadian sector. There is no question that the Bill will have impact. The Canadian Association of Oil Well-Drilling Contractors states that the cancellation of CIDA will make their prior second quarter forecast of 153 rigs drilling, down 10 per cent from 171, obsolete. In fact that figure will have to be further reduced. They are now talking about the average number of rigs running in the second quarter to be 89 or 17 per cent utilization.
Let there be no mistake that the cancellation of the CEDIP program will have a substantial impact on the Western Sedimentary Basin.
It is not just on the companies themselves that do the exploration. It is on the service companies in the industry that the negative impact will be felt. It is on those industries, for example, represented by the Petroleum Services Association of Canada which appeared before the legislative committee to make plain theirreservations with regard to the Bill.
However, the damage does not even stop there. Indeed, it extends right to the farm gate. As Mr. Bud Bell, the Vice-President and General Manager of Schlumberger Canada and the First Vice-President of the Petroleum Services Association of Canada, when asked during committee about where the people who work for the companies represented by his association, said:
They come from across Canada, but the majority of them come from Western Canada geographically. Many of them work for the services company in the winter, that are, during the summer, farmers.
This merely reinforces the point that I made at the second reading of this Bill, that many farmers, especially in Alberta, north of central Alberta, rely on farm employment to keep the farm going to tidethem over the tough times of low farm income. This Bill will impact negatively on them as well because there will not be the jobs in the smaller exploration companies and service companies that there would have been had CEDIP been maintained right through to the end of the program, projected for this December.
June 27, 1989

Therefore, there is no question that the Bill harms the small producers. It harms the servicing companies and it harms, in many cases, farmers seeking farm income who work for those companies.
There is another aspect in which this Bill is iniquitous. That is that the Government is using this Parliament to renege on a promise explicit in the previous legislation. The promise was to give six months clear notice of any alteration in the program.
There is no question that legally the Government can do this. The Government is perfectly free to place a bill before this House, have it passed through and become law and thereby simply void any prior commitment it may have incurred as a consequence of previous legislation. It can do that. The point is that it ought not to do that, especially when, in doing that, it is breaking a promise made and accepted in good faith by hard-working, small Canadian companies tiying to do a good job in the Western Sedimentary Basin. It is an improper way to conduct the public business, and for that reason alone, this Bill is unworthy of the support of this House.
As the Independent Petroleum Association of Canada noted in its submission to the legislative committee- they did not appear, but they did supply a written submission-"This measure undermines investor confidence in the integrity of Government." As was noted in its submission by the Small Explorers and Producers Association of Canada, this Bill if enacted constitutes a situation in which:
The Government violated its own covenant to give six months
notice.
This matter has not escaped the attention of the industry. Indeed, those who appeared before the committee stressed over and over again how surprised and how shocked they were that the Government would use Parliament to conduct itself in this fashion.
Last, I would like to make it very clear that it was discovered during the course of the Minister's appearance before the committee that the decision to terminate the CEDIP program was not taken in the Department of Energy, Mines and Resources, that it was not even considered within that Department. Rather an edict came from the Finance Department, as part of the Budget, that this program be prematurely terminated to save $80 million. There were no impact studies done on
Environmental Protection
the effects of this cancellation on the Western Sedimentary Basin and on Alberta. Apparently no alternatives were even considered. When the question was put to the Minister's Departmental senior staff as to whether or not consideration had been given to radically lowering the cap on the program, thereby saving at least $40 million but allowing the benefits still to flow to the smaller companies, the response was, no, not to their knowledge.
Therefore, we have a Bill that unfairly singles out small companies for punishment, we have a Bill that cancels a promise previously made by the Government, and we have a Bill the effects of which were not even considered prior to its introduction. For these three reasons, I submit the House cannot support this Bill. To do so would be wrong.
