speakeroldname: Mr. Lee Clark (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few
brief remarks on the occasion of third reading of Bill C-22. Let me begin if I may by thanking the members of the Standing Committee for the very effective and expeditious manner in which they addressed this legislation before the Standing Committee. I would also like to express my own personal thanks to the several departmental officials who were very helpful in that process.
As the members of the Committee understand, the Bill which is before the House now for third reading is very brief and a very straightforward piece of legislation. It was deemed necessary to rectify some legal difficulties encountered in the original legislation since its passage late last June.
In my opinion, the legislation before the House does indeed rectify those deficiencies. It means that we then will be in a position to enforce the regulations which were designed to come into place on July 1 of this year in order to effect the requirements of the Montreal Protocol. The Canadian Government was very happy to provide leadership at the time of the Montreal Protocol and we look forward to these regulations being in place.
I think all of us understand that the proposed emissions of CFCs by some 50 per cent which is provided for in the Montreal Protocol are no longer accepted as adequate. In fact, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) has already made a commitment that the Canadian Government will move toward the diminishing of CFC emissions by 80 per cent by the end of the next decade. Furthermore, he has accepted as an objective for the Government that we should move toward the elimination of all CFC emissions by the same date.
It is most important that all Parties work together in ensuring that the regulations in place will be effective and I think that is the case with respect to the Montreal Protocol and like all members of the House, I look forward to continuing to address this exceedingly important issue. Members on all sides now recognize the threat that CFCs represent to the ozone layer and the significance of that to the health of Canadians and citizens throughout the world.
I do hope the House will expedite the passage of this Bill as it has done to date.

Mr. Speaker, I am most happy to rise in support of this particular Bill. I must admit, however, when the Parliamentaiy Secretary to the Minister invokes the Montreal Protocol he forces
June 27, 1989

me to elaborate a little bit on our Party's position with respect to the whole question of CFCs.
This particular series of amendments was needed. Essentially when the original Canadian Environmental Protection Act was drafted by the former Minister of the Environment, he botched the job and he botched it in such a way that the current Government could not have met its obligations under the Montreal Protocol without a specific interim order unless this legislation went through. We are most happy to assist the Government in getting the legislation through but I was very disappointed that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) on February 16, 1989, stated that the CFC question was his number one priority and that he was going to begin immediately drafting regulations. In fact, we did not learn about the botch-up until May 31, so I have to ask the Minister what he was doing between February and May.
More important in the examination of CFCs, I became aware that 4,000 skin cancers every year are linked specifically to the depletion of the ozone layer, something which most Canadians are not aware of. The single largest contributor to the depletion of the ozone layer is the production of chlorofluorocarbons which are used on an ongoing basis in refrigerants and other particular products.
While I respect and understand alternative technologies in many areas are in the process of development, I do not understand nor do Canadians why the Government does not move immediately to force the recycling and recapture of CFCs currently being leaked into the environment.
Last night in our ministry committee we learned that a company in my own community of Hamilton that makes refrigerators, a Canadian subsidiary of General Electric company, Cameo purchases 300,000 pounds of CFCs per year for use in its refrigerators. Those CFCs are now purchased at a paltry sum of $1 per pound. It is very inexpensive and the company tends to use it as an inexpensive commodity. We learned from Cameo that 4 per cent of its CFCs are lost immediately during the manufacture and process and a further 10 per cent to 15 per cent of CFCs are leaked into the atmosphere on an ongoing basis during the life of a refrigerator.
Environmental Protection
We also know that at the moment there are no specific national standards with respect to the development of hermetically sealed air conditioners in automobiles, which is a very large escape source of CFCs. There is no particular national initiative with respect to companies and how they handle CFCs. We even heard by way of a presentation in the committee that VIA Rail, a crown corporation, in the City of Montreal, in the birthplace of the Montreal Protocol-

The Montreal Protocol should take effect in four days. Today is the 27th. As of Canada Day, the Montreal Protocol should take effect in the same place that it began, where it was signed. Every day, Mr. Speaker, a Crown corporation releases CFCs into the atmosphere, CFCs which we already know reduce the ozone layer and cause skin cancer. And what is the answer of the Government and of the companies that are releasing CFCs into the atmosphere?
We heard last night from the officials at Cameo that at this very moment it is in the process of doing repairs to 22,500 refrigerators in Canada and its parent company is in the process of doing repairs to one million refrigerators in the United States. When they are doing those repairs, they are deliberately permitting the leakage of CFCs into the atmosphere.
They claim that the technology is not available, even though we produced evidence that such technology does exist and indeed it is portable technology. We even asked the companies whether they would be willing to set aside or forgo their plan for repairs for a few months until they could satisfy themselves of the technology that can be used to recapture. They refused. Do you know why they refused, Mr. Speaker? Their excuse was that they represent a very small percentage of the market-place. Their percentage of the marketplace is 5 per cent. That is one company which is purchasing 5 per cent of all the CFCs in Canada. By their own declaration, the number of Canadians in their company actually working on the issue of recycling, recapture and research is two people. Two people, and they tell a parliamentary committee that they feel that they are doing enough in this area.

June 27, 1989
Environmental Protection
The company also told us that they could not move immediately because they wanted to preserve the food for Canadians by proper refrigeration. In fact, we had other methods of refrigeration before the arrival of CFCs in the market-place. Do you know, Mr. Speaker, for every 1 per cent increase in CFCs into the atmosphere, the capacity of the earth to produce food is decreased by 1 per cent. That 5 per cent ratio of CFCs used by that single Canadian company, in the Canadian context is responsible for a 5 per cent reduction in the arability of food for the world. We cannot just think about food in the context of what goes into and comes out of our refrigerator. We have to begin to think about the food in the global context.
We are among the heaviest users of chlorofluorocar-bons in the world, and if as a nation we are willing to dodge our responsibility and ignore the exigencies of the Montreal Protocol and the time bomb that is ticking on the very air which we breathe, by passing it off and saying: "Well, we only represent 5 per cent of the market-place", 5 per cent and 5 per cent and 5 per cent and 5 per cent, together a hole in the atmosphere make. That is exactly what we have at the moment with respect to the ozone layer. That is exactly why the federal Government and in particular, the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) should invoke his powers under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, under Section 35, to issue an interim order to begin to control the disposition of CFCs in refrigerants across Canada.
I was speaking to an industry person only a few days ago. He told me that at the moment CFCs are so cheap and so available that they use them as a replacement for water in cleaning the coils of their commercial refrigerators. Instead of bothering to get a water hose, they are doing repairs and they merely spray the back of the refrigerant with CFCs, which are going right into the atmosphere, which are creating holes and which are warming the climate.
We are entering what probably will turn out to be the hottest Canadian summer on record. That is not a natural phenomenon. The drought, for which Canadian farmers are still waiting to be paid, is in part a result of global warming trends which can directly be linked to the degradation which is being wrought by humankind on our universe.
Surely, if we can take some small step in Parliament, it should be an invocation of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act, of the interim orders to make sure that as well as dealing with our obligations under the Montreal Protocol, which are already out of date, that at the same time we ensure the toughest standards in the world in relation to refrigeration and in relation to the veiy things which at the moment are escaping public attention.
I asked that question specifically of the Minister only a few moments ago in the Environment Committee. I asked him if he would be prepared as an interim measure to invoke a section of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act to deal with that particular issue. The Minister, once again, was very fluid and flowery with his rhetoric but, once again, he refused to take specific action. He is studying the question. He is looking at other alternatives. This was a perfect opportunity for him to act. I must say that I amdisappointed that he is not doing more.
I am also disappointed in a decision of the committee to vote down a motion which was presented by the Liberal Party that the Bill be presented on recycled paper. It may be a small thing. It may be a nominal gesture in the fight to build a cleaner environment, but when we moved the motion to have the first piece of environmental legislation in this Parliament printed on recycled paper, it was turned down by the Conservatives.
I have to ask myself, how committed is the Government to environmental questions when it will not even recycle the paper which we use for environmental legislation, and it refuses something as simple as incorporating the concept of sustainable development into the mandate of various ministries.
I think in this particular Bill, yes, we have helped the Government and we have tried to expedite the process because we would like to see the Government meet its obligations under the Montreal Protocol.
However, the Montreal Protocol is only a beginning. We heard from Greenpeace that we have the capacity to do so much more. Then when we heard from industry what is not being done in the very specific area of refrigeration, it shocked me to know that one single company in Canada uses 300,000 pounds of CFCs a year and that most of those 300,000 pounds are put into refrigerators and leak out with very little regard to

speechtext:
That Bill C-239, an Act to change the name of the electoral district of Saint-Laurent, be read the second time and referred to a Committee of the Whole House.
She said: Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure and especially a great honour for me to speak on Bill C-239 to change the name of my constituency, Saint-Laurent, to Saint-Laurent-Cartierville.
The federal riding of Saint-Laurent includes the City of Saint-Laurent as well as the northwestern part of the City of Montreal, known as Cartierville and Saraguay.

The name Saint-Laurent has very strong affiliation with the boundaries of the city. In effect, by having the name of the riding changed, we are removing the
confusion surrounding the actual boundaries of the riding with those of the city.
During the last federal election campaign when I was canvassing door to door, many of the people in the Montreal sector of my riding did not realize that they were in the federal district of Saint-Laurent. By changing the name of the riding to encompass both the Montreal and Saint-Laurent sectors of the area, no confusion will arise.

Mr. Speaker, I can say with pride that I have fulfilled one of my election promises. I heard and listened to the people of Saint-Laurent when they told me they wanted the name of their riding to reflect who they are.

It is for this reason that I tabled this Bill earlier this session. I must express my pleasure with the fact that seven Members of Parliament from all sides of the House have agreed to co-operate and pass through all stages these Bills at this sitting. We must listen to our constituents at all times for it is on their behalf that we sit in this Chamber.
Cartierville represents 25 per cent of the total population of the riding. I am sure that those people will be pleased to see that they will be more openly recognized as an integral part of the new federal riding of Saint-Laurent-Cartierville.
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, considered in committee, reported, concurred in, read the third time and passed.

Subject to subsection (4).

and the Government's intentions than the English version. So as a Francophone, I am of course quite pleased, and I will vote in favour of the Bill. However, I wish that Anglophone and Francophone linguists in the Government would consult when drafting the respective versions of the Bill, in order to avoid these problems.

Mr. Speaker, I would first of all like to say that on this side of the House, we feel that-

This Bill is veiy narrow in its scope. It is necessary in order to implement measures that were in the intent and spirit of the law, but we have to take this opportunity to register with the Government the fact that the law known under the name of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act is flawed and must be corrected.
The first reason concerns the fact that the federal Government cannot set national enforceable standards as we experienced in the case of PCBs. The next reason is that the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) is the only person in Canada who can seek an injunction to stop a violation of the Act. Then there is the shortcoming that the law, per se, lacks a prohibition clause which does, for instance, exist in Section 33 of the Fisheries Act and which would make the release of any pollutant, not just those listed in the Schedules of the Act, an offence.
Finally, in the event of an emergency, the federal Government cannot move alone but must have consultations with the affected provinces. This, in the case of an emergency, is not a very desirable requirement.
The enforceable national standards were lost in the discussion in committee when the Canadian Environmental Protection Act eventually became law. It was lost in three stages as it went through the legislative committee process. It was in essence a political decision by the Conservative Government which was ready and willing to give up its right to establish and enforce federal regulations. That development was tantamount to the abdication of federal powers to create and allow for the formation and implementation of federally enforceable national standards.
June 27, 1989

The first practical application came about with the PCB regulations. You will recall that in the aftermath of the Saint-Basile-le-Grand tragedy and disaster the federal Government finally decided to move. The first item on the agenda was safe storage. At that time the then Minister of the Environment was quoted as saying, "The actions I am taking ensure that PCB storage sites in every part of Canada meet high national standards".
Well, within two months nine provinces had sought and obtained exemption from such standards. By May 12, 1989, all provinces except Prince Edward Island and the Territories were granted exemption from the so-called high national standards of the former Minister of the Environment.
In order to be recognized as equivalent standards, the provinces simply have to meet two criteria. The first criterion is that there must be a provincial investigation process similar to the one contained in Sections 108 to 110 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. Briefly, Mr. Speaker, these two sections allow two individuals to request that the Minister of the Environment investigate an alleged violation of the Act. The Minister must then investigate the allegations and report in writing in 90 days on whether or not charges will be laid.
The second requirement which exists under the Environmental Protection Act is that the regulations in the provinces must be the same as the federal regulations. As far as we can determine there is not a province in Canada which has the same provisions for investigation of an offence as are contained in the federal law.
It is astounding that provinces are not required to have the same penalties and fines as are contained in the federal legislation in order to be granted this equivalency. This makes a mockery of the statements made by the previous Minister of the Environment, the present one, and the Government in general that the Canadian Environmental Protection Act is the toughest legislation in the western hemisphere.
If the provinces are able to supersede federal law with penalties that are a fraction of the federal penalties the concept of national standards is evidently seriously eroded. So while the facade looks very strong, behind the facade there is weakness.
Environmental Protection Act
Furthermore, the equivalency provisions of the Environmental Protection Act, as it stands now, and the way that the PCB storage regulations were handled considerably erode our confidence in the commitment of the Government to bring in tough and enforceable national standards for other toxic substances, as in the case of CFCs, dioxins, furans, et cetera.
In their publication Healing the Sky released just a few days ago Friends of the Earth say that under the Canadian Environmental Protection Act the Minister of the Environment has the power to do several things. For instance, the Minister can ban immediately chlorofluoro-carbons in aerosols, in rug underpadding and foam packaging. He can ban chlorofluorocarbons in polystyrene foam insulation, solvents for metal cleaning, and flexible foam by July of next year. He can ban the use of chlorofluorocarbons in new car air conditioners which are not hermetically sealed as of the 1991 model year. He can ban chlorofluorocarbons used as solvents in the electronics industry and for sterilization also by July, 1991. Finally, he can require recycling, recovery, system modifications and selective replacement with alternative chillers by the year 1992.
Taken together these five initiatives, in the opinion of Friends of the Earth, could reduce the production of chlorofluorocarbons in Canada by 67 per cent within the next three years. It is important that this publication be somehow brought to the attention of this House because it is relevant to the purpose and the technical intent- but nevertheless the intent-of the Bill we are debating because it relates to chlorofluorocarbons.
But, Mr. Speaker-and this is a big "but"-in order to proceed with these five suggestions and implement them the Minister must utilize enforceable national standards. Allowing provinces to opt out through the equivalency provisions would seriously endanger the success of such a reduction program because the enforcement that the regulations would end could vary from province to province. This is where the problem would arise.
Therefore, whether it is PCBs, chlorofluorocarbons, dioxins or a toxic substance yet to be identified, the Canadian Environment Protection Act will be successful in cleaning up Canada only if it is implemented and enforced nationally. The Minister of the Environment need not grant equivalency provisions to provinces that seek them. We would urge, on the contrary, the Minister to exert the force of a strong federalism in the protection of the environment. He will achieve that end in relation to the chlorofluorocarbons and the five measures suggested by Friends of the Earth and in relation to other substances that are still to be covered in the Schedule of

June 27, 1989
Environmental Protection Act
the Bill, on which we hope there will be swift movement on the part of the Government once Bill C-22 is passed, only if he invokes national enforceable standards and makes them the instrument and the priority of the Government when it comes to cleaning up the environment.
Bill C-22 allows an opportunity to deal beyond the narrow technical scope of the Bill itself because behind the proposed changes there is this big and important question of national enforceable standards to which the Government, unfortunately, is not paying attention.
We have had this experience with PCBs. You have heard the description of what happened, Mr. Speaker. We would not like to have that experience again whereby the vast majority of the provinces seek an exemption, apply their own so-called equivalency standards, but do not have in place the same measures for compliance, enforcement and penalties as has the federal legislation. This serious shortcoming must be brought to your attention and to the attention of the Government, Mr. Speaker.
I see that the Parliamentary Secretary is listening very attentively, as he always does, and I am sure that he will register these views in discussions with his Minister. Because he believes in strong enforceable national standards I am sure that he will lend a hand in ensuring that in the toxic substances yet to be detected those standards will not be by-passed by way of equivalency sought by the provinces.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret that I did not recognize the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) before the Hon. Member for Davenport (Mr. Caccia). It was just an oversight. It is getting late in the afternoon.

Mr. Speaker, I know you were very busy just prior to this debate beginning. That probably had something to do with it.
We are on third reading of Bill C-22 which Members of this House know is rather a short Bill. It amends Sections 33 and 34 of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act. The officials like to describe it as a housekeeping matter, but in fact there are nine families
of toxic substances on Schedule I of the Canadian Environmental Protection Act that simply cannot be regulated at the moment other than through interim orders which are very difficult and unwieldy.
Of particular interest to the House, and I think to Canadians, is the reason for the urgency in getting this Bill through and why Members of this House are working together so that it can become law and so that substances such as chlorofluorocarbons can in fact be more expeditiously regulated.
Unfortunately what we have learned during the rather brief committee hearings that we have had on Bill C-22 on CFCs is that the approach being taken by the Government of Canada, and particularly by the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard), are totally inadequate. As we can see from their most recent publication of April, 1989, called Preserving the Ozone Layer: A Step Beyond, a report on options for meeting Canada's objectives to completely eliminate emissions of controlled ozone depleting substances within the next 10 years, is, by definition, an inadequate response to an extremely serious and severe global problem, namely the depletion of the ozone layer.
In this publication on preserving the ozone layer, the principal culprits or problems that we have throughout the world, and certainly in wide use in Canada, are listed in seven main categories: rigid foam, flexible foam, refrigeration and air conditioning, solvents, sterilants, bromofluorocarbons which are more commonly and widely known as halons, and aerosols. I think the first couple of paragraphs of the publication are worth putting on the record for those who want to have a better understanding of the process that has been gone through by the Government of Canada before I put some other remarks on the record as to what we should really be doing.
Global efforts to address stratospheric ozone depletion have been under way since 1981. The Vienna Convention for the Protection of the Ozone Layer entered into force on September 22, 1988.
As of March 1,1989,37 countries, representing the vast majority of the industrialized nations of the world, had ratified this Convention. The Convention provides the framework for co-operative activities, including the exchange of data or information related to the ozone layer. This Convention provides for the subsequent creation of protocols (free standing treaties) for matters such as control of specific
June 27, 1989

pollutants or families of pollutants. The first such Protocol created was the Montreal Protocol on Substances that Deplete the Ozone Layer.
The Montreal Protocol was signed in Montreal, Canada on September 16, 1987. It is clearly a watershed in co-operative and collaborative international undertakings. It introduces many new features never before established in international law.
The Montreal Protocol has two requirements for entry into force; namely, 11 signatures of ratification by countries and these countries must represent at least two-thirds of global consumption of the controlled substances. The Montreal Protocol entered into force on January 1, 1989 and as of March, 1989 had already obtained 33 ratifications, again representing most of the industrialized states of the world.
In May, 1988, Environment Canada published its first Control Options Report titled: "Preserving the Ozone Layer: a first step". This report set out a series of options to implement regulations to meet Canada's obligations under the Montreal Protocol.
The Montreal Protocol calls for a 50 per cent cut back in the 1986 levels of consumption of five chlorofluorocarbons (CFC 11,12,113, 114, 115) and a freeze at 1986 consumption levels of three brominated fluorocarbons called Halons (Halon 1211, 1301, 2402). At a series of United Nations Environment Programme (UNEP) meetings held in the Hague, Netherlands, in October 1988 the world's leading scientists expressed the consensus viewpoint that the Antarctic hole will remain unless the emissions of controlled CFCs are reduced by at least 85 per cent from the 1986 levels. The target reductions contained in the Montreal Protocol are currently undergoing international review. This review is expected to culminate in amendments that will tighten the Montreal Protocol.
Canada contributed to both the organization and conduct of the UNEP meeting in the Hague and fully supports the notion of reducing consumption further.
On February 20, 1989 the Federal Government of Canada announced that it had set as its objective the complete elimination of controlled CFCs within the next ten years.
It also called on the rest of the world to set as its common target a reduction of no less than 85 per cent by no later than 1999.
As I said, at the brief committee meetings that we have had in the last while, we learned a number of interesting things; in particular that not only is Canada not moving fast enough; most countries and most political leaders around the world are not taking this matter in any way seriously enough. I
I pointed out the seven main families of materials in use in our society that need immediate reduction and recycling and re-use. The breakdown in terms of CFCs in Canada right now are aerosols, 9 per cent, rigid foams, 33 per cent, flexible foams, 8 per cent, in the field of
Environmental Protection Act
refrigeration, 36 per cent, domestic refrigerators composing 3 per cent and solvents, 10 per cent.
As we heard from witnesses, we must move to stop the easy ones. Many of those were identified. We must make the technology available now and make the removal of CFCs, for example, from home refrigerators mandatory. Then, if one needs a reinjection of CFCs, one can take it from other units that are being disposed of for other reasons.
In regard to automobiles, as we heard from witnesses yesterday, they lose up to 35 per cent of CFCs from their air conditioning units within the first couple of years of operation because the units are not hermetically sealed. TTien there are the big refrigeration units and so on. There are ways now to immediately and dramatically reduce the amount escaping into the atmosphere. The Government of Canada and the provincial Governments are not taking serious enough action to introduce the technology, to train the maintenance personnel, to make recycling equipment available at auto wreckers, at car dealers, at gas stations and so on, to make sure that CFCs that are escaping or are likely to escape are recovered.
As we heard from witnesses from General Electric last night, one of the problems that is addressable by the Government of Canada is that CFCs right now only cost between $1 or $2 a pound. They are very inexpensive. So in fact there is encouragement to continue to allow the release and the incomplete design and construction of compressors and holding equipment that have CFCs in them.
We heard from the refrigeration people that the foam that has CFCs in it loses 10 per cent of its CFCs over the life of the fridge. As I have said, automobiles lose 35 per cent from their air conditioners. To give some idea of what kind of quantities are in your average size fridge, there are two to four pounds of CFC 11 which is in the insulation and six to eight ounces of CFC 12 which is in the cooling system.
We heard from Mr. John Bennett of Greenpeace before the committee earlier this week who gave an excellent brief called "Stop It Now'' which is its response to the Canadian CFC Control Program. Its suggestions are the following; Ban the production of CFCs and halons in Canada; expand the list of controlled ozone depleting compounds and establish a national recycling and recovery program. These seem to me, Mr. Speaker, to be things on which the Government could move if it were listening seriously enough to what the international

June 27, 1989
Environmental Protection Act
scientific community is saying, not only about the Antarctic ozone hole but about the holes that are now starting to appear over northern Canada. There may, in fact, be other holes and depletion areas within the ozone layer that simply have not yet been identified. The brief goes on to say:
There are millions of tonnes of chlorine floating around in the atmosphere destroying the ozone layer. If we do not stop polluting it now we will not be able to protect our children,-
Also included is a rather appropriate quotation from Dr. Klaus Toepfer, Environment Minister for the Federal Republic of Germany. He said:
"The affluent society is not dependent on CFCs. But even if it were, one would, I believe, have to accept this cut in living standards."
For a CFC control plan the witness from Greenpeace suggested a number of areas that need to be moved on: One, timing. Two, controlled compounds. Three, disclosure of information. Four, environmentally safe alternatives. Under the heading "Timing" we find the following:
The earth can no longer afford the cost of a slow phase-out of CFC production and use.
The Government of Canada must immediately ban the production of CFCs and halons and limit their use to an extremely few exceptions for life-saving applications.
The Government of Canada must immediately increase its commitment to preserving the ozone layer by substantially expanding the resources it devotes to eliminating ozone depletion and expanding its enforcement capability.
The Government of Canada must immediately establish national regulations requiring recovery and recycling of CFC refrigerants in all applications until new technology replaces them.
Let me say the proposal made by Mr. Bennett is so obviously capable of being implemented. The compressor technology for removing CFCs from existing units is available. It could be made substantially more compact and movable to be taken out of utility vans into the home. It can be easily moved around in plants where CFCs need to be moved between different pieces of equipment. The technology, the effort and I am sure the will of the Canadian public is there to participate in such a program even if it costs more, Mr. Speaker. We have learned from poll after poll that Canadians are prepared
to pay significantly more for a safe, healthy, clean environment. What is missing, the fundamental missing link, is political will. That political will is missing right now from the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Bouchard) to take the kinds of serious steps he is capable of taking under CEPA. It goes on to say:
The Government of Canada must immediately establish a national recycling program and not leave it up to municipalities or other governments to operate as indicated in "Preserving the Ozone Layer".
We have heard in this House many times the problems right across the country of cars simply being wrecked with their air conditioning systems in them. CFCs are released. The same is true of refrigeration units and many other things. Under the heading "Controlled Compounds" Greenpeace suggests that the list of controlled substances must be expanded to include HCFCs, methyl chloroform and carbon tetrachloride. We have yet to hear from the Minister of the Environment what his plans are on those compounds.
The Environmental Policy Institute and the Institute for Energy and Environmental Research in the United States examined various scenarios for eliminating carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform in addition to controlled CFCs and halons. The study suggests that if emissions of these CFCs decline to zero by 1995, if carbon tetrachloride growth rate was in the middle of the zero to 3 per cent range cited by the World Meteorological Organization and methyl chloroform grew by less than the WMO's 8 per cent projection, atmospheric chlorine levels would increase from 30 million tons in 1987 to over 90 million tons by the year 2000. Alternatively, if carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform were phased out by the year 2000, chlorine levels would fall from 30 million tons to 1.7 million tons by the year 2000. It is essential for the Government of Canada to ban carbon tetrachloride and methyl chloroform and to ensure these compounds are included in the international agreements on the ozone layer.
On international activity, Greenpeace states:
June 27, 1989

The Government of Canada must support an international fund to aid Third World countries in complying with a 100 per cent CFC ban.
Secondly, the Government of Canada should promote a vastly expanded international program which includes banning all CFCs, Halons, HCFCs, methylchloroform and carbon tetrachloride.
On disclosure of information, as suggested by Greenpeace, Canada should support Norway, the U.S.S.R., New Zealand and Zambia in calling for the public release of data on a country-by-countiy and product-byproduct basis for all ozone depleters. For anyone who has been around here for a while, or involved in politics anywhere, knows that access to information is absolutely fundamental to getting public support and political action for safe alternatives.
On environmentally safe alternatives, Canada should move completely away from chlorine-based substitutes, as there are a range of serious toxic pollution problems associated with them quite apart from their ozone depleting and global warming potentials. The solution to the CFC problem is in finding the best alternatives that are not synthetic. We come to the "100 per cent reduction, is it feasible?" In the refrigeration sector, a large volume of CFCs are stored in existing commercial freezer and cold storage systems. Much of the demand for CFCs in this sector is artificially created by wastage and could be met by recovery and recycling. As much as 70 per cent of the CFCs used in refrigeration is lost through leaks and other wastage.
As for foam blowing, packaging for hamburgers and fast foods, other presently available products can be substituted. Insulant foam used in building can be eliminated in most applications by use of alternatives without serious technical or cost consequences. CFCs used in solvents can often be replaced by aqueous cleaning, which preceded the use of CFC-113. Some solvent use can be replaced with organic terpenes and "clean mount" techniques. The use of halons can be avoided by installing other types of systems; for example, carbon dioxide or water sprinklers combined with other measures. Recovery and recycling of existing halons could service existing fire-fighting equipment where halons are used in life-saving applications for which no other substitutes can be found.
Plant Breeders' Rights
On ozone depletion, we find that the earth's ozone layer is being destroyed by chlorine and bromine released into the stratosphere by a group of chemical compounds known as chlorofluorocarbons and halons. The depletion of the ozone layer will result in skin cancers, eye damage and crop destruction as increasing amounts of ultraviolet radiation from the sun reach the earth's surface.
Already, British scientists and NASA have identified a hole in the ozone layer over Antarctica and a thin area of the ozone layer over the northern hemisphere has been observed. Alarmed by the rapid depletion of the ozone layer, more than 40 western nations signed the 1987 Montreal Protocol which calls for a 50 per cent reduction of CFC emissions by 1999.
Joe Farman in the New Scientist for November 1987 said:
A 50 per cent cut in world consumption of CFCs will not be enough to save the ozone layer. The emissions of CFCs are so large that they are accumulating rapidly. If we wish the amounts of CFCs to remain constant, we must cut emissions so that they are equal to the losses, that is to say, roughly 15 per cent of the current level.
Joe Farman, a member of the British Antarctic Survey, is credited with identifying the hole in the ozone layer.
In 1988 the EPA said to maintain stratosphere chlorine at current levels would require a 100 per cent phase-out of the Montreal CFCs with 100 per cent participation. In other words, just to maintain the ozone layer in its present state there must be an immediate 100 per cent reduction of CFC production.
If there is more time, Mr. Speaker, I could go on.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Mazankowski that Bill C-15, an Act respecting plant breeder's rights, be read the second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, I rise tonight to speak to this Bill being brought in under closure at second reading. It is a very complex Bill which will have a profound impact on this country and the potential food supply of this country if allowed to pass in its present form.
I recall as a young child going with my father in a Model A Ford to pick up registered seed grain from a local seed company. I remember him harvesting the wheat the next year when, in turn, he would sell that to other farmers in the area.
The advances in crop technology and plant breeding since that time have more than doubled the yields of those plants. This has been done through research by private companies as well as through the tremendous research and leadership performed by Agriculture Canada and the scientists there.
It is only in recent years that they pushed back the climatic borders by approximately 250 miles for the production of com here in Canada through plant breeding. Just a few years ago only a certain area of Ontario could produce com. Through selective plant breeding they were able to push back those boundaries. Those

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
varieties were developed to a large extent by the scientists who work at Agriculture Canada on our behalf.
This Bill disturbs me when I consider all the hunger in the world today, in places like Ethiopia. We have varieties of sorghum that will grow and thrive under conditions there. In fact, it is grown in the Sudan but is not being made available to the starving Ethiopians. In this context, we can only suggest that food is being used as a weapon. If legislation like this is passed without proper safeguards, it is not inconceivable that a few very large companies could hold the world to ransom in terms of their food supplies.
As a result of a previous drug Bill in the last Parliament, Bill C-22, we saw drug prices double in a veiy few months after that Bill became law, in spite of the assurances that this would never happen. It can happen in this case because this Bill has several flaws that I think have to be corrected, hopefully in committee if the Government intends to put the Bill through.
Let me outline a few areas of concern.
The first is subclause 2(2) and subclause 6(1) wherein there is provision that a country could protect varieties of certain species for 15 years, but in Canada that could be 18 years. I have no problem whatsoever with protecting some varieties for 18 years, but varieties of what? Grapevines or fruit trees, yes, but not seeds, not grain seed or vegetables or other types that mature in a matter of a few months or a year. Many grapevines are over 100 years old and are still producing. In fact, some of them even get better with time.
I could accept the 18-year provision for trees or grapes, but then I find that some of our Canadian scientists, some of whom are working with CIDA in Thailand, have developed new species of trees that will mature in eight years. We also have dwarf apple trees which will produce in a matter of three or four years. In committee we must look very hard at that 18-year provision. The limit for grains must be stipulated in the Bill, whether it is five, six or seven years.
My experience over the years has been that when a new variety of com, wheat, or beans comes on the market, after six or seven years that variety starts to run out, as they say. It is not as good as it was the first year it was put on the market. Therefore, there must be a
constant renewal of varieties, new developments that are disease resistant, resistant to the various types of bacteria, insects, or blights that may affect them.
Another area that I must question is that both federal and provincial Governments must comply with the provisions of plant breeders' rights. Usually what happens within a province is under provincial jurisdiction and what happens in international and interprovincial trade is under federal jurisdiction. I must wonder about why both levels of government must comply. Are we in fact imposing this on the provinces, and will they accept it?
Another area that we must look at in detail is the expansion of farmers' rights. They are mentioned in the Bill. A farmer is only given permission to grow his own seed from that which he has bought. He cannot help out a neighbour by giving him a few bushels to help him get established, or he cannot give some to a son. There was a drought in three of the last four years and farmers are very hard-pressed financially. I think there should be a relaxation of farmers' rights to enable them to give a few bushels to a neighbour or a son or to help someone in need without having to break the law.
This one is a real sleeper because it allows one to purchase seed in another country without infringing on plant breeders' rights as long as one does not plant the seed. I am speaking now of subclause 5(2). This would allow me to go to the State of Michigan in the United States and purchase seed without infringing on plant breeders' rights, but I cannot plant it when I bring it back home. If I cannot plant it, what in the world am I going to do with it? It will be treated with various seed treatments to protect it from insects and various diseases, but what do you do with treated seed? You certainly cannot eat it.
The danger in this clause is that if a multi-national seed company wanted to ensure that we in Canada are not given access to a certain superior variety of seed it can do so under subclause 5(2).
Under subclause 5(4) both the federal and provincial Governments may collect royalties on their varieties. This clause seems to make a great deal of sense until we realize that there is nothing in it that requires these royalties to go back into research in the public interest. The Government has cut research funding dramatically since 1984.1 believe that a major portion of any earnings from royalties should be funnelled back into research in
June 27, 1989

the public interest to develop new species and varieties of plant seed.
There is nothing in this Bill to prevent a company from collecting very large royalties under this legislation. In fact in England these fees start out very low and then increase over several years.
It is very simple to see what will happen here. If a company develops any variety of seed, all it needs to do is let a few bushels out on the market for the first few years in test plots and publish the results. It can fertilize these plots very heavily and grow the plants under almost perfect conditions. It can publish the yields and through advertising promote these varieties very extensively. After they are out for a few years and it has done a lot of advertising, it can start jacking up the royalties. There is nothing in this legislation to stop it.
There is nothing in the legislation to stop a company from withdrawing a popular variety of plant from the market-place and replacing it with another on which it can collect a higher level of royalties. I think that is a very dangerous clause to have in the legislation without a ceiling to protect not only the rights of the farmers and producers but, in turn, to give the companies a return on their money.
I need only think back a few years to some of the supposedly new and superior varieties of wheat that were brought into Ontario. They did not originate here. I am not going to name them, but we all know that after a few years of experience with them we found they were not as good as some of our older varieties of wheat that had been on the market for several years. They were more prone to sprouting during a season of more moisture than is normal in Ontario. The heads stood straight up when they were ripe, consequently when the rains hit, the hulls acted as a cup and held the moisture around the germination end of the seed. The older varieties would turn over and shed the rain when they were ripe. A lot of farmers bought these new varieties thinking they were going to increase their yields. Even if they did increase their yields slightly, they ended up with a lot of sprouted wheat.
With regard to the seeds, again I will use the soybean seed as an example. The price of seed went up even though the price of commercial beans dropped dramati-
Plant Breeders' Rights
cally this spring. These companies know that there is a captive market out there, and they charge what the market will bear.
Of course, this is nothing new in terms of farm input costs. For several years one chemical company was selling one particular patented type of herbicide for about twice as much in Canada as it was charging in other countries. I submit that these seed companies will do the same. They will charge whatever the traffic will bear when they get their protective legislation.
Clause 31 permits a variety to be assigned to another person. I presume that a person can be a corporation in the eyes of the law and, of course, if this is the case, there is nothing to stop a company from another country buying a variety and taking it off the market only to comer the market for its own particular products.
In Canada we already have an organization in place to market varieties produced by Agriculture Canada or the universities. That organization is SeCan which collects levies and royalties on the sale of new varieties. SeCan has about 2,200 members and membership is voluntary. In a sense it operates a partial plant breeders' rights system of marketing now, by marketing certified seed, of crops covered by Agriculture Canada's variety registration system.
One thing that is not known at this time is whether the royalties paid by our growers to foreign breeders will exceed or be balanced by royalties paid to Canadian breeders by foreign growers once a significant trade of protected varieties is established. We do not know at this time whether that balance of trade for new varieties developed will be in Canada's favour or will be against us.
I suggest, Mr. Speaker, that if we continue to cut back the research in Agriculture Canada and deprive the research scientists and the plant breeders of the funding they desperately need, the balance will very quickly turn to a deficit trade balance of seed produced in Canada.
We have persons saying that the multinationals will only dominate the industry if the public breeding program is seriously diminished and if the private varieties are superior. However, we have no commitment from the Government that the public programs will continue,

with the cut-backs in research involved in plant breeding, if it is left to the private sector outside of Canada.
I have some very serious reservations about this Bill. I hope that the Minister and the Government will consider making some major changes in committee. They have not come up with a dollar cost on the administration of this Bill. I think they should do that and look at the areas of concern that we have here in the Official Opposition.
From my own personal experience-I used to be a registered seed grower a few years back-one of the things we have to look at very seriously is the 18-year protection. Just to recap, it is far too long for any grains or seeds with the exception of grapes, orchard trees or fruit trees.
We should have a system of satellite seed banks established across Canada, not just the central bank here in the Ottawa region. We could keep samples of the various types of seeds that are grown in the Prairies, for example, in an environmentally controlled room. They could be stored for up to 300 years. These should be kept in the public trust so that no company could ever get their hands on them and destroy the parent genes and seeds. There should be satellite banks not just in the prairie provinces, but in British Columbia, Ontario, Quebec, and Atlantic Canada to protect the public interest. The cost of these would not be that great. A single room of about 400 square feet in the basement of any environmentally controlled building would be sufficient. We have also to beef up the farmers' rights and ensure that it is not a criminal act to give a bag of a particular variety of seed to a neighbour or to a son.
The fourth thing that I want to stress-and these again are my own personal thoughts on this matter-are that the royalties have to be directed back into research by Agriculture Canada. This issue is too important to be left to private corporations or the private sector.
We have some of the best research scientists in Canada. They have developed some of the best varieties in the world. Our western Canadian wheat grown out of Saskatchewan is the highest quality of wheat grown anywhere in the world. We simply cannot let those quality factors be diminished by turning it over to the private sector.

Mr. Speaker, I listened with great interest to the speech by the Member from Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson). I hope that much of what he said will be attended by the government side.
I do not count myself in any way an expert or even significantly knowledgeable about the impact of this legislation on agriculture in Canada or elsewhere. I do know that there are grounds for significant concern.
I am reminded of the debate on Bill C-22 which bore some similarity to this legislation. This legislation, however, has to do with living material. It has to do with germplasm. What this would do is provide a measure of exclusivity, 18 years of exclusivity, to those who have provided by means of genetic manipulation a plant variety that is sufficiently new, sufficiently distinguishable and sufficiently stable to be distinguished from other varieties or cultivars of that species of plant.
It is interesting that this exclusivity is based on the final product. There is nothing here which meets the test that patents are required to fulfil. It might be of use to refer back to a decision by Lord Duneden in Pope Alliance Corporation v. the Spanish River Pulp and Paper Mill, 1929 A.C. 269, page 281, where he states that a patent represents a quid pro quo. The quid to the patentee is the monopoly. The quo is that he presents to the public the knowledge it does not have.
Of course it is quite notable that in producing a new breed of plant, a new cultivar that has some significant utility, its newness, its distinctiveness, its homogeneity, and its stability as a final product are the characteristics which will determine whether a licence in effect will be accorded and whether exclusivity or a monopoly will be provided.
There is no requirement to describe the process of making those plans which have been used in developing the new breed available to others so that they can build on the germplasm pool that resulted in this new cultivar. In according a monopoly, we are denied the knowledge that usually goes with the patent. We are also denied knowledge of what plants, what germplasm needs to be preserved in the event that that new final product, the new breed of plant, the new cultivar should, as plants often do, lose their characteristics so that the process

could in turn be repeated even after the 18 years of exclusivity.
There have been a number of objections raised to this kind of legislation, objections which I think sustain the request, indeed the demand, on the part of many that this Bill be accorded broad hearings so that the public will have an opportunity to make its case.
I think it would be appropriate however to consider just for a moment what is really involved here. I am a biologist. I never really thought that living things should be the particular property of anybody. As we develop these new high-test breeds with fantastic characteristics, with the ability to withstand pests, insects, disease, climates, different soils, and so on, we have operated on the availability of genetic variation that exists within the species throughout the world.
Where did wheat come from? Where did barley come from? Where did potatoes come from? Where did the vast majority of the cultivated plants that serve human needs come from?
They did not come from the major industrial northern nations that now would impose exclusivity on a living thing. Virtually every significant food plant has come originally from the Third World, South America, the Caribbean, Southern Asia, and Africa. From the very beginning, dating from 1492, Columbus grabbed up maize, tobacco and a number of other things. He took them to Europe. In subsequent voyages there was the transport of plants from Africa and Asia back to North America, so there has been established a degree of homogeneity in availability of certain kinds of plants in the tropics. Dating from 1492 the northern industrial first world nations have taken the germplasm from the south to produce the agricultural giants that the northern nations have become.
In fact, right after the Second World War, this process went on to the extent that at the turn of the century 70 per cent of the budget of the American Department of Agriculture was devoted, dare I say it, to stealing the germplasm from the Third World. In contrast to coal, oil, and the forests germplasm was considered to be the calm and property of all mankind. We stand here today talking about taking that very germplasm that was stolen from the Third World and putting a patent on it as it is put into
Plant Breeders' Rights
new combinations. Those will be secret combinations and will provide the basis for profit for the corporations. They will argue that they have injected human knowledge into this and therefore they should be paid for it. Well, it is possible if one considers, as I did earlier, the decision of Justice Duneden that there be a revelation of the content of an invention. That might put a different shape on it.
This process, as I have said before, of stealing the germplasm from the Third World continues. Much of the variety of the germplasm exists in the land races that are cultivated in the Third World, land races which can provide the kind of variability and the kinds of genes that can be used to create new breeds. These will have new characteristics which will be advantageous in northern climes.
Let me say something about those land races just for a moment. There are two characteristics to those land races. They display a great deal of variability and a field or contiguous fields of land races may have the capacity to withstand with minor losses all kinds of environmental or biological attacks. They have worked out quite well. Those land races are still being used and will be used by the corporations that we seek to protect in this legislation to produce those new varieties with their secret germplasm content, but those land races did not just jump up there on the soil.
Those land races are the product of human knowledge in the Third World. If it is justified to provide huge profits for exclusive knowledge to First World industrial nation corporations, then why is it not of equal importance to ensure that those poor peasant farmers, who with their traditional knowledge have created something new, be similarly awarded for their contribution through human knowledge?
There is an asymmetry there that is not unusual in this world. It seems to me that this country should be seeking to resolve this situation to the benefit not of the multinational corporations but of humankind and defer to the profit of the Third World. It is of interest to us to make sure that those aboriginal species, those land races and other variations that occur in the Third World be maintained. Perhaps we can find means of ensuring the maintenance of that and find a suitable way of compensating the Third World for its contribution. There is no justice in saying that there is property resident in the

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
industrial nations but the property of the Third World is a part of a common heritage.
This is a significant and serious consideration and I know that you are pondering it with the greatest seriousness, Mr. Speaker. I hope that your colleagues, the Conservative Members on the other side, will similarly consider it.
There have been a number of other more domestic concerns raised about this legislation. Canada has done quite well really in the production of new plant breeds through the involvement of the Department of Agriculture and the universities. We produce breeds of grain, wheat and so on which are quite suitable to the Canadian climate and conditions. We have invested as a nation in this.
One has to ask a serious question: if we are going to open this up according to the multinational's exclusivity, a licensing of an 18-year exclusivity, is there not a danger that given the history of this Government inevitably the private sector will overtake the Government and industrial sectors?
Those areas will be increasingly devoted to basic research while, in fact, the private industry-and read there multinational corporations-will take over by deliberate intent. Remember this is the privatization Government: "We will take over by a deliberate intent the production of new breeds of plants for the farmers of this land". I
I do not have to tell you what the implications of that might be because the implications are clear. Monopolies and oligopolies will be established in which relatively few large companies will take over and, of course, prices will rise for the farmer and the cost of food will rise for the consumer. There is another element in this that I think should concern everybody. That concern resides in the list of corporations which are engaged in plant breeding. I am sure that you are going to be very interested in this: Shell, Sandoz, deKopp-Pfizer, Upjohn, Ciba-Geigy, and ICI. That sounds like a list of companies that produce chemicals and pesticides.
I know you are not a devious man, Mr. Speaker, and so you would not want a devious company. I am sure that you can understand that there might be a terrible
temptation out there, given the power of genetic engineering, the power of my own field, indeed, biology, to manipulate and that unbeknownst to the farmer those companies might very well be producing plants which are dependent upon pesticides and herbicides. What a trick that would be: sell the plant, you cannot get the new breed from anybody else. You plant that devil and find out it will not grow without 2,4D.
This has been a notion that has been dismissed by some but it is very difficult not to be extremely suspicious when we read the names of the companies which have the greatest interest in all of this. I think that we should know a good deal more about those possibilities before we allow this Government to push this legislation through without considerable thought. We have a good, solid plant breeders' effort in this country right now through Government and the universities that serves the farmer well. If the farmers are served well, the consumers are served well.
I do not see that there has been provided significant justification for a change in that situation, given the considerations involved. So I say to you, Mr. Speaker, not from a position of erudition but of concern, that this is not a piece of legislation which should be passed by one o'clock tonight. I hope that it will be given months of consideration by all of the interested parties, consideration of the interests of Canadians generally, farmers specifically, our role in the world and the interest which we should have as Canadians to ensure fairness not only within our own country but internationally. This would ensure the maintenance of the germplasm so necessary for securing our future and the availability of food, and that nothing will restrict the amount or the availability of the germplasm pool. This is really the common heritage of all of us and not that of Shell, Sandoz or any of those other big guys on the other side of our southern borders.

Mr. Speaker, following the thoughtful intervention of the Member for Lambton-Middlesex (Mr. Ferguson) and the Member for Windsor-Lake St. Clair (Mr. McCurdy), it makes me wonder whether there is much that can be added to what has already been put on the record.
On the other hand, some points have to be stressed again, and perhaps some new territory has to be covered. It seems to me that with this plant breeders' rights Bill we are debating what could be described as the heart of
June 27, 1989

the concept of sustainable development, particularly as it affects certain parts of the world.
Once again, this Conservative Government has succeeded in not practising what it preaches. Alas, this measure reveals also the limited understanding on the part of this Conservative Government of global environmental and developmental issues. It is a very distressing conclusion that one has to arrive at, after learning by way of a very interesting process, the implications of this plant breeders' rights Bill. It has certainly been quite a learning experience for me. It seems that a background picture needs to be given in order to appreciate the implications of this Bill.
The genetic resources essential to world agriculture- and I am heavily drawing from material prepared by genetic resources of our world organization-are increasingly controlled by multinational corporations. New crops are developed for economic reasons, including higher yields, uniformity, stability and ease of transportation, at the time and expense of public objectives, including nutrition, environmental protection, Third World development, as others have already stressed, and the protection and preservation of smaller-scale farming.
The new varieties are genetically uniform and therefore susceptible to wipe-out by disease or bad weather. The original varieties are disappearing, resulting in a dangerous depletion of the gene pool, to which the Member for Windsor-Lake St. Clair just referred.
What Bill C-15 seems to be doing, if it is implemented, is to reinforce monoculture, chemical agriculture and finally, private control of this precious public resource which is called seed. Plain, important, vital seed. To increase funding to Canada's world-class plant breeding program within Agriculture Canada and the Canadian universities to ensure a truly Canadian response to the environmental and food scarcity problems facing the world today is the objective we would like to see translated by this Bill. However, we do not see it. With the plant breeders' rights legislation, knowledge becomes an industrial secret and research becomes accountable to corporate interests and to considerations related to profit-making. That is not the way to go. In detail, the measure would lead to the use of more pesticides in food and agriculture. In the 1988 edition of
Plant Breeders' Rights
The Economist-l do not know which month exactly-it reported and I quote:
Chemical companies have spent $10 billion or so in as many years buying up seed companies worldwide -
It lists companies such as Pioneer Hi-Bred, Sandoz, Dekalb-Pfizer, Upjohn, Limagrain, Shell Oil, ICI, Ciba-Geigy, Orson and Cargill as the world's 10 largest companies in the business of seed. Seven of these 10 companies are also involved in crop chemicals. That is the important linkage which one has to keep in mind in order to understand the implication and the impact of this measure. At least six of these companies already sell seeds in Canada.
If the plant breeders' rights proposal Bill becomes law, then the trend will escalate. More than 50 per cent of seed research and development within private industry is focused on building the tolerance of new seed varieties to higher and higher concentrations of agricultural chemicals produced by these same companies. That is where the interesting link emerges. Canadian farmers will most likely be forced to bear the cost of seed royalties as well as increased input costs. The increased cost of food production will of course eventually be passed on to Canadian consumers who have already stated loud and clear that they do not want harmful chemicals in their food. Currently there are 4,000 registered commercial and restricted pesticides on the market in Canada.
The second impact of this proposed legislation would be to limit sustainable agriculture. Many farmers see organic farming as being one way to reduce the effects of the current financial and environmental crises facing Canadian agriculture. Fewer inputs are needed in organic farming and costs are much lower. Net income is often much higher in organic farming then in conventional chemical food production. The health of consumers, of the environment, of livestock and of family farm members is, of course, better protected through organic farming. We have seen on The Journal in recent weeks of a farmer who, because of the use of pesticides over a period of time, incurred a form of lymphoma.
If plant breeders' rights are adopted in Canada, organic farmers and converting farmers will not be able to get the seed varieties they need, varieties that are not

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
dependent on pesticides and fertilizers to grow well. That is where the crux of the matter lies.
In addition, there is the decline of the gene pool which has been so well covered by those who have spoken before me. It is important to know that when seed companies develop a successful variety, it becomes a dominating seed on the market, but new varieties, I am told, typically rest on a narrow genetic base. The seeds are genetically uniform. Thus if one plant is damaged by disease, pests or bad weather, the entire crop is likely to be affected, creating widespread destruction or even a world-wide catastrophe. When a variety proves susceptible to a particular threat, breeders' usually go back to more robust, traditional varieties in order to find the genetic material they need to overcome the difficulty. According to some estimates, we have already lost over 50 per cent of the world's major traditional agricultural crops.
The danger to the gene pool is particularly great in the Third World where many of the world's centres of genetic diversity are located. Traditional crops face a triple threat of war, environmental degradation and replacement by the same genetically uniform varieties developed and used in industrial nations. We have no idea what genetic material is being destroyed or of its value to future generations. If environmental conditions change through the greenhouse effect, for example, hardy traditional varieties will be essential to breeding new varieties which can adapt to the new conditions.
Some of the threatened genetic resources from Third World countries are now stored in seed banks located in the industrial countries. However, the integrity of these collections is by no means assured, given inadequate funding and the trend toward privatization in the hands of multinationals. For instance, I am told that the repository at Cambridge University is now the property of Unilever.
The impact on the Third World can be summarized by saying that the crops developed by the multinational seed companies are designed to be grown with capital and technology-intensive farming techniques. In Canada this encourages the decline of the family farm in some cases. In the Third World, it exacerbates economic injustice as large land-holders drive peasants off their small plots of land. Third World countries develop
massive debts and balance of payments deficits as the cost of imported agricultural seeds, machinery and chemicals rises much faster than the export price of the crops produced.
It is particularly ironic that the Third World must now buy seeds from the north since the genetic resources on which these seeds are based were taken mostly from the Third World without compensation. Therefore, it would be much better if this Bill were to be withdrawn and Canada were to join in the international debate without committing itself to any single system, especially when these decisions impact so heavily on the economies and the people of the Third World. The changes being considered could also render Third World germplasm subject to patents in the north and additional royalty payments could equal 10 per cent of the total Third World debt per annum.
In response to corporate moves like plant breeders' rights in the industrialized world, the United Nations Food and Agriculture Organization is currently reviewing its commission on plant genetic resources and is considering farmers' rights, supplying intellectual property rights for Third World farmers, which could profoundly affect Canada's access to its major source of breeding stock in the future.
It may be fairly said that this is the first time the House of Commons is dealing with life patenting. While the Bill is of course limited to plants, the legislation also pledges Canada to participate in the International Union for the Protection of Variety of Plants. It has already announced that it would alter its system in order to allow member states to accommodate wider forms of life patenting including the patenting of specific genes and of livestock.
Finally, the issue that really brings us to our feet is the matter of exclusive monopoly. The notion of plant breeders' rights goes well beyond offering an opportunity for a return on costly breeding investments through royalty payments. The plant breeders' rights as envisaged in this Bill grants exclusive monopoly over access to a plant variety. The plant breeders' rights in countries where it has been adopted has increased crop genetic uniformity, reduced the quality of innovations in plant breeding and allowed corporate power to become even more concentrated. That is something that we Liberals do not like to see happening.

The problem is that our market is small, much of it is dominated by multinational corporations owned abroad. Effective research and development requires a significant scale of operations. The principal beneficiaries of monopoly rights of plants in Canada are likely to be multinational corporations. This is certainly the case that we have seen with industrial patents. We know that multinational corporations have the resources and the experience to begin claiming breeders' rights immediately and to control the claims of less well-endowed rivals.
With the shift from the public sector to the private sector, another consequence would be that the open exchange of scientific information will be curbed in the interest of commercial secrecy.
In conclusion, plant breeders' rights is a consequence of the development that was set in motion by the Free Trade Agreement. I will be glad to expand on that point at the next opportunity.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise tonight to speak on this Bill. I take it that it is so important a part of the Government's agenda that it invokes closure on such a Bill.
This Bill is much more than an agricultural Bill. Many more people other than farmers are concerned about plant breeders' rights legislation. It concerns all who are concerned with the increasing concentration of power with multinational corporations. It also concerns all of us who are concerned with Canada's food system and the world's food system. That means all of us.
My criticisms of this Bill are based on many things. It is an insidious Bill. The issues are economic, ethical, social, political, moral, and ecological. For tonight's address, I am going to concentrate on three areas. First, I am going to talk about the environmental concerns, then my concerns about the corporate concentration aspects, and finally the international development aspects of the Bill. I hope by then to bring it all together. Although I make each of those three categories distinct for the purposes of my address tonight, they are all interlinked.
First, I will address the environmental concerns. We have heard much from scientific experts, particularly those on the environment committee of the Royal Society about the dangers of mono-cropping. This Bill is pushed by large multinational corporations, those U.S. agri-business firms that have developed mono-cropping
Plant Breeders' Rights
to the state of a high art. They are the ones that are behind this. The environmental degradation that goes along with mono-cropping is well known. The vulnerability that exists through mono-cropping is also well known. Yet, the Bill, because of corporate concentration, will encourage mono-cropping.
Not only do we suffer from environmental vulnerability, but financial vulnerability. As many farmers know, if they have only one crop which is devastated then they are out of luck and do not have anything on which to fall back. We have seen this in North America, and we have also seen it overseas where a farmer has only one crop and it is devastated by pests or blight, and then the farmer is out of business for that year.
We must also be aware of the environmental concerns because of genetic manipulation of seeds. Seeds could be manipulated so that they are dependent upon a particular type of pesticide or will respond only to a particular type of fertilizer. Although we have been assured that no corporation would ever do that, there are enough of us who are sceptical about those assurances that we should reconsider this Bill.
The Bill has a history. This is the fourth time that plant breeders' rights legislation has been brought before the House, and it looks like this one will be successful. We must understand the motivation of why now? Why is this legislation being brought in now? Similar legislation was brought before the House in 1980, but it did not get past second reading. In January, 1988 it died on the Order Paper.
We have to understand that the timing is important. Although Members opposite get tired of us talking about the Free Trade Agreement, it is important for us to understand that the U.S. Government has openly argued that food products should be patentable. It has asked Norway for example, to patent food as well as pharmaceutical products. It is all part of the right wing agenda that we have witnessed over the past year. We saw it with the Drug Patent Act last year, and now it is plant breeders' rights. The free trade agenda is implicit in this legislation. It is through the Government's willingness and lying down in the face of U.S. pressure that it has decided to invoke closure on this plant breeders' rights legislation. This brings me to the corporate concentration. It is the U.S. agenda that we are following here, let us be clear about that. This Bill sets a precedent in life patenting, as my colleagues have pointed out. This Bill has an insidious nature. Although it has been put across

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
as an agricultural Bill, as something that we should not worry about, it is much more than that.
Think of what it means to set a precedent for patenting life, Mr. Speaker. Think of where we are going. Think about the path upon which we are embarking and what it means.
Under European and American plant breeders' rights legislation 90 per cent of seed patents are held by a handful of multinationals. After the year 2000, it is forecast that from 10 to 20 major corporations will dominate the seed markets. That does not give me any reassurance since what we are doing is inviting a monopoly situation in terms of controlling not just our food supply but the food supply of the world. I do not like to have large multinational corporations having any more control of my life than they already do.
The type of corporate concentration we have seen in the early months of the Free Trade Agreement will only increase with the passing of this legislation. This legislation should be reconsidered. We should take a long hard look at where we are going, not only in terms of environmental concerns but in our concerns of the path we are going down on life patenting. We are giving over the control of our food supplies to those multinationals which have not exactly shown the kind of sensitivity to the needs of ordinary human beings, whether they be here in Canada or elsewhere in the world.
There is more to this measure than the bottom line. This is where the moral questions come in. I
I would like to address my final comments to the international aspects of this Bill. Although Europe and North America were the first to patent genes, the genetic base for major crops originated in what we now call the Third World. Representatives of countries in North America, Europe and the Soviet Union have collected seed in the developing world and brought this germ plasm back home to store in gene banks.
