As one expert in the field has pointed out, it does not thrill Third World countries to think that their genetic diversity, something which they have given to us, is now subject to patent.
I visited Africa and in particular northern Ethiopia which happens to be where genetic diversity has been so well developed over many centuries. When the Ice Age was occurring, what is now known as Ethiopia was where the seeds were developing. We have taken from that country, or it has given to us freely, and we are now going to be using what they have given to us for profit. The type of vulnerability that is invited by this Bill will hurt us, but it will hurt those developing countries even more.
Large companies are claiming ownership of products which are the result of farmer genius over thousands of years. When I was in Eritrea, in northern Ethiopia, visiting agricultural research farms, I saw the benefit of the genius about which this article speaks. The farmers of that country have a great respect for their land and for the fact that crops must be diversified. They do not believe in mono-cropping or laying out by the hundreds of acres any one crop. Diversification is practised in order to regenerate the land. This is the same lesson that scientists from the Royal Society have been telling us. Yet this legislation pushes us away from that way of doing things.
As a developed country, we have the responsibility to stand fast in opposition to this legislation. The green revolution promised increased food production in the Third World through high yield wheat and rice varieties and the ingredients of modem agriculture. However, the green revolution has failed those countries. We have to go back and learn from their expertise and not be so ethnocentric as to think we know it all. I think that I have enough humility to know that I do not know it all. I just hope that Members opposite in the government ranks will take a little humility and recognize that they do not know it all either.
The crops that are mono-cropped are more vulnerable to total and widespread failure if faced with less than favourable conditions. That is one of the environmental concerns about which we have been talking. Not just the environment suffers, but the ability to feed ourselves is lost.
Canada has an important role to play. We should be standing fast in opposition to this type of legislation for environmental reasons and because of the resistance to corporate concentration, which is certainly not in our interests, and because of our role in international development. Canada has an integral place in the global village. It is the only developed country other than
June 27, 1989

Austria, Finland, Norway and Greece not to adopt plant breeders' rights. We must stand firm against privatization and corporate control, control over the world's food system. That is what we are talking about here. Such control over the world's food system will bring long-term dependence. Dependence on whom? The large multinational corporations. It will bring vulnerability both economically and financially, as well as political instability, not just for the less developed nations but for us. This is a global village. Canada has a role to play as the conscience of the developed world.
I ask that this Bill be reconsidered in that light.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to participate in this one-sided debate on Bill C-15, a Bill which introduces plant breeders' rights to Canada for the first time. As often is the case, this Bill has been and will spark much heated debate within farm groups, church groups, political parties, provincial governments and even labour unions. This Bill has economic, social and moral implications which have not been adequately addressed. With closure having been invoked this evening, those issues will not now be adequately addressed. Therefore this important Bill will be vehemently opposed by many of our citizens who are disillusioned with the way this Government is addressing their legitimate concerns.
On the surface, the idea of plant breeders' rights makes sense. If an inventor designs a new or an improved type of machine, his time, expense and effort are recognized. The inventor patents his invention. He sells the rights to manufacture his invention to other people, if he chooses not to do so himself, and he collects royalties on the sales of his creation. He is rewarded. His rewards spur others on to develop new advances in a broad spectrum of endeavours.
An author is similarly rewarded, if the product of his pen results in sales, whether great or small.
It is well recognized in our society that people will be rewarded for their labour. Canada has never had this system extended to cover the development of new distinctive living organisms. The development of new plant varieties has always been carried out by Government and universities for the public good and the advancement of plant science. These two agencies have
Plant Breeders' Rights
been quite successful in developing improved plant varieties which are suited to the regions of Canada where special types of seed are needed because of our relatively short growing season. It can be said with certainty that the development of the Marquis variety of wheat by a plant breeder in our Department of Agriculture resulted, to a large degree, in the settlement of the Canadian West.
The development of new varieties of rapeseed, hybrid com, soya beans and potatoes have greatly benefited regions of Canada, and have greatly benefited our farmers and consumers.
Most of our important agriculture crops are subject to variety registration by Agriculture Canada under the Seeds Act of 1923. The Seeds Act covers crop varieties that are made, sold, advertised or imported into Canada. The Seeds Act ensures that inferior varieties, the role of which would be detrimental to Canadian agriculture, do not enter the Canadian market while desirable new varieties can be approved for sale or importation.
Now the Government, with the introduction of this Bill, is extending the opportunity of developing new plant varieties to the private sector who, if their developments qualify under the Seeds Act, would be able to collect royalties for a period of up to 18 years.
The question is: Will the federal Government withdraw its support from Agriculture Canada once the private sector expands its efforts in developing new plant varieties?
Of course, the Government says that it would never do that. But this is the same Government that said during the election campaign of last year that regional development programs would not be affected by free trade. There will be tremendous pressure on any government that is dealing with a large deficit to withdraw from competing with private industry in a duplicating operation, especially if the private industry we are talking about are multinational corporations.
Therefore, there will be pressure from within and without for government to get out of the plant breeding business. The chance is very great that government research will become merely a back-up to private industry rather than a competitor, as has happened in other

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
countries like the United States, that have similar legislation.
Also in the initial stages of private industry entering the plant breeding field, the Government will lose many of its top scientists as the multinationals lure them away with large salaries and other inducements.
I would like to believe the Government when it says it will not abandon the field, but I would rest easier if it were embodied in this legislation so that it cannot abandon Canada's commitment in plant breeding that we have had for over a century.
Second, there is absolutely no commitment to fair play to developing countries where, astonishingly, all of the world's major food crops originated. These developing countries have given freely to us in the industrialized world their rich supply of germplasm for crop variety breeding.
We in the industrialized world are almost devoid of primitive or wild seed supply from which we can tap the strong genetic material needed to develop new strains of seeds. The source of that raw material is diminishing as developing countries copy our mono-culture practices.
What we have been doing for the past number of years is collecting the raw material, the genetic material we need to develop new plant varieties from the developing countries and banking them in temperature controlled gene banks. This ensures our supply of raw material while we encourage the source countries to follow our practice of mono-culture and the larger production which results, while decreasing the growing areas of their wild seeds. What must be incorporated in this Bill is an amendment which prevents these gene banks from falling into the hands of the multinationals. If new large companies gain control and ownership over the genetic supply of raw material, as they are beginning to do in the United States, then we will all, here and in the Third World, be totally dependent on the goodwill of these corporations for our food supply.
Corporations do not have a conscience and if they control seed, fertilizer and pesticide production in one company it will spell disaster, especially for developing countries.
Therefore, vigorous public sector breeding programs and government controlled gene banks are absolutely necessary in preventing monopoly control of plant breeding in Canada. Granted, Canada will have access to varieties of plants from other countries which may have a positive impact on our economy, and Canadians will be able to be rewarded monetarily when our new varieties are exported to other countries. This is not happening now. We are exporting our progress in plant development for nothing.
But there is one thing that will happen for sure, the price of seeds will rise higher than the inflation rate. Farmers will be forced to pay the higher costs or risk being left behind when new high volume crop varieties are developed. This has already happened in the United States since plant breeder legislation has been adopted.
Finally, with the new technologies now being applied to the breeding of new plant varieties and indeed in creating new types animal life, perhaps Canada should defer this legislation in order to have it conform to the results of the UN study on the world-wide implications of plant breeding which is now under way.

speakeroldname: Mr. Peter Milliken (Kingston and the Islands):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it gives me great pleasure to speak tonight on Bill C-15, an Act respecting plant breeders' rights.
Several speeches have already been made on this subject tonight and I hope that I will be able to say something of general interest to Members to convince them, especially the Government Members, to vote against this Bill.

One thing we are labouring under tonight is a closure motion. I could not go on with the Bill without expressing my distaste at the activities of the Government in invoking closure again tonight. This is the seventh occasion in this Parliament that the Government has chosen to use closure to cut off debate on its legislation. No other Government in the history of this country has used closure so frequently as this Government. Frankly, it is a disgraceful performance. The Government is obviously fearful of bringing its legislation before Parliament and having it exposed to the light of public scrutiny.
June 27, 1989

If I had introduced legislation of the kind the Government has, I would be embarrassed as well.
It seems to be a persistent practice on the part of the Government to move closure at the earliest possible opportunity. This Bill has been debated part of one day, for two and a half hours, prior to tonight's sitting. Tonight the Government introduced closure on this Bill. It did the same thing last night and the same thing on five occasions prior to that. It is becoming a disgraceful habit.
I want to read the words I quoted in the House on December 16, 1988, when I quoted the former Member for Yukon, who said in 1964:
The procedure of closure has been repugnant to the sense of fair play to the Canadian people. My own personal view is that never in Parliamentary debate should there be a muzzling of free debate.
Tonight we are seeing a muzzling of free debate. I submit the Government is ashamed of the Bill. It is ashamed of most of the Bills it has introduced. It is invoking the closure rule to cut off debate and limit it so the public will not hear about the evils of the proposals it is putting before Parliament. It is time the Government discontinued this practice and made a promise to discontinue its use in the future.
I am not seeking to blame the Government for all the evils of this Bill. I think that perhaps it is the result of some misguiding on the part of the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Mazankowski). He made a credible speech in the introduction of the Bill a few weeks ago. I do not think he took an unduly vigorous approach in supporting it. I can understand why, because he must have some doubts about some of the items proposed in the Bill.
The Bill will allow companies and individuals to patent new seed developments. As plant breeders develop new strains or varieties of seed, they will be able to protect those varieties by a patenting process similar to the patent that is given in the development of new business techniques or instruments of production. I
I suggest that this control given to seed companies will lead to a control that can be extended to the whole food production cycle. Let me give some examples to explain why I feel it will lead to the control of the production cycle, not just in Canada but on a world-wide basis. That is a major reason for our concern tonight. If we give away the control of the production of the seeds, which in
Plant Breeders' Rights
effect we will do under this Bill, the thin edge of the wedge is in and there is potential for control on a much wider scale of the food production industry of the world.
Hybrid seeds are perhaps the easiest example and so I would like to talk about them for a minute. I want to make it perfectly clear to you, Mr. Speaker, and to all Hon. Members, that I do not claim to be an expert on this matter. I am not a farmer and I am not the son of a farmer, nor am I a seed producer or the son of a seed producer. I am not an expert on these matters at all but I have done some reading on this subject and it has caused me great concern.
Hybrid seeds are produced by the crossing of plants which breed on themselves. In other words, they do not require cross-pollination to produce seeds. The hybrid seed that is the result of the cross-breeding of these two types of plants will result in the growth of a plant that often possesses the best characteristics of the two parent plants. The result of that is that the hybrid seed will normally produce a plant that grows twice as fast.
As a gardener, I have grown things like broccoli and I will use broccoli as an example, because Members will understand that. There are hybrid broccoli plants available and non-hybrid plants. The advantage of the hybrid is that it usually grows faster and usually produces larger heads of broccoli than the non-hybrid plant. The disadvantage of the hybrid plant in normal, everyday parlance is that it does not itself produce seeds that reproduce its strong characteristic. If it produces seeds, they fall back to a weaker plant which will not produce as large heads and will not produce as vigorous growth as would the hybrid parent, if there were such a thing. So you need to keep crossing the two in-bred plants in order to produce the hybrid.
If one of these companies patents its hybrid it will retain the right either to produce the seed exclusively or to licence out the production. In other words, the production of the hybrid seed will be the property of the owner of the plant breeders' right, as it were, in this product.
What is the risk of this? Let us suppose there is one strain of broccoli that becomes the leading hybrid strain and it is sold on a world-wide basis and most growers of broccoli grow this particular strain produced by Company A and its licensed affiliates. The sale of the seed is

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
obviously then controlled by the patentee, the person who has the plant breeders' right on that seed.
If in a particular year that company were unscrupulous enough to withhold all its seed and refuse to sell any of its seed, clearly the world production of broccoli would drop off substantially, presumably in quality and certainly in quantity. This is because there would not be many other seeds around. If there were one dominant brand, people would not be producing other seeds. Also, the other seeds would be for lesser quality plants of broccoli. One can well imagine, therefore, that the price of broccoli on a world-wide basis would substantially increase by virtue of the operation of the law of supply and demand.
Let us look at what would happen the next year. The company has a great supply of hybrid seeds that it has been building up. It did not sell any the previous season. The price of broccoli has skyrocketed. It is clear that the price of the seeds it is offering for sale would then follow suit and skyrocket. I do not hold the grudge against large multinational companies which my friends in the New Democratic Party obviously do, I do not say that everything they do ipso facto is bad. However, we face the risk that an unscrupulous company might control the production of a particular seed for its own profit advantage at the expense of other people. I am also not a believer in the completely free market concept that is espoused by some of my hon. friends opposite. I think they realize their mistake in adopting that position, at least I hope they do.
The other difficulty is that if we agree to this Bill we become part of an expanding world-wide network controlling the production of seeds because most of the other industrialized nations have already adopted legislation similar to this legislation and they are now part of this expanding network. I suggest that if we avoid joining in this particular network we will not suffer any disadvantage. Indeed, a suggestion was made by the Minister that if we did not join we would not then get seeds that are available elsewhere. However, I have never heard anyone suggest any variety or type of seed which is available elsewhere and not available here because of the lack of plant breeders' rights rules. I tell Hon. Members opposite that before I could possibly be persuaded to vote for
a Bill of this kind I would want some very firm evidence that its non-adoption would be substantially detrimental to the interests of our country because I have seen no such evidence. I suggest there is no such evidence.
The second reason for looking at this Bill with great skepticism, and indeed rejecting it at this point, is the fact that many of the new strains of seeds being developed today-and I am going away from hybrids and talking about almost any seed or plant that is developed-is developed by large multinational companies which also produce chemicals and pesticides. It is clear that those companies would find it to their advantage to produce seeds that grow better when they are subjected to extensive spray from pesticides or other types of pest controls and/or fertilizers.
The production of the fertilizers and the pesticides is done by these companies for the purpose of earning a profit. If they could produce a seed or plant that was dependent on their particular kind of fertilizer or their particular kind of pesticide, sales would clearly increase because if they can sell the seed they will sell the chemicals with it.
In my submission the sale of both the seeds and the chemicals constitutes something which is, in my view, undesirable. We have many natural occurring seeds or seeds which have evolved through hundreds of years of use in cultivation by farmers and growers of seeds in various plant stocks. All of those are currently available throughout Canada for our use to the extent that we wish to have them. We do not need to grow particular ones with pesticides or with fertilizers. Those help in the growth, perhaps, but they are not essential. Why we would aim for the development of strains of plants that are fully dependent on particular chemicals is beyond me. Yet that could be one of the effects, and I suggest that it will be, of the adoption of Bill C-15.1 urge Hon. Members to look at that very carefully before they vote willy-nilly for this Bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: Has that occurred in the desert countries?
My hon. friend asks whether that has occurred in the desert countries.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:
The 15 countries that have adopted it.
June 27, 1989

No, I do not believe it has happened in the 15 countries that have adopted it because, I suggest to my hon. friend, they have not been able to get control on a world-wide basis at this point and thereby take full advantage of the fact that these seeds are then controlled. However, I will tell him one thing that has happened in those countries as a result of the adoption of this kind of legislation, and that is a very significant reduction in public participation in the development of new seeds through government payments and so on. There has been a significant reduction in many countries. Second, there has been a general takeover by the large multinational companies of the small seed development companies in the countries. That has happened on a regular basis. That is an undisputed fact and I hope that when the Bill goes to committee my hon. friend opposite will get on the committee and hear the evidence of this fact and use it to advantage. It may persuade him to vote against this Bill.
The third reason that we ought to consider rejection of this Bill is that the effect on the Third World I suspect will be ultimately devastating.
I think, Mr. Speaker, you are aware that in times of drought or particular problems in the Third World, the industrialized world ships into that area its seeds, its plants, its products to help get things going again. In other words, there is often the situation where there is a complete dying out or destruction of seed stock in one of the developing countries, and we then fill the gap with seeds that have been developed or produced in some other part of the world. If the parts of the world that become subject to plant breeders' rights end up using a limited variety or a number of strains of seeds, then it will be that limited number of strains that will be sent to the Third World for their use. If they require the use of pesticides or fertilizer for their successful propagation, or if they are ones that are not well suited to their growing conditions, it is going to create additional problems for food production in every part of the world. I
I suggest that the ramifications of this part of the policy have not been fully explored. We need a detailed study on this. The various groups in this country which-have come out against plant breeders' rights have all expressed a very grave concern on this matter. I invite Members to read about and familiarize themselves regarding those concerns because it is an extremely
Plant Breeders' Rights
serious risk. There is no reason today for Canada to join the expanding, if it is any longer expanding, group of industrialized countries which feel that this kind of legislation is helpful. I suggest that the only persons who really benefit from it are the seed companies.
I am not opposed, and I do not believe anyone in this Party is opposed, to seeing that persons who develop new seed strains or varieties are paid on a reasonable basis for their important work and effort, but it is not necessary to adopt patents in order to ensure that some such arrangement be made. There must be another method the Government could explore.
In preparing for this speech, I do not want to suggest that I read everything on plant breeders' rights and did all the work myself. I want to say that I have been assisted greatly in the preparation of my remarks by Rick Munroe who is one of my constituents. He lives on Howe Island, one of the islands in my riding of Kingston and the Islands. He is a farmer there, and he takes a very great interest in this subject, but not through any particular axe to grind or anything of that kind. He is just interested in this issue. He has thought about it, read extensively about it, and has written a few notes, or perhaps you could call them essays on the subject. I would like to refer to some of his ideas. I am not going to quote directly from his writing, but I want to mention some of the things that have caused him concern which I believe will cause concern for Hon. Members if they think about these things before they cast their vote on this Bill.
He indicated to me that 15 years ago the southern com leaf blight threatened the genetically uniform American hybrid com crop. This is a case where there had been a strain of com developed on a hybrid basis that was used extensively throughout the United States. He indicated that the blight was halted by breeding in genetic material from a very rare com variety from Mexico. The question he asks is, if we are going to adopt this plant breeders' rights business and start exporting our seeds abroad and displace the local seeds that are regionally generic, are we then going to destroy those seeds? Are we going to lose the seeds that are generic to a region and replace them with the hybrids that we in fact have developed? If that happens, will we then put these other generic seeds to the point that they are extinct? Will we in fact destroy them and lose the possibility of transferring the genetic material from these rare seeds to our hybrids to save them from this kind of destruction? I do not think that

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
question has been addressed. I do not think it has even been thought of in dealing with this legislation.
Second, he refers to the errors that can occur when one gets into genetic breeding. I see the Hon. Member for Macleod (Mr. Hughes) is here with his cheshire-cat appearance, and I am delighted that he is here because he is very interested in this question. I hope he will vote against this Bill.
The interesting ones that he pointed out as new genetic forms of life were the gypsy moth and the killer bees. He points out that the gypsy moth and the killer bees were introduced quite deliberately by scientists who thought that they knew what they were doing. The mistake was made and these things got out. The Fear is that if we have plant breeders' rights, the plant breeder is liable to make similar mistakes and release a kind of seed or plant that should not be out. If we are going to be rushing through a patent process to get these patents applied for, it may be that there could be errors in the system and that these seeds could be released. We will face the same kinds of problems with these plants as we are facing with killer bees. Maybe we will have killer plants or something that grow up and eat the wheat in the Macleod constituency. I do not know. The risks are there.
I do not in any way make light of them, Mr. Speaker. I think there are risks that ought to be faced by the Government in particular as it considers whether to proceed with this Bill. I
I know, Mr. Speaker, you will realize notwithstanding my comments at the outset dealing with the deplorable use of closure in this case, I have not sought to be partisan in my dealings with this Bill. What I am trying to do is persuade the Hon. Members who support the Government to urge their Ministers of Agriculture- there are three of them for Heaven's sake-to take another look at this legislation and see if they cannot do something to stop it or slow its progress so we can have a long, hard look at the proposals and hopefully reject it.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I regret that the Hon. Member's time has expired. On a point of order the Hon. Member for York South-Weston (Mr. Nun-ziata).
Mr. Speaker, I think if you seek it, you will find unanimous consent for my friend and colleague from Kingston to continue with his excellent remarks.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Is there unanimous consent?
Agreed.
No.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad for the chance to speak tonight against Bill C-15, an Act respecting plant breeders' rights. The problem with the Bill is that like some of the Members across the way who keep shouting, it does not respect anyone else's rights. TTie Bill respects the rights only of the plant breeders and wants to push them to the exclusion of all other rights except to the extent that plant breeders are taken over by the chemical companies. That is why we in the New Democratic Party oppose it.
Our principle is a democratic socialist principle that production should be carried on to meet the individual and social needs of people and not primarily for profit. That is why we maintain that it is necessary to curb and control and sometimes even put monopolies directly under democratic public control. In fact what we want to do is democratize the economy. Of course that brings us into collision with the Members opposite whose respect for democracy is so little that they are using closure three times within a week because they do not have the patience to debate the subject when they are sure that they can just hammer it through with their majority.
In other words, their principle is, let the monopolies control. Since the monopolies control their Party through the Business Council on National Issues, naturally they are saying: "Let the monopolies control this country".
This debate is very much like the debate of a year or two ago about the patenting of prescription drugs in which the same Party, the same Government, insisted that the drug monopolies should be allowed bigger profits through patenting than they were already getting.
June 27, 1989

They promised all kinds of jobs in return for that, but they would not guarantee it, nor would they make that a condition of receiving the profits. Profits were guaranteed and the jobs we can whistle for.
What this legislation wants to do is to patent life forms or to enable those who have the fortunes, the wealth to do research to own life forms and the use of life forms through their patents. This will mean that not only will certain plants become the property or the seed of those plants become the property of a few, but according to the people who are engaged in it, such as the Unionfor Protection for New Varieties of Plants, they will alter their plans to accommodate some aspects of biotechnology, possibly including livestock patenting. In other words, there is no boundary when we get into this field strictly between patenting of plant forms and patenting of animal forms. Nor is there a boundary between the patenting of animal forms and the patenting of human forms. These people are willing to lead right on to try to patent and own human beings in a way that the slave holders of past time never dreamed was possible.
In other words, it is a system of enslavement that these people are pursuing. One of the earliest results of it will be a sharp rise in the cost of seed which will put many farmers in this country and many more farmers in other countries of the world, especially in the south, into a loss position. At present about 4 per cent of the production cost of Canadian wheat is in the seed. Europeans are already spending five times as much but it is predicted that as biotechnical patenting increases, the farmer's share of the cost for the seed and the crop may rise about 50 per cent, 50 per cent of the cost going for seed.
The problem is that these companies producing the seeds are being reduced by takeovers. In the last 20 years there have been over 1,000 corporate takeovers of seed companies. In the 1970s there were about 30 companies that produced crop chemicals. Now there are about a dozen and within a decade the industry predicts there will be only six crop chemical companies. They are the ones which are taking over control of seed production so that in another 10 years or so there may be only 10 or 20 major corporations in the seed market. That is bad news for farmers and it is bad news for people who like to eat. In other words, our eating is going to be controlled by
Plant Breeders' Rights
these seed companies and by the chemical companies that control the seed companies.
Some of this is illustrated in a very good book published this spring called From Land to Mouth by Brewster Kneen. It is a study on the food system. He points out some interesting examples. For example, a couple of centuries ago Sri Lanka was self-sufficient in food. When the British Empire came along it wanted Sri Lanka to produce tea rather than the rice and textiles needed. Changes were introduced into the agriculture and now after the British and U.S. changes of bringing in wheat, Sri Lanka is being told to grow things like oil palms for the global market and it is not producing so much of its own food.
A further example he gives is that in the GATT discussions the Canadian representative, the Minister for International Trade (Mr. Crosbie), was not speaking for the ordinary people of Canada, he was speaking primarily for the big trading companies of Canada. They point out also, for example, that under an executive exchange program David Gilmour,a vice-president of Cargill Limited, a Canadian subsidiary of Cargill Incorporated, was on loan from Cargill to Agriculture Canada to assist in drafting agricultural policy for the Conservative Government. Cargill continued to pay his salary when he occupied an office on the top floor of the Carling Building beside the Deputy Minister of Agriculture. In other words, under this Government, Cargill, the great grain company dominating the grain markets of the world, was allowed to dictate Canadian government policy at GATT.
In the past we talked about trade, which means trade between partners. In other words, there is some mutual respect between one trading partner and another. Now the emphasis has shifted to export. It does not matter who the other guy is, push it out at him, push the grain out there, push it to the Soviet Union, to China or to Syria. It is not a matter of partnership anymore. It is just a matter of a one-way street. Now, with plant breeders' rights or so-called intellectual property rights, what we will get is control of world trade and export by the companies which have the wealth to own the patents.
For example, Ciba-Geigy, Bayer, Sandoz from Switzerland, Rhone-Poulenc from France, Cyanamid, Du Pont from the United States, BSAF from Germany and ICI from Britain. The people who are actually growing the food will be working, even half way around the world, for these great companies. The people who grow

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
the food will not set the wages they get nor the prices at which the food is sold. That will be done by these few companies that will try to reach all around the world just for their own profit.
This sort of thing is not all in the future. Mr. Kneen, and I quote from the bottom of page 103, said that in Thailand today farmers are not permitted to grow the native varieties of rice. The Government requires them to grow only the hybrid varieties, the seed of which the farmers have to buy for each crop. In other words, for thousands of years the farmers have been independent and by their own skill were able to maintain themselves and build communities. Now they will, in effect, be employees of some European or North American company from whom they will have to buy the seed every year. They will become totally dependent upon those seed-producing companies.
The problem is that plant breeders' rights are part of an over-all totalitarian approach by the large companies. When some of us were young we joined the Army, sometimes with misgivings-the Canadian Armed Forces, the Army, Navy or the Air Force-because we were told it was necessary to kill in order to stop Hitler's totalitarian push.
Now we are getting totalitarianism of a different sort based on these large companies which want to control not only the land on which people produce food but the food that people eat. It is part of the over-all drive based on the high interest rates and low commodity prices that dominate most of the Third World, most of the nonwhite former colonies of Britain and North America. In those countries high interest rates and low prices for agricultural products are both fixed by the banks primarily of North America and Britain in which the real interest rates for a decade has been far, far higher than it ever was before. The real interest rate to be calculated isthe difference between the London Inter Bank Offer Rate and the annual per cent change of commodity prices.
For example, in 1981 the London bank rate was 16.6 per cent. The commodity change was a negative 15 per cent. The real difference those countries were paying was 32 per cent. The situation went on like that through most of the 1980s. In 1987 the real interest rate which these countries were paying, taking into account the
price differential as well as the bank rate, was about 10 per cent.
For those years from 1981 to 1987 the average actual interest rate being paid by the so-called developing countries was about 15 per cent. No wonder they are in debt. No wonder there are wars as the allies at the banks try to maintain military control in order to get those debts collected.
The problem that we have is an old, old problem, even though there are some new wrinkles to it. It is at least two and one-half thousand years old, as we find if we read the Book of the Prophet Isaiah, Chapter 5, beginning at verse 8. This is a warning to the people nowadays who want to do as they did then and simply take over other people's land.
"Woe to those who join house to house, who add field to field, until there is no more room, and you are made to dwell alone in the midst of the land. The Lord of Hosts has sworn in my hearing, surely many houses shall be desolate, large and beautiful houses without inhabitant."
That, of course, was the Jewish Scripture. It comes in very strongly into what we call the New Testament, the Christian Scripture, in the letter of James, Chapter 5.
"Come now, you rich, weep and howl for the miseries that are coming upon you. Your riches have rotted. Your garments are moth eaten. Your gold and silver have rusted and their rust will be evidence against you, and will eat your flesh like fire. You have laid up treasure for these last days. Behold, the wages of the labourers who have mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud. Cry out, and the cries of the harvesters have reached the ears of the Lord of Hosts. You have lived on earth in luxury and in pleasure. You have fattened your hearts in a day of slaughter. You have condemned. You have killed the righteous one and he does not resist you."
If we go the way of this plant breeders' rights law, that is what we are asking for: Destruction.

Mr. Speaker, at some risk, if I were to take seriously the remarks of the previous speaker, I have decided to participate in this debate. I frankly have succumbed to the temptation because I am simply sick
June 27, 1989

and tired of hearing the twaddle and the nonsense coming from the side opposite.
The fact is that the merits of plant breeders' rights have been debated here and elsewhere, off and on for many years. The suggestion that this legislation has not been adequately discussed is ludicrous.
What we are talking about tonight is simply referring the matter to a legislative committee in order that there can be some hearings and the Bill studied in some detail, and back to the House it comes again.
I believe that the time has come for serious consideration and the passage of the legislation. Plant breeders' rights legislation-I am going to call it PBR from now on in the interests of time-is in place in 18 countries in the world.
In fact, Canada is the only major agricultural nation which does not have such legislation. To listen to opponents of this Bill, one would think otherwise, that plant breeders' rights was something new, something unusual and something from outer space. We are talking about killer plants, Mr. Speaker. Maybe we are going to have killer plants which eat Members with red ties. I do not know, it is possible. However, the facts show otherwise.
Why PBR? The intent clearly is to enable plant breeders to collect reasonable royalties for new and distinct varieties which they develop through research. Breeding new varieties is expensive. It costs money. It is a matter of economics and a matter of simple equity that successful plant breeders should receive the return on their investment of time, of expertise and indeed, of money.
The royalties will encourage private sector plant breeders to increase their research activities. Public sector research will also be enhanced by the royalties which will be ploughed back into further public sector research. The result clearly should be an increase overall in research in this country.
In Canada right now, I believe that we need new varieties which will improve yields and which may be more resistant to pests and diseases. PBR will enable us to have improved and expeditious access to these new varieties.
Plant Breeders' Rights
Bill C-15 will also allow for the injection of higher quality foreign varieties which are adaptable to the Canadian environment. In the absence of PBR, breeders outside of this country are hesitant to market their new varieties here because their product has no legal protection. Canadian farmers are not able to gain access to certain protected varieties which are popular in the rest of the world. This could present a problem to our exporters who find themselves unable to produce the protected varieties which are in demand in some world markets.
Clearly, Bill C-15 will create new opportunities for the export of many excellent Canadian varieties. Without PBR, Canadian breeders may be unwilling to introduce new varieties on which they have spent considerable time and money.
The over-all impact of this legislation will be to strengthen the base for plant breeders in Canada. In the result, the entire agricultural industry in Canada will be strengthened. My Province of Saskatchewan, and my constituency in particular, are heavily dependent on agriculture. PBR will be good for the Saskatchewan food and agriculture industry and that is why I support this legislation. It is also the reason why I hope that my socialist colleagues in the Province of Saskatchewan will see fit to cast aside their philosophical opposition to this much needed legislation.
It is instructive at this point to look at the situation in other nations, the impact of PBR elsewhere. The United Kingdom provides an excellent example. Since their legislation back in 1964, the U.K. has seen a tremendous growth in productivity which has dramatically converted it from being a net importer of cereals in the 1960s to being a net exporter in the 1980s. As much of this growth relates to the improved varieties as it does to improved husbandry and to other increased inputs, the quality has improved as well as the quantity.
British crop varieties are now exported throughout the world. Wheat into Europe. Barley, into New Zealand and Spain, roses and top fruit root stocks, into growers world-wide. As of last year, the British industry, I am told, was comprised of some 52 plant breeders and agents for foreign breeders. The participants range from publicly funded institutes to small private companies, to divisions of multinationals. Dire consequences of multinational take-overs are nowhere to be seen.

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
If the U.K. has been able to reap these benefits from PBR, imagine that there are indeed similar advances available to Canada through this legislation. With their knowledge, expertise and creativity, Canadian plant breeders have virtually unlimited opportunities.
At this point I would like to examine some of the opposition to PBR. It appears to me that the Liberals as usual are split. Members have made the halfhearted argument that the 18-year period of exclusivity rights is too long. However, the fact is that the 18-year period complies with the international convention for the protection of new varieties of plants.
If Bill C-15 proposed a seven-year or a ten-year period, we would not be able to satisfy the requirements of that international convention, nor would we be able to enjoy the benefits of reciprocity with the many other nations which are bound by the convention.
Further, 18 years is the maximum period of exclusivity. This right can be terminated sooner in many cases, and probably will be. In fact, Section 6, subsection (2) of the Bill provides for the payment of an annual fee to maintain that right. Under Section 35(l)(c), that right may be revoked for non-payment. Thus, the breeder will only retain protection on a variety if there is a sufficient return to justify payment of the annual fee. If the right is revoked, the variety becomes public property.
We have also heard the concern that Government plant breeding programs will decrease as a result of PBR. The Minister of Agriculture, Mr. Speaker-and I should digress here because I think I heard the Member for Kingston and the Islands (Mr. Milliken) suggest that there was something wrong with there being three Ministers of this Government devoted to agriculture. The fact that there are three Ministers devoted to this area indicates the tremendous importance which the Government of Canada attaches to the agricultural sector.
The Minister of Agriculture reaffirmed recently the commitment of this Government to the maintenance of public sector plant reading research. In this year alone, more than $23 million will be spent by Agriculture Canada on PBR. In the words of the Minister, and I quote: "Agriculture Canada has been in this business. It is in the business and will continue to be in the business".
Our friends in the NDP, of course, are against this Bill, as they are against anything which departs from the status quo. The NDP are misnamed. There is nothing new about them at all. They are against change. They are in fact the arch conservatives in this country. We on this side are the Progressive Conservatives. We on this side see the need for change and the need to move with the times.
While I am digressing on this point, I must say that I was amazed by the comments of the Hon. Member who spoke previously and referred again to the matter of the pharmaceutical patent legislation. I am amazed by the strange attitude displayed by Members opposite relative to innovation, to invention, and to initiative. I recall the remarks made when we were debating Bill C-60 in the previous Parliament, the copyright legislation. At that time, I heard all sorts of sanctimonious mutterings about the imperative to reward artists, musicians, and writers. That is good and that Bill passed.
What I hear from over there is that if we are talking about a song, music, a play, a book or something that is artistic, it should be given all sorts of protection. They want to recognize it and talk about the creative genius of the artist, his remuneration, and recognition. All of that is good, but why on earth would equal treatment not apply to someone who comes up with a new drug for the benefit of mankind or who comes up with a new plant variety which can benefit all of mankind?
Why is it that the inventor, the builder, the creator in a field outside artistic endeavour is someone to be denigrated as members of the Opposition do? All I can say on this topic is that Members of my Party and I say that we should at least afford to plant breeders the same kind of rights and recognition as has been afforded to the artistic community.
The Hon. Member for Mackenzie has warned us of the dire consequences of plant patents. Under this legislation, we are not talking about plant patents or the patenting of any other life form. Bill C-15 deals with plant varieties in an extremely specific way. It proposes a limited right that applies only to the reproductive material of plants. It is the same legislation that is in place in most of the nations with which we trade in seeds and
June 27, 1989

other plant reproductive material such as bulbs, rose bushes, and the like.
Opposition Members try to imply that Bill C-15 would reduce the exchange of genetic information. They conclude that a plant breeder, having discovered a new and distinct variety, would secrete it away and not allow anyone access to it. Surely this legislation will increase, not decrease, the exchange of genetic information.
Indeed, with the current set of circumstances, potential useful foreign varieties are not available to Canadian producers. With the passage and implementation of Bill C-15, there will be an incentive for foreign plant breeders to share these varieties with Canadian producers. There will be a two-way street. Plant breeders will be able to obtain a financial reward for their efforts and the producers will have new production opportunities as well as increased potential for even greater yields plus enhanced protection from pests.
It is for these reasons that Bill C-15 is supported by a great number of farm and horticultural organizations from coast to coast. They include the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, the Canadian Horticultural Council, SeCan Association, the Canadian Seed Growers' Association, the Canadian Seed Trade Association, Flowers Canada, the Canadian Ornamental Plant Foundation, the Canadian Nursery Trades Association, the Western Canadian Wheat Growers' Association, the Agricultural Institute of Canada, the Canada Grains Council, and many more. These organizations and their members are fully cognizant of the opportunities they are currently missing.
At this point, it is important to recognize that there is a second way in which this legislation will encourage the sharing of genetic information. The International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties specifically prohibits the monopolizing of the genetic information in plant varieties. Article 5(3) states that authorization by the breeders shall not be required either for the utilization of the variety as an initial source of variation for the purpose of creating other varieties or for the marketing of such varieties. Bill C-15 is written to conform with this convention. The clear intent of the Bill is that plant breeders will continue to use existing varieties for breeding new varieties.
Plant Breeders' Rights
Another opponent of this legislation is the coalition known as GROW, Genetic Resources for Our World. One of its concerns is that this legislation will result in a dramatic increase in the price of seed. One of the outspoken opponents of the legislation has suggested recently that farmers' seed costs will quadruple. What he fails to mention is that farmers are in no way forced to use new seed varieties. They can continue to use their own seed, for example, which is unaffected by PBR, or they can purchase unprotected varieties. Even for protected seed varieties, it is predicted by experts that the increasing costs will be less than changes caused by supply and demand.
As well, one can assume that competition from foreign and new Canadian varieties is expected to hold down price increases. Moreover, improvements in yield, increased resistance to disease, and other positive improvements in available seed stock will far outweigh any increase in seed prices.
Another point that has to be kept in mind is that if a plant breeder is found to be charging excessive royalties or is intentionally keeping the market short in order to collect higher prices, any individual can apply to the commissioner of plant breeders' rights for a compulsory license which would give the individual the right to produce that variety. This measure ensures that all varieties are made available to the public at reasonable prices.
Of course, those on the far left have been telling anyone prepared to listen that this legislation will lead to takeovers of the industry by those nasty multinational corporations. What they fail to understand is that our seed industry is too large and diverse to be effectively taken over by foreign countries or anyone else. To be a target for takeover, a company has to have a breeding program and or protected varieties. At the present, private sector breeding in Canada is a distant third behind Agriculture Canada and university programs. The possibility of a corporate takeover in the industry is simply out of the question.
Furthermore, as indicated earlier, and I invite opponents of this Bill to examine the situation in the U.K., the legislation has been in place there since 1964. There has been plenty of time for this touted corporate takeover, but it simply has not been the case. An examination of other nations with plant breeders' rights

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
legislation indicates that there are many, many hundreds of concerns that are involved in the process.
The opponents of the Bill, GROW, Friends of the Earth, and the like, have raised the argument that the Bill will allow the large seed companies to breed seeds that are dependent upon specific weed killers. This view fails to take into account the reality that the so-called dependent varieties would have a limited appeal to a producer who has the option to purchase public sector varieties or unprotected varieties. It seems to me just common sense that farmers would also shy away from a variety with high input costs as a result of its dependency upon a specific chemical.
Those in the left wing coalition have also raised the argument that plant breeders' rights will lead to genetic uniformity which will inevitably result in future catastrophes, another potato famine. Once again, they fail to grasp the true essence of the legislation before us.
By providing an incentive for even greater investment in plant breeders' programs, both in the private and public sectors, the chances of increasing genetic diversity are enhanced because only those varieties which are substantially different from other existing varieties will be recognized under plant breeders' legislation.
In closing, I want to say that perhaps the silliest and most revealing argument against plant breeders' rights is that put forward by GROW and others in the coalition that the Bill is somehow linked to the Canada-U.S. Free Trade Agreement. The old free trade bogyman is being dusted off again. The Hon. Member for Etobicoke North, in an unguarded moment, was honest enough to say that every sparrow that falls from the sky will be laid at the feet of the Free Trade Agreement. Here we go with another sparrow.
This legislation has been around in one form or another since 1979. How on earth can it be affected by a 1989 bilateral trade agreement between Canada and the United States? This argument reminds one again of this blind opposition to change, to trade, and to anything new that characterizes the arch-conservatives of Canada, those people in the left wing masquerading as progressive people when in fact they are the most reactionary in this nation.
The Government has great confidence in the people of Canada. We know that with the implementation of Bill C-15, Canadian plant breeders will prosper and so too will producers.
I would like to conclude by saying that there is nothing sinister in the legislation before us. It is a Bill that I believe will increase the level of plant breeding research in Canada, the results of which will enable producers and farmers to stay competitive in a modem world. The legislation does so by providing researchers with an incentive to increase their activities in order to create new varieties with greater yields and enhanced resistance to disease and pests.
Canada is the only major agricultural nation in the world which today lacks legislation of this kind. The time has come for us to get out of the dark ages, get in step, stop talking about PBR, and implement this Bill. Let us get it off to committee where it can be dealt with in some detail. I look forward to the eventual passage and utilization of the Bill for the benefit of all Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to have the opportunity this evening to address Bill C-15, the plant breeders' rights Bill. I have profound and grave concerns about this Bill, although I would like to state at the outset that I believe that plant breeders are entitled to certain rights. My concern relates to the implications of how far this particular Bill goes. Another concern is the greater implications of this Bill which I feel are not being well addressed and are not well known by many people who are debating the Bill and who will be voting upon it this evening and at other times.
My concerns with regard to this Bill relate to various areas. One relates to the environmental issues, moral and ethical issues, food security issues, and how those food security issues impinge upon the well-being of Third World countries that represent the majority of the population of our world.
Through this particular Bill we are favouring multinational corporations. In fact, the multinational corporations that will most benefit from this Bill are companies involved in the production of chemicals. These companies have the funds and the wherewithal to finance the
June 27, 1989

research and development of different seeds. In many cases, they pay for that research themselves.
However, it is well known that in various agricultural colleges, departments of research could not well survive without the funds made available from those companies. Therefore, the independence of research is taken away as research is directed into certain areas. The areas of concern to me are where research and development are put into the production of seeds that are dependent upon the very chemicals that those companies produce. If I were a corporate president whose company produced chemicals, I would love the idea of doing whatever I could to promote the sale of the chemicals. What greater thing could a company think of than having a greater dispersion of its chemicals over the lands all around the world?
In Canada, many farmers who buy the product of producers of seed are not aware of the fact that the seed is so dependent upon the chemicals that must be applied simultaneously with the seed purchased.
In this regard, my experience has been in the Third World. I have had some experience in Africa which has experienced serious drought in the past years. As a member of a committee, I helped to select projects that were to receive Canadian funding for production in Africa. We saw the harmful effects of the seeds that were chemically dependent. It was not only the cost of the seed, but it was the cost of the chemicals, the fertilizers, the insecticides, and the fungicides that had to accompany the particular types of seeds that were being made available and which in the end we did reject despite the grave needs of the area, of which we all know.
The poor people of the world cannot afford the seed, let alone the chemicals upon which those seeds are dependent. It is not only the seeds and the cost of the chemicals themselves, it is the cost of the technology to apply the chemicals. Education and knowledge are required in knowing how to apply those chemicals not only in the correct order and timing, but also safely. I have seen many illnesses develop among poor people who were handling chemicals, who did not have the equipment to apply them safely, and who suffered serious health effects as a result.
In one program in which I was involved in Central America, the program was supported by a northern Government, an aid providing Government through the help of a multinational corporation. Very poor farmers in this country had benefited from a very small land reform program. Landless peasants suddenly had some land.
Plant Breeders' Rights
However, they were given the land on the proviso that that land would be productive.
Those farmers knew how to produce crops for their own self-sufficiency. They could feed themselves with small resources. Instead, those farmers were enticed, with large resources, to move away from the production of self-sufficient and self-sustaining food crops into cash crops for export. They were given many financial and capital resources in order to divert their production into those areas. They were told that they would receive not only the seed and the chemicals, but all the technical assistance necessary in order to produce productive crops that would bring them good cash income.
Many countries in the Third World have been motivated into producing these cash crops. Countries that were self-sufficient in food production are now finding that they experience crop failures for a variety of reasons and that they are now net importers of the food they need to sustain themselves.
What happened with the program to which I was referring was that the farmers took all the resources. They took out loans in order to cover their part of the bargain, so to speak. They received the seed, the chemicals, and the technical expertise. They got their crop off the fields and it was ready for export. This crop was very labour intensive.
At the point when the crop was to be exported, a review was done of the cropping procedure and it was found that, at one point, one application of a chemical was made incorrectly and the crop could not be exported. The poor peasants lost everything. They found themselves without the food they needed to eat because they had been diverted from that type of production into a cash crop for export. They had no cash, they lost their land, and they were deeply in debt.
That example explains one of my concerns about this Bill in that it supports most particularly multinational corporations that will have more and more ability through this Bill to gain control of Canadian breeders and companies that produce.
This Bill has implications as far as getting patents for life form itself. I believe that germplasm is a basic resource for all mankind. It is global resource. It relates very much to world food security in general. There is a profound distinction that must be made between the applying of patents to intellectual property, to technologies of various sorts, and the technology which relates to the very production of food upon which we are all dependent. We have to make a distinction between the various patents which we are approving and making possible. I believe that we must look very carefully at any

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
patent that has an effect on the food security of our world.
When companies are paying and supporting the research of seed that is dependent upon chemicals, there are profound environmental problems as well. The application of chemicals or fertilizers, insecticides and pesticides has a very deleterious effect upon the soils of our land and upon the waters into which they flow. This is producing seed which is vulnerable to epidemic. Again, this is a food security problem of which I feel we must be more aware.
I hope that when this Bill is discussed in committee many of these issues will be addressed and that we will bring before the committee witnesses who can speak much more profoundly than I to the issues I have raised this evening.

Mr. Speaker, of all the debate that we have heard tonight I think the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia (Mr. Wilson) had the most articulate position of any taken this evening. I think he fully described what this Bill will do and what it should do. The bottom line of his position is simply this: it will make a stronger agricultural sector in the country from one end to the other.
That is what this Government has been attempting to do since 1984. It has been attempting to create a strong farming community. This measure is part and parcel of that.
This is evident in some of the figures the Minister of Agriculture has used in some of his speeches over the last number of months. Presently in Canada we have a very strong agricultural sector with only one out of twenty farmers at what we would consider a risk stage as far as finances go. Of all the farmers in the country 60 per cent of them do not need operating loans. The reason for that is very simple. It is because we have
looked after the farming community of Canada, something which we will continue to do.
Farmers are extremely hard working and Canadian farmers in particular are very successful. They provide for their families and their communities. They are really the backbone of the nation. They contribute immensely to our economy and to our society as a whole. We do not want to forget that.
This Bill is very important for me. I come from Atlantic Canada where the climatic conditions are different from the other parts of Canada. What this Bill will do is meet some of the needs of a region such as mine. The geography and the climate of eastern Canada, particularly New Brunswick, are somewhat the same as certain parts of Europe. There are certain strains of grains in Europe, potatoes and other root crops which would prove to be very successful in Atlantic Canada. Those particular crops, if we did have the right to use them in Canada, would make us much more successful in Atlantic Canada.
We have to import a great deal of grain into Atlantic Canada. That is subsidized by the federal Government, as most everyone on both sides of this House will realize. Because it is subsidized it means that Canadian taxpayers are actually paying to put grain into eastern Canada. If we could have access to some of those species which would produce a higher grade and survive some of the climatic conditions we have in Atlantic Canada, we would all be better off. For that reason I believe this legislation is very important.
As a Government we feel very strongly that plant breeders' rights legislation is long overdue in Canada. Not having it has been detrimental to the plant breeding industry in Canada. The Member from Saskatchewan alluded to that fact. It has been very difficult without it for a number of people. It has nothing to do, as the Opposition has attempted to point out, with multinational corporations. The fact of the matter is that all the nations of the world that have used plant breeders' rights do have such legislation. There is a multiplication factor present. In other words, it encourages more businesses to get into the business of plant breeding.
June 27, 1989

The Netherlands, which was one of the first countries to institute such legislation and which did so in 1941, has 983 businesses in plant breeders' genetics. That number has increased significantly every year. It has nothing to do with multinational corporations. There are many small businesses in that area as well.
Denmark and France have the same proportions. The United States in 1970 instituted the same type of legislation. It has 786 companies involved in this area.
We are one of the few industrialized countries in the world that has not gone that route. I feel that it is time that we do so.
Why?

I will answer that question put to me by the Opposition. At the present time it is difficult for Canadian breeders to ensure that their varieties are protected in other countries. It is plain and simple.
In Nova Scotia, a successful plant variety well suited to processing called Shepody was given to McCain's by Agriculture Canada. As you know, Mr. Speaker, McCain's is located in my riding. It is a very important part of my riding. The potato industry is a very important industry in New Brunswick. The company's French office was able to protect that variety under French plant variety protection, thus securing a return on Canada's research investment.
We had to go to another country via the corporation to get protection for that variety. Obviously, it is preferable to pass our own legislation so that we can consistently enter into reciprocity with other nations and not give away our hard work paid for by Canadian tax dollars or private industry. We do not want to give it away.
Similarly, Canadian growers often face problems when trying to import varieties since many foreign plant breeders are reluctant to export their products to Canada, knowing that they are not protected by any comprehensive legislation. This Government understands their concern and knows it is reasonable since a great many varieties of ornamental plants commercially available in Canada have been copied or pirated from foreign plant materials. The horticultural industry in particular needs access to imported varieties, as do potato growers.
In addition, without plant breeders' rights we may not be in a position to face competition from those who have
Plant Breeders' Rights
not bothered to invest time, money and energy in plant research and development, be they foreigners or Canadians. Our breeders must be compensated through royalties for investments of millions of dollars.
Plant breeding costs money-a lot of money. It involves a great amount of risk. As you know, Mr. Speaker, it generally takes 10 years to 15 years to select a variety that can be sold commercially. During that period breeders have to cross numerous plant varieties and produce numerous parent lines. Seed is then obtained and varieties tested. From these hundreds of varieties only a few make it to the market-place. It demands great patience and can be subject to many pitfalls, which is why plant breeders must be compensated through royalties. Profit is not a dirty word, although I guess it is if you are a socialist. However, that is precisely one of the reasons why we need plant breeders' rights. If we have a healthy agricultural society and Canadians are concerned about feeding the hungry of the world, one way to do it is to develop the varieties that can be used to create wealth in this nation. We know that the wealth in our nation is shared by many nations in the world and, in doing so, we can secure a food policy for all the people of this earth. We are not being narrow at all when we are looking at plant breeders' rights. We are looking to the good of humanity, not being selfish.
Absolute nonsense.

We cannot underestimate the importance of plant breeding in Canada, and we will not lose this opportunity to strengthen the agricultural sector.
Let us consider the comments of a former Minister of Agriculture, Eugene Whelan, in 1980, when that Government attempted to bring in its own plant breeders' legislation. Mr. Whelan had this to say about plant breeders' rights:
The basic idea behind any proposed legislation protecting the work of a plant breeder, is to give recognition to the breeder for the work he's done in breeding and introducing a new plant variety. Right now inventors can patent their gimmicks, and writers get royalties on the books they get published. Plant breeders, although they are pretty much the same as authors and inventors, have no way of benefiting from the work they do.
That is a quote from Eugene Whalen, that fellow with the funny green hat. He was not a bad Agriculture Minister after all.

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
Mr. Whelan went on to state:
I'm a strong supporter of our Canadian plant breeders. Their efforts have contributed a great deal to the success of Canadian agriculture today. I want to see them encouraged, and I want to see them get the protection for their work that they deserve.
This legislation will give them the protection for the work they do. They deserve it.
It is surprising to realize the number of people in the House on the opposition side who actually support this legislation. Unfortunately, they are not here tonight. There are a few ragtag renegades from their Party-I am not referring to the Member for Gloucester (Mr. Young) who is a good New Brunswicker. There are a few on that side of the House who support this legislation but they are very silent tonight. I am very pleased with that silence.
It is an historical fact that the settlement of the Canadian West was to a large degree facilitated by the development of a single superior variety of wheat, Marquis, produced in Ottawa by a plant breeder with the federal Department of Agriculture. Members opposite do acknowledge that this was a result of the Canadian Government. It is interesting that they would do so.
Farming has always been crucial to our country and new and improved varieties are the foundation upon which it is built. It is embarrassing to see the role which plant breeders have played in Canada's history when one notes how Canada ommitted itself from the history of plant breeders' rights. The agricultural sector has been waiting for a long time, while other nations passed the legislation they so desire.
In 1923, the Canadian Horticultural Council recommended legislation for plant patents. However, nothing was done at the time. Meanwhile, the Netherlands passed plant breeders' rights in 1941, Germany in 1953, and Denmark in 1962.
By 1961, the International Convention for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants was drawn up among six European nations to promote continuity and the exchange of plant breeding and germplasm. In 1964 the United Kingdom passed its legislation.
In 1970, the United States introduced the Plant Variety Protection Act. France also adopted plant
breeders' rights in 1970, as did Sweden in 1961. During that decade 11 other countries passed similar legislation.
That same year in Canada, the University of Guelph sponsored a conference on plant breeders' rights which was attended by interested organizations. That conference recommended that PBR was essential to our country and that legislation be passed.
In 1972, the Canadian Agricultural Services Co-ordinating Committee agreed that plant breeders' rights would be desirable in Canada. The committee is a broadly based organization with representation from provincial Departments of Agriculture and industry. It also includes deans of agriculture from Canadian universities. That prominent organization asked Agriculture Canada to draft proposals for legislation.
In 1980, Hon. Eugene Whalen who was an ardent supporter of plant breeders' rights, introduced Bill C-22. It was essentially the same Bill that we are introducing, but it died on the Order Paper. In that same year, Australia and Ireland acted and passed its legislation.
In January, 1988, the Hon. John Wise introduced into Parliament a plant breeder's rights Bill, essentially the same as Mr. Whelan's. Again, it was not passed because an election got in the way.
The Government never got around to doing anything.

speakerposition: Minister of State (Privatization and Regulatory Affairs)
speechtext: You were not even here.

Had their not been an election, I am sure the Senate would have held it up like it did with so many other Bills that we introduced which were good for the country but which the Senate obviously did not want to pass. That is what they did with the Free Trade Bill and the Child Care Bill. I am sure they would have done that with the plant breeders' rights Bill if it had passed this House.
Except for some minor legalistic changes, it was the same Bill we are debating today. The agricultural sector is behind us and it is time for the Government to adopt that legislation. It will create an incentive for further development of plant varieties, which we need in Canada.
Plant breeders from Hungary, Japan, Ireland, Sweden, Switzerland and Australia have already gained from breeders' rights legislation in their own countries. We as Canadians can do the same thing.
June 27, 1989

Let Canadian breeders benefit from this proposed legislation too. We know that in order to obtain some return on their varieties, Canadian breeders need reciprocity. Many of their products can sell well elsewhere, but we must act to give them the mechanisms to protect their work domestically and internationally.
Without Bill C-15, our producers are being denied the best varieties from Canadian and foreign sources. The absence of plant breeders' rights legislation leaves Canada out in the cold. Our country and Norway are the only developed nations in the world not to have some sort of mechanism to protect the work of their breeders. We must recognize this fact and move forward with this proposed legislation. I trust that Members of the House will help us do so.

Mr. Speaker, we have been listening to the twisted malinformed ragtag minds of the group who call themselves Progressive Conservatives. It is unfortunate that none of the regressive convertibles have taken the time to read Bill C-15, something that many Canadians would be interested in knowing about. There was only a couple of hours of debate before the Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), who calls himself a western Canadian, and calls himself the Minister of Agriculture, brought in the guillotine, the savage choking off of debate before Canadians know what is really being brought before the House.
This is a very important debate because it is about the privatization of life forms and genetic material for profit. Of course, this is just the second chip. We saw the drug patent legislation brought forward by the so-called Progressive Conservative Party. That was, of course, just a chip in relation to the free trade deal, a piece of legislation which is now known from coast to coast and from north to south in this country to be harmful to Canadian consumers in terms of drug pricing.
The only Tory plank that we have heard in here all evening is that Eugene Whelan liked the idea. If that is the sole foundation of Conservative policy it should be enough for a few of the rank and file on the government side to smell a rat and to vote against it.
Plant Breeders' Rights
Let us have a look at the Bill, Mr. Speaker, something which I am sure no one on the government side has done. They do not want to be confused with facts. Clause 5 says:
Subject to this Act, the holder of the plant breeder's rights respecting a plant variety has the exclusive right
(a) to sell, and produce in Canada for the purpose of selling, propagating material, as such, of the plant variety;
I think there are a lot of Canadians out there who would like to know what that means. Let us go on to Clause 6 which says:
The term of the grant of plant breeder's rights shall, subject to earlier termination pursuant to this Act, be a period of eighteen years,
Now we know what the Act is for and how long the period is. Let us now look at the offence section. It is always interesting to know where Conservatives are coming from. Let us have a look at what would happen to the granny on the Prairies growing daisy seeds, British Columbians on Vancouver Island who are growing some pear trees and have been giving them away or selling them for many years, or New Brunswickers who are producing their own spud varieties, if they wanted to continue selling or propagating seed and were not participating in this new bureaucracy, this massive red tape being proposed by the Conservatives. They can be convicted under a lot of clauses but Clause 53(4) says:
An individual who commits an offence-
