(a)	is liable on summary conviction to a fine of not more than five thousand dollars; or
-if the Minister of Justice decides that he does not like the person particularly-
(b)	is liable on conviction on indictment to a fine of not more than fifteen thousand dollars or to imprisonment for a term not exceeding three years,
So you go to jail for three years and pay a $15,000 fine for giving somebody some asparagus.
Let us have a look at what some people have to say about that. The cart is, as you know, way before the horse, as is always the case, it seems, with this Government which is wandering all over the map in terms of policy.
We know that Canada desperately needs a debate on genetic engineering and biotechnology. I have had it on the Order Paper for more than one Parliament. Does the Government ever take the opportunity to get involved in an important and fundamental debate that this country

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
and many countries around the world need? Not a chance, it wants to privatize and give it all over to their pals the multinationals.
How many Members in this House know that already 10 per cent of world trade is in chemicals, pesticides and herbicides? This comes at a time when Canadians are demanding a change in terms of the products that we collectively eat, chemical and pesticide-free food. For example, in the Province of Quebec a provincial poll was done earlier this year. Twenty-five per cent of the residents of the Province of Quebec want chemical and pesticide-free food.
I know that the Deputy Prime Minister often reads Harrowsmith, one of his favourite publications. An article entitled Profitable Patents reads:
While the proposed patent system appears logical and fair on its face, there are those who believe it to be neither necessary nor desirable from the public's point of view. Plant patents will have one inarguable effect: greater profits for those who sell seed. Holding ironclad rights to a particular new seed gives the marketer a new selling tool, with guaranteed royalties-often 10 per cent of the seed price for the breeder, his sponsor or the organization which has bought the patent.
The prospect of these greater profits, along with a growing awareness of the potential value of good seed in an increasingly hungry world has suddenly lured a number of unlikely corporate players into the seed breeding and marketing arena.
As soon as plant patenting systems were planned and legislated in Europe and the United States in recent years, seed companies began to be snapped up by mega-corporations, often those already having interests in agricultural chemicals and food products. Britain's plant patenting system was instigated in 1964. At about that time Ranks-Hovis-McDougall, one of the "Big Three" in baking and flour milling in the British Isles, purchased scores of agriculture-related businesses.
In his report to company stockholders in January, 1964, the chairman of Ranks said that the corporation had "secured substantial additional interests in business trading directly with farmers and we have been engaged during the year in building up this activity-by the acquisition of further businesses and by strengthening the links between the various companies".
Ranks, incidentally, owns several businesses in Canada, among them Georgian Bay Fruit Growers Ltd. and the Gattuso Corporation, manufacturers of spaghetti and pasta products.
This is a very interesting part, this is why I know that the Deputy Prime Minister read this section of Harrowsmith before he came up with this dire Machiavellian plan
of bringing this in hoping that Canadians would not know that second reading was going on under the threat of closure. The article continues:
Seed patent legislation was the subject of a 40-year controversy in the United States, with critics predicting dire consequences if the law were passed. Nevertheless, on Christmas Eve of 1970, the Plant Variety Protection Act was hurriedly approved in Washington. Bernard Leese of the U.S. Plant Variety Protection Office, now says that it was "rather an expeditious act on the part of Congress- everyone wanted to get home for the holidays".
Also in the Harrowsmith article, which I think is particularly true, under "Transient Politicians" is the following:
What very large corporations want, they generally get. Leonard Silk wrote in a March, 1974 editorial in The New York Times, "The danger is not that corporations will pursue their pecuniary interests-but that they will corrupt and capture the powers of government and transfigure national values and institutions to serve their corporate interests."
It is interesting to note that both Ranks-Hovis-McDougall and Ciba-Geigy were known contributors to the Conservative party in Britain and that party, under Sir Alexander Douglas-Home, was in power when the Plant Varieties and Seeds Bill was passed there in 1964. In Canada, both the Liberal and Conservative Parties have expressed support for plant patents.
We are now starting to get to the interesting material, Mr. Speaker. Let us take a look at what actually happens under the heading "Out with the Old".
It reads:
Public breeders routinely produce standard varieties that are economical for the farmer or gardener. It takes seven or eight breeding generations longer to develop a standard rather than a hybrid tomato, for instance, but after that it is very easy to produce additional seed. Hybrid vigour, the aspect that makes hybrid com so attractive, is more prevalent with some crops than others, and is determined in part by the plant's method of reproduction. While hybrid corn is often markedly more productive, standard tomatoes and peppers may be little different from their hybrid counterparts.
"We've tested a thousand or so different hybrids," says Dr. Ernest Kerr, "but none of these were equal to the best standard varieties of tomatoes."
Nevertheless, standard Canadian-bred tomatoes like Veeroma, Sub-Arctic Maxi and Moira may eventually disappear from the catalogues to make room for new, lucrative hybrids and patented varieties -hybrid or standard.
Maclean's of March of this year points out what happened in the United States last year in an article called "A harvest of toxin". It reads:
June 27, 1989

Readers who waded through the exhaustively researched 6,500-word story-
-in the Wall Street Journal, hardly a left-wing magazine, Mr. Speaker-
- learned that last summer's drought may have left up to 30 per cent of the United States' com crop-which provides more than one-third of the world's supplies-contaminated with a natural toxin 100 times more deadly than industrial polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs).
In fact, the story, in part at least, was already known to most American growers and processors of food, as well as to the Canadian agencies charged with safeguarding the country's food supply. They have known since last autumn that summer-long high temperatures and low rainfall produced ideal growing conditions for Aspergillus Slavus, a fungus that attacks ears and kernels of heat-weakened com.
There was less to reassure Canadians, however, about the safety of more than 340,000 tons of American com-and no fewer than 32 varieties of processed corn ranging from commeal to tacos- imported in Canada each year. That com is supposed to meet standards set by the United States Food and Drag Administration, Blewett told Maclean's. But, as Journal reporter Scott Killman noted, "Those who regulate grain elevators lack money and manpower."
The Quaker Oats Co., which owns the world's largest cereal mill at Cedar Rapids, Iowa, tests six samples from each truckload of com -and last fall was turning away as many as one in five because of aflatoxin contamination. The danger is greater for Third World consumers who are major buyers of U.S. com, and often lacks sophisticated testing facilities or strict food-quality regulations. Indeed, medical journals record the deaths of about 100 people in Indian in 1974 -
And it goes on. So we know what some of the problems are with some of these hybridized, highly patented and restricted varieties that are controlled by the chemical companies.
Tories do not want to talk about monopoly control, but let us have a look at the facts. There have been 1,008 corporate take-overs of seed companies since 1969. Many of the purchasers also sell fertilizers and chemicals. In the 1970s there were 30 companies that produced crop chemicals. Now there are about a dozen and within a decade the industry itself says there will only be six remaining. Under the European and U.S. PBR legislation, 90 per cent of all seed patents are held by a handful of multinationals. After the year 2000, it is forecast that from 10 to 20 major corporations will dominate the seed markets. Seed and fertilizer companies may continue to buy up and hold patents on seeds, making it harder for
Plant Breeders' Rights
farmers in Third World countries to get the seeds they want. These companies are focusing greater research efforts on developing pesticide resistant seeds rather than pest resilient ones.
Let us take a look at how long this debate has been going on. I refer to an article written a decade ago by Carol Allen called: "Life is Not a Bed of Patents". This was written in respect, of course, to the now Conservative icon, Eugene Whelan-the Conservative icon on plant breeders' rights.
What is the difference between patenting a tomato and patenting a light bulb?
That is a question that not too many Tories could answer.
This question was put to me by a querulous Seed Trade Association officer who thinks we should permit patents and royalties on new plant varieties. He appears baffled that the idea of levying royalties in living, growing things, the source of human food, is repugnant to me.
If he really does not understand the difference between living and inanimate matter, he must be vastly perplexed that his 30-watt bulbs do not seed themselves and grow into 100 watts. The self-evident fact is that no one invented the tomato. We do not "invent" life. Nevertheless, many industrial countries (the U.S. and the U.K. among them) do grant plant patents, euphemistically called plant breeders' rights or PBRs. Since Bill C-32, which would give such rights to Canadian breeders, has been placed on the parliamentary order paper by Agriculture Minister Eugene Whelan, this particular bit of lunacy could become a domestic reality unless we scrutinize its implications. The fact is, we may be about to leap on the band wagon just as others, chastened by experience, are preparing to leap off.
Agriculture Canada insists patents are just basic human rights extended to breeders and that they will not affect farmers significantly. But fanners in other countries who have lived with patents are already disillusioned. Swedish, Swiss, U.S., British and German farmers, for instance, are disgruntled about higher seed prices.
Since the advent of patents and the move away from public breeding in the U.S., the National Farmers' Union has complained that seed prices rose 150 per cent between 1972 and 1977, more than any other component of the agricultural inputs. Many of the new patented varieties of seeds, though they do produce higher yields, are more vulnerable to disease.
Furthermore, wherever patents exist or are pending, they have created a virtual stampede to the seed business by multinational chemical and pharmaceutical corporations in pursuit of royalties. Small seed companies are vanishing as motes into a vacuum run by companies like Ciba-Geigy, Upjohn and Royal Dutch/Shell. In the last decade, roughly 40 small U.S. seed companies engulfed in this acquisitive romance. In Canada, Stewart Seeds is now owned by Ciba-Geigy, while Warwick Seeds is owned by Pfizer.

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
It all makes corporate sense, but not necessarily good farm policy. What could be more manifoldly profitable than to market seed, fertilizer and pesticide, all neatly interdependent, from one tidy carpetbag? But do we really naively expect the seed arm of a multinational corporation to search eagerly for a patentable variety of plant that requires little input from its pesticide and fertilizer arms?
Patents attract multinationals: multinationals flourish by massmarketing uniform products, not by custom-tailoring products to small, specialized markets like Canada. TWo thousand traditional vegetable varieties were dropped last June from the European Common Catalogue. Britain alone lost 500 vegetable varieties in July when the country's seed regulations made it a crime (punishable by a fine of 400 pounds) to sell or catalogue any variety not on the list.
I suppose this will be the next step by the Tories.
It is estimated that Europe is faced with the loss of three-quarters of its vegetable material in the decade.
Yet Eugene Whelan and Bill C-32 are still holding hands. As prominent a body as the Food and Agricultural Organization Secretariat to the United Nations opposes patents because they restrict free exchange of information and plant material among world breeders. An internal FAO document also states that patents have resulted in monopolistic practices, crop epidemics in the Third World and a narrowing of the genetic base upon which all plant life rests. And this in a field where tolerances are astonishingly thin: though there are 300,000 higher-order plants on the planet, more than 90 per cent of human nutrition derives from only 30 of them; only 30,000 have been studied, and by the turn of the century 50,000 may have vanished forever. Nevertheless, Canada ignores the warnings of informed bodies such as the U.S. National Farmers' Union and blithely considers turning over this fragile balance to a multinational-dominated business.
Why should Canada join this demonic parade to genetic wipeout? To be as neglected in the global seed market as we are in the pesticide field, where we make do with the products designed for warmer climates and larger markets? Make no mistake: in the political world of multinational agri-business, a tasteless tomato can bounce pinkly through a harvester like an Indian-rubber ball and survive a 2,000 Km truck trip undented and collect royalties will win every time over a tastier, more nutritious but squashable and unpatentable tomato. Mass production and mechanization have already produced the rubberized tomato and make traditional varieties shockingly scarce. They have also routed 6,000 small Canadian growers in the last 25 years.
Greater profits and increased uniformity are not everything.
Quality counts, as does designing a crop for its growing conditions; as does, most crucial of all, preserving old plants in the genetic pool that we may need to correct our mistakes. To say nothing of the quaint notion that many of us share that living plants should be accessible to all humankind, without royalties.
This is what I consider to be a truly excellent article by Carol Allen.
There is a growing coalition to which the Government does not want to listen. Let me just give one final quote from a letter by Susan McIntosh, the Coordinator of the Grow Coalition on Pesticides. In 1988, the economists reported:
Chemical companies have spent $10 billion or so in as many years buying up seed companies worldwide -
She lists Pioneer Hi-Bred, Sandoz, Dekalb-Pfizer, Upjohn, Limagrain, Shell Oil, ICI, Ciba-Geigy, Orson and Cargill as the world's ten largest seed companies.
Seven of these ten are also involved in crop chemicals and at least six sell seeds in Canada already. This trend will escalate if PBR should become law.
No Member of Parliament, no Canadian citizen should support Bill C-15 as it is proposed. It is a scurrilous and wrongful Act.

speechtext:
That indicates the level of debate which some of the NDP Members are able to achieve. They think that nationalizing everything is the answer.

They honestly hold that view. In spite of the fact that in every socialist country of the world socialism has failed and failed dismally.
What was the secret, Mr. Speaker? As you well know, it was when we tried that experiment in the western world. It was to say to people "You can own a piece of property. You have the fundamental right to speak. You have the fundamental right to association and you have the fundamental right if you come up with something new and creative, whether it is an industrial design, a piece of music, or whether it is a car or a truck, you have the right to own that and for a period of 17 years you get to develop that product and collect a royalty if someone else wants to build it".
Under that system of private property, of land, fundamental rights, including the rights to patents, we developed wealth and created a lifestyle that has put all of us at a standard of living that is truly incredible. But it all goes back to those fundamental rights.
Then governments came along. During the 1970s, because some drug companies were charging too much, different nations responded in different ways. Some of

them took away their patent rights, which is the way Canada went. Other countries handled things in a different way. They put in price review boards so that they were more regulated. Let me ask the NDP this: what other countries now have plant breeders' rights. You would think that it is all going to go away. It is not going to go away. You either steal from the Third World or you don't survive.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext: What about Australia, Belgium, Denmark, France, all socialist nations? speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
speechtext:

One is foresight and the other one is hindsight.

The Hon. Member for Regina Wascana (Mr. Schneider) said one is foresight and the other is hindsight. Those are my sentiments exactly.
I do not think the Members opposite do know any more and that is why I think they will no longer be the government of Saskatchewan, for example, after the next provincial election. I will put any money on that, although I am not a gambling man. What this debate is all about is the privatization of seed versus a vision of the modern family farm which can survive a corporate onslaught which the Progressive Conservatives are unleashing on the farm community.
As I stand up to speak here tonight, I am not only standing up as the Member for Prince Albert-Churchill River, approximately 20 per cent of that population are

farm families. There are quite a few of them because they are relatively small farms, probably averaging four quarters of land in our constituency. About half of the farmers are combined income farmers and work off the farm. It does maintain a large rural population, with
3,000	people in the area of Buckland alone.

It is not because I believe that profit is a dirty word or that Members on this side of the House believe that profit is a dirty word. It is a methodology that from time to time Conservatives do manage to sell. They sold it successfully in 1982 in Saskatchewan. They sold it again in the last federal election to a large portion of the population, certainly not though in Saskatchewan, British Columbia and the Maritimes. Nevertheless, they do sometimes try and convince people that people on this side of the House, be they New Democrats or Liberals, somehow or other with New Democrats profit is a dirty word.
There are all kinds of business people who are members of the New Democratic Party, including the MT .A for Prince Albert-Duck Lake, whose campaign I managed and who had strong support from the Prince Albert business community. We were in that constituency. Years later, it turned out that he had. That was some-

thing he did because he believed in John George Diefenbaker, as a lot of people in that part of the country did.

John George Diefenbaker led the charge, not only in this House but in the country. There were a lot of people from all kinds of different philosophies who followed him.

That is the way the Members opposite have become about closure. They have used it once, they got away with it in free trade, so all the way through this session it is closure, closure, closure. It is not a crisis like the pipeline debate was. Nobody is arguing that. I think the fall of this Government in the polls-we are not high either, but the Government has fallen very dramatically-is because of the perception that is spreading through the country that there is an element of arrogance and shoving things down people's throats about this Government that they just simply do not like. I
I could understand why closure was being brought in if there were some kind of crisis in the country. If we had just got through this seeding season and the farmers had run out of seed, and there was not good seed for the people to sow, then there would be a crisis in the country that would perhaps justify taking a radical measure like this on an issue which is not particularly earth-shaking as far as the general health of the country is concerned, but it is an important symbolic issue. There is no crisis. We do not need new seed next year or the year after. We are doing very well.
Is there a crisis in production? There is no crisis in production. We had a problem with drought last year and we are still working out the details of that. Canadian farmers can produce. The Canadian research establishment has done very well for us. We run one of the most modem and efficient farm economies in the world. That was with public seed production. That was with institutions like the Canadian Wheat Board. That was with a country elevator-based railway system. I do not think those ideas are particularly old fashioned. I think those ideas just do not fit in with the philosophy of Members opposite.
Another thing that would have called for closure is if there had been such a crisis that it required this kind of radical action. If the farmers themselves were clamouring for this legislation, it might have been justified. However, I have not seen any farmers marching on Parliament Hill lobbying for plant breeders' rights. Not one farmer from my constituency has written me a letter saying that he wants plant breeders' rights, and there are some former Conservatives in that constituency as well as plant breeders.
The Government says that it has consulted with farm groups. One of the authors of the very good report on Indian post-secondary education which came out tonight had a chance to see for himself what the people thought of the Government's consultation process. Couldn't name one, though.

Earlier in this debate, the Hon. Member for Swift Current-Maple Creek-Assiniboia (Mr. Wilson) said that there were several reasons for this particular legislation. He said that one was to enhance our exports and another was to practice better husbandry. However, he offered no compelling argument other than that Conservative Members think that is true.
We are producing lots of grain for export and we could produce a lot more. We could invest more in plant breeding, and I think we should. It does not matter whether it is private or public investment. The point is that those resources should stay in the public domain so that seed is available to everyone as it has always been. Farmers can afford high quality seed. It is a national and international resource and should be treated as a public resource.
Then the Hon. Member said that some of the provisions in the Bill, including the 18 years of the patent's lifespan and the exchange of information, were because of an international convention that we needed to become a part of. The international convention is made up of those countries which, as the Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) so eloquently outlined, took their cues from large multinational corporations and did their bidding. Sure enough, a farming system evolved which followed that kind of philosophy.
The Hon. Member mentioned 18 countries. What about the other 160 countries in this world? Only 12 per cent of the countries of this world belong to that convention. If we join that convention, we will have to play by the rules of those 12. If we become the lucky 13th, we will not be able to do anything with the other 159 countries where much valuable work is going on. If Hon. Members think we will be better off with the 12 than with the 159, they should check out which countries those are and what kind of agriculture they support.
The Hon. Member also said that this Bill was not related to free trade. He said that no matter what happens, if there is a tornado or some other natural catastrophe, Members of the Opposition will jump up and down and say it is about the Free Trade Agreement.

This isn't a natural catastrophe, this is a man-made one.

As the Hon. Member has pointed out, this is a man-made disaster, not a natural one. It is linked to the Free Trade Agreement, if not precisely to the language of the free trade legislation, though there is some evidence that that might well be true. This Bill represents a philosophy that is very much a part of free trade.
I fully accept the Hon. Member's criticism of people wrapping everything up in free trade, but that is because free trade is symbolic of the Government's whole philosophy, which is that large foreign corporations are more important than family farms, that the jobs of people in Ohio are more important than the jobs of people who work at the Inglis plant in Toronto. Those are the kinds of judgment calls Members opposite are prepared to make. Government Members will have to excuse us if, whenever we see that philosophy in action, we start talking about free trade. I think that is something Members opposite will have to get used to because Canadians everywhere see it in those same terms.
We have been told that we have to adopt this line of thinking to become competitive in the modem world. We have been told that the agricultural industry can only survive in the modem world if we adopt that kind of thinking. Government Members go so far as to say that Members who might oppose this Bill might be reactionary and might not want change or progress. That is relatively hard to take coming from a political tradition that has brought many of the institutions that have contributed immeasurably to the agricultural wealth of Canada, ideas like the Canadian Wheat Board which a Conservative Government brought in. The Hon. Member said that it was an old-fashioned idea which symbolized the NDP, and I think in some ways it does. We do not think that the Wheat Board is old fashioned, we think it is doing very well. If Canadian farmers are to beat American farmers, they will do it through the Canadian Wheat Board, not through Cargill, because Cargill has a conflict of interest. We are better off with our own Wheat Board, and I think most farmers believe that as well.
The difference between us is whether we see the farm community as being composed of owner-operators and large enough numbers of them to support small communities, or whether the rural community is seen as a series of large agri-business corporations. We think that the modem approach to the Saskatchewan economy has to be that the small farmers have access to the technology,

the capital and the export opportunities as well as the large fanners. It is becoming very clear that with the philosophy of this Government, along with the philosophy of its colleagues in the Saskatchewan legislature, that kind of small farming community will no longer exist and the Government makes no apologies for that.
The reason I am opposing this Bill is because I want to see a competitive modern farm sector in Canada. With the Progressive Conservative approach, we will not get that.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to rise in the House at this late hour to speak to Bill C-15, Plant Breeders' Rights. This legislation is long overdue. Plant technology has changed as much in the past 25 years as have medical advances and computer technology.
Canadian farmers are demanding hardy, high-yielding seeds and plants that work in concert with modem farm management practices. To compete in the world market, Canadian farmers require seeds that are stable and predictable, that have a specified growing period and that are disease and pest resistant.
These seeds are the result of extensive research and years of experimentation. Currently, the bulk of this expensive, painstaking research is done by Agriculture Canada and universities. The private sector has been unwilling to put time and resources into research whose results are not protected by law. Canada lacks a legal mechanism to protect the inventors of new and better varieties of plants and seeds. This need has not gone unrecognized. Plant breeders' rights have been advocated by a number of agricultural groups in Canada since 1923, when it was recommended by the Canadian Horticultural Council that legislation protecting plant breeders' rights be created. More recently, plant breeders' rights legislation was introduced in the House of Commons in 1980 and 1988.
The Bill now before the House dealing with plant breeders' rights has the same intent as the previous Bills. The purpose of the legislation is to grant the breeder of new varieties of plants control over the multiplication and the sale of productive material. The breeder will be entitled to a royalty if others sell the variety he has
produced. The rights in this case work like a patent or copyright.
The implementation of plant breeders' rights in Canada will have a positive impact. The beneficial effects will include increased investment in plant breeding by both public and private sectors; improved varieties available for Canadian producers from both Canada and from other countries; and a return of royalties on Canadian varieties sold at home and abroad.
Plant breeders' rights legislation applies to new, distinct varieties. Varieties already on the market are not eligible for protection. Once a new variety comes on the market, a breeder cannot prevent others from using it in breeding programs.
The demands of the modem world, complete with pollution, international subsidy wars, and highly technical agricultural practices, make the protection of plant breeders' rights absolutely necessary to encourage the development of high-yielding, disease-resistant crops. This legislation is designed to encourage research and plant breeding in Canada.
One of the most important benefits of plant breeders' rights legislation is that it offers financial incentives to the private sector to become involved in plant breeding. Presently, the majority of research and plant breeding is done by universities and Agriculture Canada. Unfortunately, those institutions cannot keep pace with the world-wide gains in plant technology.
To date, the private sector has steered clear of plant breeding research because their results would not be protected. This legislation will encourage the private sector to become involved in research. The royalties from the sale of seed or plants would ensure research funding on both a public and private level. In this way, Canada can be competitive on the world agricultural market.
Ten years ago while visiting Britain, I had occasion to visit canola test plots. The British refer to them as trials. The area covered 100 acres, and was owned and operated by the research division of a seed retail company. Of course, in England, plant breeders' rights legislation exists and the private sector receives royalties on plants.
Competition between the organizations involved in the development of new varieties of plants will ensure that seed prices are not substantially increased. Any cost
June 27, 1989

increase in new varieties would be offset by the benefits of improved yields and increased disease and pest resistance.
There are also safeguards in the legislation to prevent excessive pricing or restrictions of seed supplies. Farmers will always have the option of using their own seed, using unprotected seed, or using the protected new varieties. I believe that many farmers will be willing to pay a little more at the outset to reap the advantages of new varieties.
In the late 1970s when I was with the Alberta Agriculture Research Council, the Alberta Government, together with a number of other provinces and Agriculture Canada, spent large sums of money on plant breeding and research of rapeseed. As a result, the canola plant was developed. This development was beneficial to producers and consumers. For farmers, it was a cash crop and allowed them to diversify. Canola seed-crushing plants were built to produce canola oil for cooking and meal for animal feed. Canadian consumers had a Canadian-made oil second to none in the world for quality and at very competitive prices. Canola became the Cinderella crop of western Canada. We were able to capture 65 per cent of the oil and fats market in Canada. That is an outstanding achievement. If there had been plant breeding rights at the time of the canola development, the private sector would have played a large role in the research and development, thus saving taxpayers millions of dollars.
Canada is one of the agriculturally developed countries that does not have legislation protecting plant breeders' rights. Canada now is in a position to learn from the experiences of other countries and implement the very best and most effective legislation. Most countries have noted very positive effects. For example, the United States documented, 10 years after the implementation of plant breeders' rights, that the legislation provided farmers and consumers with a large number of plant varieties yielding larger and better quality crops. In addition, the United States found that the plant breeders' rights inspired the private sector plant breeding that resulted in the development of more and better varieties of plants.
Certainly, the United States is not alone in recognizing the benefits of plant breeders' rights. Australia implemented legislation in 1987. The International Convention
Plant Breeders' Rights
for the Protection of New Varieties of Plants established an international union to protect plant breeders' rights. The international union has some 18 of the leading agriculturally developed countries in the world as members. Plant breeders' rights legislation has found tremendous support in Canada's agriculture sector. Nationally, the supporters of plant breeders' rights include the Canadian Federation of Agriculture, Canadian Horticultural Council, SeCan Association, the Canada Seed Growers Association, and a number of other associated groups.
In closing, let me emphasize the importance of plant breeders' rights to all Canadians, producers and consumers. I strongly believe that this legislation is imperative to the future well-being of Canadian farmers.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, tonight we have had an opportunity to see very clearly what is wrong with Canadian politics. Let me start first with the disingenuousness of the Liberals who have had the nerve to rise and criticize this piece of legislation. Granted, some of them were new Members, and perhaps the old Members have not told them what the Liberal position used to be on plant breeders' rights. I have been around here for a while. I remember that the Liberals were intending to bring in this legislation prior to their defeat in 1979, and had it on their legislative agenda from 1980 to 1984. The fact that they can get up and make the kind of speeches that they have been making tonight goes to show one of the major problems of Canadian politics, that is, the insincerity, the duplicity, the hypocrisy of the Liberal Party when it comes to this and many other issues.
Rip Van Winkle.

The Liberal Members who are upset about this happen to be sitting on the other side of the House at this moment, which seems to me to be a great symbol of just exactly what I am talking about.
I listened with interest, as I always do, to the Hon. Member for Lethbridge (Mr. Thacker), whose former riding was Lethbridge-Foothills. That used to be the name of his riding. I have not quite mastered all the names of the new ridings.
I think he puts the government case very well. I do not agree with the government case for this particular

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
legislation. However, as I listened to the Hon. Member from Lethbridge he started out by giving us an interpretation of Canadian history which is fundamentally flawed. He said that the way we built this country was only through individual enterprise, through the exercise of private property and entrepreneurs taking risks-the whole Conservative mythology about how Canada came into being.
The fact of the matter is that that is not how the country came into being at all. If one wants to be an advocate of that particular view of private property, and how economic activity is generated, and how particular countries have been built, then that is fine. However, do not distort Canadian history in order to make the case. The fact of the matter is that the country developed as a result of a very creative mix of both public money and political vision and private property and private investment, the CPR being an example thereof, as well as Canadian institutions, Crown corporations and other things we have come to see as part and parcel of the fabric of the country, like the Canadian Wheat Board for example. These do not conform to the Tory mythology about how Canada was built.
They are making a serious error when they get up and try to lead us to believe that that is how the country came into being. They may want to take the country in a particular direction-that is fine. It is their right to argue for that direction. It is the right of the Government to bring in legislation which takes us in that direction. However, please do not pretend that this is perfectly in keeping with Canadian history because Canadian history is something else all together.
Our argument on this side is that the public sector, whether it be in the form of Crown corporations or in the form of research done by universities and government Departments, have played a vital role in making us the kind of country that we are today. Many of the victories that we have won in the agricultural sector, whether it is the more recent one concerning canola or whether it is other former victories with respect to the development of various kinds of wheat, are things that happened because there was a- public commitment to this kind of research and because the results of that research were made widely available. All this happened without the desire for profit that the Hon. Member from Lethbridge
says is so absolutely indispensable to anything good happening.
The fact of the matter is that societies can do good, productive and creative things without being motivated purely by money. I know that goes against the Conservative view of the world. The fact is that many good things have happened in this country without that kind of motivation. What we are saying is that we would like to preserve the mix of public and private, of things still being done for the good of the country or for the good of agriculture, or as the case may be.
The Member from Lethbridge says that we do not want to enter the modem world, that the NDP wants to keep the country back from modernity. If the kind of modernity that the Conservatives want us to enter into is a world in which everything is motivated only by the desire for profit, in which everything is regulated by the market-place, then, yes, that is the kind of world that we do not want to enter into and that we do not want our country to enter into. Unfortunately, that is the way of the world. The Member from Lethbridge is right about that. The question is whether or not in Canada we are going to acquiesce to these global trends, whether we are going to have what I would call an accomodationist stance toward these global trends, or whether we are going to, in concert with other countries, resist these global trends.
It may be difficult to do this. It is going to be particularly difficult for us to do this after the Free Trade Agreement because the Free Trade Agreement for many of us is the symbol of Canada giving up on that tension between public and private, giving up on a mixed economy, giving up on what has made Canada a particularly successful country.
I think members of the Government should remember that the kind of country that we have is not the kind of country that has been created only by individual enterprise. It is the kind of country that has been created by this creative mix of the public and private sector. What they have done through their actions in the Free Trade Agreement and through this action, and through many other acts that they have taken and some that they still plan to take, has broken that tension. From here on in it is the market-place alone. If that is the kind of brave new world that the Government wants to lead us into,
June 27, 1989

then we make no apologies for resisting that brave new world.
What is that new world all about? It is about control. It is about who is going to make the decisions that determine the very nature, in this case of plant life, on the planet. I cannot for the life of me understand why Conservatives who are very concerned about government control, who are very concerned about unaccountable power, want to turn over to a handful of global corporations the power to determine the whole botanical life of the planet. On what possible grounds would people who are concerned about excessive control by anyone want to do that?
Yet that is what the Government is asking us to do in this particular instance. It wants to worsen a situation that is already with us. That is the fact of these large global corporations, which as far as I am concerned are analogous to the biblical powers and principalities. These are the institutions which in a very short time will control everything, if there is not a will on the part of Governments to defend the public interest, whether that is the environmental public interest, or, in this case, the genetic public interest in terms of preserving various kinds of species or plant species in the Third World or elsewhere. We have this very tragic trend in absolutely the wrong direction.
It is all part and parcel of the globalization of the economy. With that globalization has come increasing concentration of power. These are the people who want to talk about competition all the time. However, their policies lead to more and more concentration of unaccountable power, global corporations which are accountable to no one, which have assets in many cases bigger than any nation state in the world, corporations which can play one country off against the other, one province in a country off against the other, one state off against another. This is called free enterprise. This is called freedom. This is not freedom. This is the newest and most diabolical form of tyranny that one can imagine, that this kind of power should be in private hands and should be beyond the reach of Governments and that the only occasion on which Governments become involved is to facilitate this kind of control, which is exactly what this Government is doing tonight by bringing in this legislation.
Plant Breeders' Rights
I think it is unfortunate that the Government will get away with this. It has been a long battle. One of the first speeches I made in the House of Commons in the fall of 1979 was on this particular issue, when the Conservative Government of the day tried to bring it in. We have seen since then how the Government has succeeded in doing this with respect to drug patent laws. Now it is doing it with respect to seeds for plant breeders' rights. I heard the Hon. Member from St. Albert, I believe, say that public investment will continue. We heard that during the debate about the drug patent laws.
And it is. Admit it.

Not public investment. One of the first things that happened after the drug patent law was passed is that Connaught Laboratories, which used to be a publicly owned corporation and something of which Canada was proud because of its good research, was sold to an American company. That really helped a lot. That was part and parcel of the vision of Canada the Conservatives say they will preserve.
You don't like success.

The Member from Calgary says that I do not like success. I do not call having all the new kinds of plant life in the world owned by a handful of corporations success. She and I have a different view of what success amounts to. I don't think success is something that can be measured in terms of the quarterly or annual profit margins of a variety of different multinational companies.
I do not believe it is success to carry vertical integration to its extreme so that there would be what I call bio-integration, the same multinational corporation owning everything, beginning with the seed put in the ground. It will be bred to use that company's herbicides, to respond only to its fertilizers-
Oh, oh!
It's happening.

All the way from the furrow in which the seed is placed to the kitchen table owned by the same multinational corporation. If the Member from Calgary calls that success, then I reject that success. I call it tyranny. It is turning over our lives to a handful of unseen people in a boardroom who make decisions about the whole country while we sit here and have to listen to people like her call it success. It is disgusting. That is not success, it is failure of the worst possible kind.

It is failure to imagine a world in which people can do things co-operatively, through the public sector, and do things as part and parcel of a vision of what the country should be rather than how institutions can make money in the country or the world by developing a monopoly on new kinds of seeds, drugs or whatever the case may be.
We managed to be very successful in many respects with the Government involvement. The Government was involved, along with universities in the development of canola. Is the Member saying that was a failure?
The Member for Calgary Southwest (Mrs. Sparrow) is so psychologically damaged by the National Energy Program-
You are right.

-that she cannot imagine anything good happening in the public sector. In the name of that paranoid reaction to the National Energy Program, the whole damn country is to be destroyed in order to satisfy Tories from Alberta who developed an aversion to the public sector in the early 1980s. For that, the whole country has to go down the drain. It is disgusting.

Mr. Speaker, in this House we always have activists, lobbyists, and other interested Parties who are constantly asking politicians to pass legislation. Often this legislation has to do with changes in technology such as this Bill before us today.
However, this is not a Bill that is tinkering with an established procedure. This is not a Bill that is ironing out a new wrinkle in an existing process. We are, on this Bill, breaking completely new ground. We are embarking on a new course.
Biotechnology is fundamentally different from any other aspect, any other Bill that this House has introduced before. This is a new technology. This is a technology that is codifying the development of new variety of species of plants.
Biotechnology, generally, deals not only with plants but certainly the development and improvements of animal species. In fact they present to us an opportunity for a better society. There are some very good benefits with respect to biotechnology. A better aspect of biotechnology is that of profits. This is an area of research and development that promises to provide those who are making the development massive profits. In fact, it has been said that it is going to be like a new unit of power.
We used to have, at one time, the gold standard. Now we will have the gene standard. Why do we want to move in such a direction? The answer is patently obvious. We want to move in that direction because we want to solve real problems that exist in society in this country and elsewhere in the world today. We want to prepare and develop a better world. We want to develop an easier life. Those are very laudable goals. Those are things that we all strive for. We must be careful in solving the problem that we do not create new and different problems, ones that are actually worse than the problems we are attempting to solve. My caucus and I have a concern with this particular Bill. The Government is endorsing a process and is setting out on a path that it
Plant Breeders' Rights
does not comprehend. It does not realize what kind of road it is sending this country down.
Biotechnology offers us a means to solve many agricultural problems. It offers to solve production problems for farmers to provide better varieties of grain that will grow in shorter periods of time and avoid frost. It will provide better yields, allow producers to utilize new and other varieties that otherwise would not have been able to be used. It perhaps will provide the consumer with safer, cheaper and possibly healthier products. At the same time this technology threatens not to aid producers but make producers a slave to this new technology.
We are dealing here with plant life. This is the thin edge of the wedge of biotechnology. We welcome biotechnology if those who control and steer the direction of this instrument do so with the benefit of mankind in mind. This Bill dealing with plants only asks and presents some very fundamental questions. Who is controlling this new technology, the massed propagation of plants, plant tissue culture, the monocolonal antibodies and cell fusion?
Is it going to be the Ph.Ds that are working in universities, those who we expect are going to control that? That is not going to be the case. It is going to be a handful of large companies, so-called agri-business which are going to control, develop and monopolize this area, not only plant breeders' rights but later animal breeders' rights. We are just on the threshold of this massive technology which Canadians should not only look forward to but look forward to with some caution.
This has been the subject of much discussion and much debate. There have been numerous conferences held on biotechnology. Certainly one of the most well known was the 1987 Dag Hammarskjold seminar on the socio-economic impact of new biotechnologies on basic health in agriculture.
Let me state one of its conclusions. The greatest threat in the new biosciences is that life will become the monopoly property of a few giant companies. In the key countries the products and processes of biotechnology either are or are becoming patentable beyond the wildest dreams of the industrial barons of the past. The whole gene revolution is on the verge of becoming private

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders ' Rights
property. Of all technologies this life derived technology must remain in the hands of the people.
This is a conclusion of a conference of scientists from around the world, scientists including people from Canada. In fact, the Government would have received a report from this conference. This Government has chosen to ignore these experts and individuals who devote their lives to science. This Bill codifies what the Hammarskjold seminar feared most.
We should be looking at plant breeders' rights and biotechnology, but we should be very careful about how that development proceeds. The Government has ignored that conference, those conclusions of world experts as it has ignored other experts in the world. If the goal of science is to serve humanity, then let science serve humanity.
Many countries are dealing with this problem. Members opposite spoke of this much earlier. They spoke of numerous countries, including the United States which has a tremendous influence and effect on Canada. The United States not only allows plant breeders' rights but also plant patents, plant cell culture, and engineered organisms.
The Americans have taken a step ahead of us. The United States considers a lack of patent protection to be an unfair trading practice. That was brought up at the GATT negotiations. Canada has been under pressure from the United States about the subject. The United States has demanded that Canada adopt similar laws to the United States for pharmaceuticals and plant varieties. You can see in the recent past that this Government caved in to U.S. demands on pharmaceuticals.
We had a nation that for 20 years had some of the cheapest drugs in the world. This benefited Canadians, but Canada passed a law providing protection for drug corporations.
And it created all kinds of jobs.
The Government promised that this type of legislation would create research and development and hundreds of jobs.
Thousands.
These jobs simply have not materialized.
Come up to Ontario and I will point them out to you.

The Government is now caving in to the pressure of the United States Government on plant breeders' rights. Mark my words, this is the beginning. Certainly there will be pressure from the United States to have treaties not just for plant breeders' rights but for animal breeders' rights. That would be the next stage. Perhaps legislation will be introduced next year or in the next session.
We want to improve the quality of life and have a better community, but this Bill does not provide the protection needed to guarantee the decent quality of life Canadians deserve and have come to expect.
Canadians attended the Hammarskjold seminar. Reports were presented to the Government which indicated that plant breeders' rights promised to increase production and reduce costs, but the conclusions of experts, not politicians, of people who work in that field and devote their life to it, said that that was not likely to be the case. They concluded that it will aggravate genetic erosion and likely to increase the dependence of farmers. It will further concentrate the power of transnational agri-business. In other words, there will be a concentration of power into fewer and fewer hands at the ultimate expense of producers.
There is more. Certainly plants go into producing a large number of drugs that are utilized in the pharmaceutical business today.
That is why it is not uncommon to have a company which is involved not only in pharmaceutical drugs or chemicals but also in seed production. This Bill simply allows them to further concentrate that monopoly which they are developing.
In health, Mr. Speaker, the drug companies will say that they will provide more effective diagnostic tools and new ways to prevent disease. The Hammarskjold Conference concluded differently. These experts and these people who devoted their lives to this type of work-and not politicians-have concluded that the pharmaceutical industry more likely will focus upon the most profitable opportunities and divert attention from basic health requirements. In other words, the bottom line. These are experts who have reported to government and who have lobbied governments. There is one tragic flaw and one tragic problem that these experts do not have. They do not have a lot of money. They do not have the power that the dollar bill brings when we are talking to people like Cargill and Shell Oil and other companies, like the Eli Lilly Company. Those are the companies to which this

Government listens. Those are the groups on which this Government focuses its attention. That is who it listens and responds to, as opposed to experts and people in the field who are devoting their lives to this problem. That is what is wrong with this Bill.
Members opposite tonight with respect to plant breeders' rights, were saying that this will be a benefit to farmers and producers. It is already happening in other countries where plant breeders' rights has been established. Seed corporations who have patented their particular seed and who have the protection-and in this case it is going to be 18 years-are lobbying governments to say that farmers should not have the right to retain seed.
It is expected that in certain countries there will be the introduction of laws to demand that if farmers retain seed they should pay a royalty to the companies. Is that benefiting farmers? Is that a government which is doing what it can for the small producer? Is that a government which is devoted to maintaining agriculture and a rural structure? I do not think so. That is a government that is passing legislation that is simply going to concentrate the wealth of this nation into fewer and fewer hands. That is the difficulty that I have with this Bill.
The idea is fine, but it needs massive amendments. This is a government which is setting a dangerous and potentially destructive course for this country. The potential profits in this area are mind-boggling. There are millions and millions and millions of dollars to be made in this area. The potential benefits are there as well.
However, when a small group of corporations have a monopoly, they dictate what sort of production will be happening in the rural areas of this country. Contrary to Members' saying, "don't worry, don't worry", if this Bill is allowed to pass unamended, unchanged, it is going to be destructive to the family farms in this country. It is going to be destructive to rural Canada.
Members opposite talked before about when the Drug Patent Act was passed there would be jobs created in research and development, but they have not material-
Plant Breeders' Rights
ized in this country. They are not going to materialize under plant breeders' rights either.
These companies are in the business of making a profit. We cannot blame a company for being in the business of making a profit. Its shareholders appoint directors to work each year to make the company a profit. If those directors do not make that company a profit, those directors should be fired. That is how the system works and it is fair. There is nothing wrong with making a profit.
This Government should not be passing legislation which is simply giving the agri-business corporations of this world a licence to print money which is going to put a lot of dollars in their pockets and going to show a lot of increased revenue for those corporations. It is going to simply spell one more expense. It is going to mean one more expense for family farmers and one more in which they are being controlled. This is a government which talks about free enterprise. This is not free enterprise. When this materializes down the road, these corporations will have a say in what people plant, when they plant it and how they should plant it. That is the problem with this Bill.
These corporations are not trying to develop a plant which is resistant to various insects and other problems which exist in fields and in crops. Rather than developing a pest resistant variety, they are focusing on gene transfer for pesticide resistance because that is where the money is. If they can develop a crop variety and show that it produces well and convince producers to buy it, they will do that.
What will happen is that as varieties disappear, as they inevitably will, then producers will be forced to follow the tune that these agri-business companies maintain. That is the conclusion of the conference. That is the conclusion of experts who are concerned with this area.
This is a Bill which is only at second reading, thank goodness. I certainly hope that in committee we can effect some changes to the Bill and come back to this House with some recommendations so that it provides some protection for the producers of this land that does not give everything to agri-business and does not cave in to agri-business.
I and my colleagues will be working very hard to see that this Bill is either defeated, or if not defeated, that it is presented to this House in a fashion which reflects and represents and is responsive to the needs of average

June 27, 1989
Plant Breeders' Rights
Canadians and not agri-business. It is my hope that that will be the ultimate result of this Bill. The objective is the same, to provide a better lifestyle, a better world for all of us. This Bill is not a Bill for Canadians, it is a Bill for agri-business.

speakeroldname: Mr. Murray Cardiff (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister, President of the Privy Council and Minister of Agriculture):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is with pleasure that I rise to speak to Bill C-15 at this late time and at the last event and speech that we will be giving in the House of Commons as we wrap up for the summer session.
We will have the opportunity of going home and seeing the wonderful plants that are growing which have been the fruits and work of many of our plant breeders.
We have heard many arguments against Bill C-15 over the course of second reading debate. Some have suggested that plant breeders' rights will destroy world gene resources or adversely affect less developed countries, or lead to the patenting of human life. Bill C-15 does not do these things, and during the course of debate, my hon. colleagues in the Opposition have at times forgotten what plant breeders' rights are all about.
Bill C-15 is about joining with 18 of our most significant trading partners in signing the international convention for the protection of plant varieties. Bill C-15 is about ensuring a place in the world for Canadian varieties so that Canadian efforts can be rewarded abroad. Bill C-15 is about allowing farmers and horticul-turalists to import exciting new foreign varieties which are unobtainable until we have our own plant breeders' rights legislation.
Bill C-15 is about offering private breeders incentive to undertake this important work despite its risks and its expense. Bill C-15 is about ensuring that Canadian farmers have access to the best possible varieties, whether they be foreign, private or public. In short, Bill C-15 is about benefiting Canadian agriculture which in turn benefits all of us. When agriculture is prosperous, Canada is prosperous and everyone does well.
Let me begin with the suggestion that this is patent legislation. In fact, it is quite obvious that this is not patent legislation, nor will it lead to any. If it were, we
would be debating an amendment to the Patent Act. Instead, we are discussing plant breeders' rights legislation.
Because the Government recognizes that this is a sensitive and complicated issue, we have chosen to deal with it separately. In such a manner, we believe we can best protect the interests of breeders, farmers and the country as a whole.
Equally, this Bill in no way authorizes anyone to patent human life forms. It merely allows plant breeders an opportunity to be rewarded for their hard work, and 18 years has been designated as the period of protection for a variety under Bill C-15.
There are a number of reasons for the choice of 18 years. Generally, out of one million initial crosses, plant breeders find only four potential varieties. These will take 10 to 15 years to develop at a cost of $3 million to $5 million. Out of this work will arise varieties which often last only a few years before they are superseded by other new plants.
It is essential that the really outstanding varieties help to pay the costs of plant breeding programs. There are varieties which have lasted well beyond the 18-year period. For example, Thatcher spring wheat was registered in 1935, Selkirk wheat in 1953, a red clover called Alataswede in 1923 and Climax, a timothy variety in 1947. Those of us in the agricultural industry know the value of Climax, one of the best timothys that has ever been developed in this great country. I think that says something for the early plant breeding programs and for the dedication of plant breeders many years ago who did not have the technology and tools to work with we have today in developing varieties.
After the 18 years, these successful varieties would, of course, become public, but if breeders are not given time to recoup their investment, seed prices would necessarily go up. Currently, in other countries with PBR, royalty rates are approximately 6 per cent to 8 per cent, but the length of protection is essential to maintaining this low level.
The Hon. Member from Regina said that he accepted the principle of royalties. A Member of the NDP said that, though he did not say how the royalties should be paid.
June 27, 1989

My colleague, the Hon. Member for Algoma (Mr. Foster), has suggested that the period be reduced to seven years. Not only would this tend to have an inflationary effect upon prices but it would do nothing to improve our external situation.
We have indicated our intention to join the 18-member international convention so that we might enjoy the benefits of reciprocity with these major trading partners. Lowering our period of protection in this way would no longer meet the requirements of the convention and we could not ratify the agreement. We would remain incapable of securing foreign imports or of protecting our varieties abroad.
The absence of variety protection can also have a detrimental effect on the industry by artificially restricting and extending attempts to control seed. Contractual arrangements are currently made between growers and some seed companies in an attempt to ensure some return on their product. Members of the House of Commons who are farmers know that to grow a variety of seed that they know by name, they have to sign a contract to obtain that seed and they have to agree to return it back to that supplier because there is a lack of patent protection for the variety. To me, that makes a mockery of the system and is not fair to farmers because it restricts good seeds to certain individuals and puts us in an uncompetitive position.
This creates a great deal of paperwork and complicates matters for the grower and the company alike. The agreements have no cut-off. This Bill C-15 offers. Nor does the current situation allow the Government to intervene in the national interest. As well, foreign countries do not recognize this contractual agreement as a parallel system and will not enter into reciprocal agreements.
We need plant breeders' rights. I am very happy to see this legislation read the second time tonight and go to a legislative committee for deliberations. This issue has been debated for many years. Finally, it will provide great assistance to the agricultural producers in Canada in competing on the world market.
The Government has been far-sighted enough to ensure that some means exist by which we can maintain the system in an equitable manner. Clauses 32 and 33 provide for a compulsory license which could be granted in the event of unnecessarily high royalty rates or unfair
Plant Breeders' Rights
distribution. This system is in place in many UPOV nations but its use has rarely been necessary.
The enforcement of this Act will not be applied to our grandmothers who wish to trade plant slips. The Hon. Member for Skeena (Mr. Fulton) referred to the clauses in the plant breeders' rights Bill relating to penalties for offences. He implied that the penalties applied to people giving away seeds of protected varieties, and this is not so. The offences in Bill C-15 relate to such issues as false representation and abuse of trust. They do not relate to the selling of protected varieties. If someone sells another person's protected variety, it is a civil and not a criminal offence.

Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I suggest that the Hon. Member who just misquoted me read Clause 6 of the Bill and Clause 51, the offence clause. He just misquoted the legislation his Government has brought in. I think that is quite improper and quite misleading to those viewing these proceedings.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: That is debate. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I simply want to say again that if someone sells another person's protected variety, it is a civil, not a criminal offence. It would be up to the owner of the rights to enforce his or her own rights, and that is quite clear in the legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a point of order. I know what the Hon. Member just said. What he said was false. It is improper for a Member of the House to impute false statements to another Member.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary has the floor.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, to make compulsory automatic licensing as effective as possible, we have chosen the route of maximum flexibility. By selecting an advisory committee and implementing specifics by species with regulations, we have allowed for a system which will take the nuances of this vast nation into account. With this method, the unique situation of maritime potatoes will be handled in a manner different from that of Red Spring wheat or that of a new breed of red roses, or of any roses.
It has been suggested that those provisions are not enough, that multinationals will take over and gain a strangle-hold on our farmers. At this time, seed development and marketing in Canada is largely in public or small private hands. Large multinationals do not at this time play a significant role in the industry. The ongoing global process of mergers and diversification in all

Plant Breeders' Rights
sectors may have an impact upon the industry, but this is not anticipated to be a direct result of plant breeders' rights legislation. There have also been suggestions that the chemical companies associated with those multinationals would try to breed varieties which are dependent upon specific pesticides and fertilizers.
Before I was elected to Parliament, I was the chairman of a marketing board in the Province of Ontario marketing white beans. In 1977 there were extreme weather difficulties in the same manner as we had a drought last year. In 1977, particularly in Ontario, there was a strain of enthracnals that was new and came into our white beans along with the wet weather. Our plant breeders responded very rapidly. We said that we were going to use chemicals to control the disease. However, within three years, our plant breeders worked together and chemicals were used for a very short time until a variety was bred with resistance to that strain of Delta enthracnals.
I know that we have dedicated public breeding programs in this country. I want to acknowledge the fine work that they do, and the effort that is being made to breed varieties with resistance to the many diseases that are there to rust and smut.
How is this Bill going to help?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
This Bill will help do all those things, because it will allow the plant breeder to recoup and put more dollars back into the development of the breeding resources, and resistance is as important as new varieties. Many times, it means taking present varieties and assuring their continued viability by breeding in resistance to the various sectors.
I do not know if the Hon. Member lives on a farm or is familiar with the growing of beans, barley, com, or any of those products. I invite the Member to come to my farm and look at the crops that we grow. I would be very happy to have the Member come to western Ontario some time and look at some great crops in that area.
I would be delighted to do so, and I will make a speech when I am there.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext: I invite the Hon. Member to come when we are baling hay.
Is that where you learned to shovel it?
You fork it, you don't shovel it. We have to teach these guys everything.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
It has been suggested that those provisions are not enough, that multinationals will take over. I do not agree with that. The ongoing global process of mergers and diversification in all sectors may have an impact on the industry, but this is not anticipated to be a direct result of plant breeders' rights legislation. I want to reinforce that point, as much as I can.
The task of plant breeding is so complicated that it is highly unlikely a plant could be bred for a specific chemical. That is not what the interests of our plant breeding programs are, and have not been, and will not be.
In the event that this did occur, the variety would still require registration under the Seeds Act to verify its merits and suitability before it could be sold. There is a process of licensing before that could ever happen. There would also be competition in the market-place from other private breeders and public-sector programs that would be producing varieties without such limitations.
Ultimately, the decisions must rest with fanners. Those decisions should stay with the farmers, because they provide the bread-basket of this great nation of ours. Many of them came as immigrants, and perhaps for some people it may be a long time ago, but when one looks at world history, the fanners are pioneers. Many were our grandfathers or our great-grandfathers. I believe that the farmers have responded to the needs of this country, helped it grow, and will continue to make it grow if we give them the room to do so.
Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Farmers will not buy a product which requires high input unless the benefits are sufficient to support the initial investment. Farmers are good shoppers and good buyers. They have always had choices and they will continue to have choices, because the farmers will demand that that choice be there. I have lived on a farm all of my life, worked with farmers, and I know how they feel.
June 27, 1989

At one time I represented all the white bean farmers in the Province of Ontario, and I do know how they feel about plant breeders' legislation.
White beans are like little white pearls. They are the greatest product one could ever get hold of. They are an exportable product. In 1972, 20 per cent of our white beans were exported. By the year 1980,80 per cent of our beans were exported at no sacrifice to human consumption. This happened because we were leaders and because we had varieties acceptable throughout the world. It is one thing to grow beans, but quite another to have varieties that are acceptable with good cooking qualities and storing qualities.
We must never forget that farmers are intelligent customers. Farmers are businessmen. Farmers have to carefully consider factors such as input yield, and ratios. They look at all those things when they look at what varieties they are going to choose from. They do have many varieties to choose from. Let us never underestimate farmers, because they do make intelligent decisions.
As a result, farm organizations are supporting this Bill in large numbers. Groups such as the Western Canadian Wheat Growers, the Canadian Grains Council, Canadian Nursery Trades Association, United Grain Growers, Canadian Seed Growers Association, Canadian Ornamental Plant Foundation, and one close to my heart, the Ontario Bean Producers Marketing Board, to name only a few are supporting this Bill.
When my hon. friend is helping with the hay, we will give him a good feed of beans.
Beans are good for the heart.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
All those people feel that this Bill will benefit agriculture and benefit Canada. The Hon. Member for Northumberland (Mrs. Stewart) has suggested that this is not enough, that we must benefit the Third World as well. Like all Hon. Members, I too wish that there were easy solutions for the social and economic problems facing the developing world. Even if all Members of the House devoted all their time and energies to the issue, we could not solve all the problems. Why should we expect Bill C-15 to solve all those problems? Plant breeders' rights are designed to address issues in our country and in our dealings with our major trading partners.
Plant Breeders' Rights
It's a kowtow to the U.S.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Privy Council; Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
While we are doing that, it strengthens the viability of our farms and our agriculture industry in this country. Who could argue against strengthening the opportunities for agriculture? In fact, the difference between our northern climate and the tropics prohibits effective seed trade with the Third World. Even if a distribution system were in place, and the equipment was there, places such as Uganda and Malaysia would still not become major markets.
However, our Government is concerned about their food resources, and to ensure that varieties are developed for their countries, we offer them our fiscal and technical support. CIDA contributed $18,250,000 in 1988 to 17 different research institutes specializing in developing agriculture. That is a lot of money. There are also a significant number of bilateral agreements which offer technical advice or specific services between our country and less developed ones. The International Development Research Council has also funded seed projects worth almost $3 million in 1988.
